headline: TIENTSIN QUIET.
text:
POLICE AND UNRULY STUDENTS.

FIRM ACTION TAKEN

The Chinese police have decided to release all the workers arrested recently provided they obtain shop guarantees to return to work and do not have anything to do with further strikes and disturbances.

All the students have not yet been released, the police demanding that those who have gone out of town return to their homes. Those having homes here are being held until they obtain guarantee that they will not again interfere with the workers and will remain in their homes until the schools recommend. Also they must agree to resign from the Students' Union.

The situation is now very quiet.

headline: CHINESE LESSONS.
text:
NUROPEAN WHO SACKED

Although he gave notice to his Chinese teacher after receiving but a few lessons in July, it was pointed out to Mr. S. J. Squire, Hongkong Electric Company, in the Summary Court yesterday that he made himself liable to the month's full payment.

The Chinese teacher sued Mr. Squire for the month's full wages ($15) also for $15 in lieu of notice (producing in this connection a document which stated that he was entitled to this amount).

This, Mr. Squire said that he had not seen until the plaintiff brought it to him in August, and Mr. Justice Wood held that not having seen or signed it he was not liable under it. An order was made for Mr. Squire to pay the $10 full month's wages

headline: FAELEN INDEED. / PLIGHT OF EDMUND STINNES. / FROM RICHES TO RUIN.
text:
"How are the mighty fallen," makes a suitable headline for the plight of the heirs of the late industrial king of Germany, Hugo Stinnes, whose eldest son Edmund to-day is hard pressed to pay £5,000 wages to 2,000 employees in his motor car works owing to the refusal of the banks to grant further credit.

Edmund appealed to the Prussian Government for a loan of 8,000,000 Marks to avoid closing down the works, and is approaching another bank to advance the wages due to-day.

headline: BELGIUM'S DEBT.
text:
AMERICAN COMMISSION'S WORK

Washington, August 14. President and Mrs. Coolidge this morning motored from Swampscott to Plymouth on a visit to the President's father.

Mr. F. Mellon and Senator Smoot of the Debt Funding Commission are also on a week-end at Plymouth. It is understood that they desire to communicate to President Coolidge the latest developments of the debt negotiations with Belgium, and get his advice. The Belgian representatives are also keeping in close touch with their Government and are only proceeding upon instructions from Brussels.

headline: END IN SIGHT?
text:
FOREIGNERS IN CANTON AGAIN.

AMEEN'S GATES.

News reached Hongkong on Saturday that Shameen's gates had been re-opened and that intercourse between the French and British Concessions and Canton city had been resumed.

Shameen is, of course, connected to the mainland by two bridges. The “east” bridge is that leading into the French Concession and the “west” bridge links up the British Concession with Shakee.

It was stated that the decision had been arrived at to allow Chinese who had, at the time of the Yunnanese siege, deposited valuables and other property in Shameen for safe keeping, to withdraw whatever they wished. Another part of the report to hand was that domestic and other Chinese employees, formerly of Shameen, had indirectly signified their intention to return as opportunity occurred.

On inquiry from the best informed source in the Colony, it was learned by the “China Mail” this, morning that Shameen's gates are still closed. Their reopening had not even been discussed, nor would such a step be contemplated until adequate protection was given by the Chinese authorities on the spot. Shameen was still, virtually, in a state of siege. Nothing had been done to change conditions.

However, Canton's "gates," meaning the right of entry into the city, were opened on Saturday. It is surmised that the report referred to mistook Shameen for Canton. Foreigners, with the exception of British, are now allowed in Canton for purposes of ordinary intercourse. The supposition is that a beginning has been made to restore trade.

Trustworthy Chinese business circles express the opinion that the trouble, as far as Canton was concerned, would "blow over" in less than three weeks from to-day. A Chinese merchant with large interests in Canton predicted to a "China Mail" reporter yesterday that most of the Chinese-owned river steamers, if no others, would be running between Canton and Hongkong again, by the 15th of the 7th moon if not earlier, the equivalent of "that date" being September 2. He had reason to think that the huge army of unemployed in Canton were getting restless, that the "professional labour bosses" were becoming alarmed as to the outcome, and that negotiations had been made by those indirectly interested but not directly concerned, for river shipping to move again, with the object of facilitating a gradual return to normalcy.

Macao Steamer Back.

This afternoon, the s.s. Chuen Chow (Captain Jones) put in at Hongkong again after having tied up at Macao for the second or third time since the strike began. For a reason which has not been given, the crew have not made the voyage, lying up and then making a fresh start again.

Poultry and Livestock. Housewives were pleasantly surprised yesterday morning when hawke s offered fowls in the street at 65 cents per catty, which is about equal to 50 cents per pound, for live chickens, and capons at a slightly lower figure. Later in the day the price went down to 58 cents per catty which is about the figure in ordinary times. This sudden drop is attributed to a very large shipment having arrived. The source has not been divulged, but the Chinese are particularly grateful for this bit of enterprise. Arrivals of cattle, pigs and other livestock have also been reported, but the market prices for meat are still prohibitive.

The engagement is announced between Vivian Geoffrey, second son of the late Mr. F. Smyth, of Hongkong, and Mrs. Smyth, of The Red House, Oxshott, Surrey, and Joyce, only child of Captain F. Cresghan Osborne, C.B., R.N., and the late Mrs. A. R. Cresghan Osborne, of Dillon Park, Langley, Bucks

headline: TROUBLE AT SHEKKI.
text:
News has reached Canton that disorder has broken out at three important villages near Shekki,

Whampoa Cadets who were sent there, so it is stated, as the nucleus of the “nationalisation of property” (Soviet) experiment have fallen foul of the local “Man Tuen,” which are really civil guards.

The Cadets were fired at first, when they lost over thirty men in casualties through trying to overrun some padi-fields.—They took instant revenge on the civil guards and the situation is now tense.

headline: NO BOYCOTT. / HOIHOW SHIPPING UNFETTERED.
text:
RESIDENT'S REPORT.

The reports as to a trade boycott of British and Japanese goods being prosecuted with vigour at Hoihow would appear to be without foundation for a resident of Hoihow who arrived in Hongkong by the Talkwa Maru (leaving Hoihow on Friday morning), reports that a full cargo was brought to Hongkong, this consisting of 230 head of cows, over 200 hogs and large numbers of chickens.

This resident reports that there is absolutely no attempt on the part of the students to prevent shipment of freight either to Hongkong or Hoihow and states that when the boat left shipments were arriving regularly from Haiphong, Hongkong and Bangkok.

There had been a boy in the town of Hali-man Island, according to our informant, is determined that none shall occur. He has arrested and executed four or five students who were known to be Reds from Canton and were attempting to stir up trouble. There is absolutely no anti-foreign-feeling at Holhow, according to this same source, and the women and children who left for Holhow were all now returned. The women and children of question set a banana cell on their own in Canton and no one could have brought them to the home.

headline: TRAMWAY COMPANY. / SOCIAL GATHERING AT THE DEPOT.
text:
VOLUNTEERS THANKED.

A volunteer worker of the Tramway Company during the strike writes as follows:—

Eleven o'clock yesterday morning saw the disbandment of the volunteer car drivers and conductors when a group photograph was taken, including the tramway officials.

In a short speech, just after the photograph was taken, Mr. L. C. F. Bellamy, the General Manager, on behalf of the Tramway Company, said that they were very sorry to lose such a fine body of men whose loyal co-operation helped them to see the strike through thick and thin, besides contributing in no small measure towards organising and training new men to undertake permanent work. It was, he said, with mixed feelings that he parted with the volunteers, and he thought—although he hoped nothing untoward will happen to have recourse to their services again—it would be much more appropriate to say "Au revoir" than "Goodbye." He also paid a tribute to the very efficient manner in which the volunteers carried out their duties. Mr. Bellamy's speech was received with much applause and hand clapping, after which the gathering dispersed.

I understand that the Tramway Company intends to present the volunteers with autographed copies of the group photo, and I think I voice the sentiments of all the volunteers when I say that we shall cherish the same as a memento of an unusual and extraordinary incident in our lives. In closing, I beg, on behalf of my co-workers, to tender the tramway officials our very hearty thanks for the gentlemanly and gallant treatment, accorded to us during our term of service.

headline: LIBEL ACTION.
text:
CHINESE PAPER TO PAY

UNRESERVED WITHDRAWAL.

Allegations against the morals and honesty of the Chinese manager of the Kwangtung Industrial Bank are contained in an article appearing in a local Chinese newspaper on June 10, in respect of which legal proceedings were instituted this morning.

No defence was offered, but the printer—and publisher of the newspaper had already submitted a withdrawal and apology and agreed to pay $5,000 and costs, and this morning's proceedings were for an order to be made along those lines by the Chief Justice.

Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by Mr. G. K. Hall Brutton) was for the plaintiff (Ching Pikkam), and Mr. Y. K. Mok (instructed by Messrs. Lo and Lo) for the defendants (Lai Ki-nam). The newspaper in question was the “Tai Kwong Po,” and following is the article in question, which appeared in the issue of June 10:—

“Since Tang Pun-yan has had the intention of carrying into effect the ‘great eight districts’ policy he is making a display of the influence of the eight districts very actively. Recently he has organised the ‘King Ngai’ Bank as well. Banking is, in fact, a business for the benefit of the people, but to the eyes of the militarists it only serves as a means to suck the marrow of the people. Moreover, the chief manager of the Bank appointed by Tang is a fickle young man, Ching Pikkam. Ching had been a private secretary to Li Lit-kwan (Li Lieh-chun) and is a favourite of Yeung Yan-ping. In the second year of the Chinese Republic, 1913, through the recommendation of Yeung, he was employed as a proof reader in the “Kwok Man Yat Po” at Singapore. As Ching was addicted to the cup and woman he stole over $1,000 from the funds of the said newspaper and absconded to Hongkong with a female. For this reason the said newspaper nearly stopped publication. Now Tang has appointed this man as chief manager to the Bank and it may be inferred that they will help each other in the commission of evils by defrauding the people and causing a mess to the money market of the eight districts. At present on hearing the news the overseas Chinese residents who are natives of the eight districts are proposing to lodge a protest by sending telegrams to Tang.”

In submitting defendant's apology and the conditions contained in it which met with the plaintiff's requirements, Mr. Zejtlyn said that the stipulation with regard to publication in two English Hongkong papers was made because the Bank in respect of which the plaintiff was manager made its appeal to both European and Chinese clients. Following is the apology, signed by defendant and addressed to

"You have commenced an action against me, as printer and publisher of the "Tai Kwong" Newspaper, claiming damages for libel contained in an article published by the said "Tai Kwong" Newspaper on June 10, 1925, which article is set out in your statement of claim in the above action." I now confess that the statements relating to yourself contained in the said article are absolutely untrue and without the slightest substance in fact. I hereby unreservedly withdraw every word in that article which in any way reflects on your character. I admit that there never was any foundation for any of the charges contained in the article. I deeply regret that they were ever made, and I tender you my sincere apologies therefor. I agree to pay the sum of $5,000 as damages and in addition your costs as between solicitor and client, and consent to judgment being entered therefor and to this apology being read out in open court and embodied in the judgment. I also undertake to publish this apology in the "Tai Kwong" Newspaper on three consecutives.

headline: HIS MASTER'S CAR.
text:
WAS HE JOY RIDING OR TESTING IT?

JNDIAN CHAUFFEUR'S CASE.

Taking his master's cur out with his own friends in it and without permission was the reason given in the Summary Court this morning for the dismissal of an Indian chauffeur who claimed his wages for July up to the 23rd., the day on which he was dismissed, and a month's wages in lieu of notice ($106 in all).

The car was a 1925 model Buick seven seater, supplied to the plaintiff's master (Mr. Shewaran) by Mr. A. H. Rowe, managing director of the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxicub Company. It was the latter who had seen the chauffeur out with the car, and had informed the owner accordingly. The plaintiff said that he had had to make minor adjustments in the mechanism of the car and had gone out on the occasion in question to test whether they held good or not. The man whom Mr. Rowe had told the Court he had seen sitting on the door of the car was there because he did not wish to dirty the car with his clothes.

Mr. Rowe, in evidence, said that the car being a new one with a six month's guarantee, he had told the chauffeur, whom he had personally introduced to the owner, that he was to come to him (witness): if anything was wrong and not to attempt to make repairs on his own account. This was done in accordance with the wishes of the owner.

Mr. Howe further said that the car was being driven very fast when he saw it in Stubbs Road on the day in question. It had to pull up near the Bowen Road turn and the back wheels skidded for some distance.

Mr. H. S. Fitzroy, for the chauffeur, suggested that the man on the footboard or sitting on the door might have been listening for some slight defect in the engine, but witness said that no one who knew anything about motoring would suggest such a thing. The wind would be whistling past the ears of a person in that position. On being informed that the chauffeur had said that he paid witness commission for introducing him to the buyer of the car Mr. Rowe stated that this was an absolute fabrication. The case is proceeding.

headline: NO FIGHTING.
text:
OPINION ON CANTON OFFENSIVE.

THE WAICHOW SITUATION.

A Mr. Lau, who formerly held a high command under General Chan Kwing-ming, has informed the “China Mail” that little concern has been felt by the general’s subordinates in the hinterland of Swatow, over the punitive expedition despatched by Canton against Waichow.

According to Mr. Wong, some of the senior generals now holding territory under General Chan's banner are now in Hongkong to attend the funeral of the father of General Ip Kue (Chan's right-hand man and Chief Director of Military Operations), the old man having died at his house in Kowloon City (near the Sung Emperor's Pavilion). Other generals have just returned to their commands after interviewing Chan in Shanghai. It is unlikely, therefore, that Chan's men will march to Waichow to aid its holder Yeung Kwan-yu in his opposition to Canton. It is known that Kuomintang troops have arrived at Sheklung but the feeling is that Canton will have its hands full with recalcitrant (anti-Bolshevik) leaders nearer the capital.

headline: IN OTHER PLACES.
text: From inquiries made in another direction it appears that the trouble near Shekki—reported in yesterday's issue — has been quelled, the local civil guards not being able to resist the detachment of Whampoa Cadets. Considerable attention has also been diverted to General Tang Pun-yan, who holds Hainan (the "eight districts") as people are looking to him to unite General Leung Hung-kai (Kuomintang, reputedly anti-Bolshevik) who holds the territory between Tang and the districts near Canton.

headline: SIR EDWARD STUBBS.
text:
SHANGHAI'S NEWSPAPER'S COMMENT.

Sir Edward Stubbs, when he relinquishes his Governorship of Hongkong to take up a similar appointment in Jamaica, will no doubt find ample scope to employ those great qualities of governorship and administrative ability which have characterised his work in the neighbouring Crown Colony, remarks the "North China Daily News." Sir Edward will follow a line of distinguished governors, among them in recent years being Sir Alexander Swettenham (whose action on the occasion of the great earthquake of 1907 caused so much comment): Sir Sidney (now Lord) Olivier, who was Secretary for India in the Labour Government, who was at one time a famous Fabian and is a brilliant scholar; Sir William Manning; and Sir Leslie Probyn. The record of Sir Edward Stubbs at Ceylon and at Hongkong has shown clearly that he is more than a worthy successor to whoever may have gone before him at Jamaica, and there is not the slightest doubt that the Colony is getting a Governor in whom it may place the utmost confidence.

headline: ANOTHER STRIKE.
text:
SHANGHAI POST OFFICE TROUBLE.

CHINESE DETECTIVE MAULD.

Nearly a thousand postal employees, comprising clerks, sorters, postmen, and coolies, struck this morning demanding a substantial

Employees Union, shorter hours payment for overtime, gratuity of a year's pay for every 10 years; immunity of strike leaders, right to demand abolition and rejection of unequal treatment and a guarantee that foreigners would not be employed after 1925

The strikers this morning attacked a Chinese detective and battered him with stools and chairs.

Tie detective finally used his revolver and wounded a coolie in the leg.

The police rushed to the scene and restored order.

A detachment of marines from His Majesty's Concord is now guarding the Post Office.

The strikers have issued a pro- elaboration complaining of being badly paid and compelled to work I'k• cattle, while foreigners occupy superior positions and draw en- emours salaries.

A meeting of strikers decided to withdraw the demand that only China should be employed in the Post Office after 1926.

headline: BOGUS CONSTABLE.
text:
UNPROVOKED ASSAULT ON

An unemployed Chinese was charged before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning with impersonating a Police officer and assaulting a coolie employed at the Yaumati Police Station.

The case against the accused was that he put the complainant through a search at Reclamation Street, and, the result not being satisfactory, he assaulted the complainant.

After hearing evidence, His Worship sentenced the accused to one-month's hard labour.

headline: NOT DETAINED.
text:
S. S. FOO CH.E O N G "STRANDED" AT PAKKAI.

Definite news is now available regarding the 8.8, 100 Chsong which was, some days ago, suspected of having been detained by Chinese at Pukkai, the part of Kongmoon.

The steamer was on the Macao. Kongmoon ran and did not return after leaving Macao one evening. It has been stated that the Macao authorities had taken steps as the vessel was under the Portuguese flag, her port of registry being Macao.

It has now transpired that some bare-faced intimidation at Pakkai caused the crew to desert. Hence the ship is now tied up there awaiting a new crew to bring her back. The officials at Pakkai are reported to have denied interference.

There is still no direct communication between Macao and Canton, the last batch of delegates from the Strike Executive at Canton being very definite about the matter. However, the tow-boat is now running again between Macao and Shekki, where passages can be obtained, under 'passports' from the strike office there, for Canton. Passenger fares on the tow-boat are high owing, it is stated, to'squeeze' having to be paid for the privilege of keeping up the service.

Two modern Portuguese warships are reported to have reached Macao.

headline: STINNES' EFFORTS.
text:
SUPPLY OF CHEAP CARS FOR GERMANY?

AMERICANS IN THE MARKET.

While Edmund Stinnes is continuing his efforts to get financial assistance from the Prussian Government to prevent the closing down of his motor works, it is reported that a representative of a big American automobile concern is contracting with Stinnes with a view to the purchase of the entire works and their extension for the purpose of the mass production of cheap cars which are badly needed in Germany. Meanwhile the workers are still deliberating over Edmund's offer though they have not yet received last week's wages fully.

Official notification of the unknown whereabouts of the Yue Ying Wu is contained in a Harbour office notification calling on all ships to look for possible signs of the missing ship. So far none has been reported.

In accordance with the quarantine regulations of the Merchant Shipping Ordinance it is proclaimed by order of His Excellency the Governor in Council that Shanghai is a place at which an infectious or contagious disease prevails.

headline: AN ACT OF WAR? / REPORTED CANTON SHIPPING RULES.
text:
TREATIES VIOLATED?

British

Boycott

Shipping regulations which may amount to a declaration of war are reported to have been imposed by Canton, but whether they have official backing remains to be seen.

Japanese?

headline: HITTING HONGKONG.
text:
The Chinese authorities have drawn "up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.

All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union. The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.

It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.

headline: LOCAL COMMENT.
text:
Opinions in Hongkong vary as to the outcome of the telegram. A gentleman who controls a fairly large number of ships vitally interested in trade with Canton pointed out to a “China” Mail” reporter that such a state of affairs had existed practically from the beginning of the “strike.”

"With the exception of ships under the Chinese flag," he said, "all vessels calling at Canton have been interfered with, even Chinese-owned shipping under foreign registry. Latterly Chinese steamers have discharged and loaded at Canton, but," so he believed, "only under payment of'squeeze' to strike officials who work hand in hand with administrative politicians. More recently some foreign tonnage had reached Canton, such as tramp and chartered ships with cargoes of rice from Bangkok, etc. Even food boats had to be'squared' before they could be cleared."

Continuing, the speaker said he took the message to mean that the so-called Canton Government had now actually come out in the open to sponsor the activities of the Strike Executive which was probably the “Anti-Imperialist Union” referred to in the cable. Certain shipping would continue to call at Canton, without coming to Hongkong but trade would suffer to an untold extent if British and Japanese hulls were prohibited.

Another gentleman, connected

headline: CANTON MOVES.
text:
TREACHERY TO CRUSH ENEMY.

HONAM BOUGHT OVER?

The “China Mail” learns from a reliable source that the Kuomintang Government is attempting to buy over General Li Fook-lam's troops before crushing him, so as to extend their power and remove opposition.

General Li has several thousand Cantonese troops who have been in Honam (the island opposite Canton) for some time. He is accused of refusing to obey the Bolshevik order to prohibit gambling and opium—from which are derived substantial revenues.

Recently General Li has moved his troops into surrounding villages for fear of being disarmed by the Reds and news has reached Hongkong that the Red leaders are aiming at "buying over" some of his detachments before challenging him to battle. At any rate, without support, Li would have been an easy prey for the Reds. No news is to hand regarding General Young Hung-kai, another Confidence officer who has since told in the Reds "This is my own 출탈패앗길" (the hinterland of

with river shipping, noted the fact that Hongkong would still be in communication with Canton if the order ever took effect, because there was nothing to prevent steamers running between Canton and Macao, and between Macao and Hongkong. This speaker expressed some very pronounced views. He said that the Kuomintang were imposing their will on the merchants regardless of whether foreign trade was crippled or not. In his opinion if the drafting of the rules could be legally brought to the door of the Kuomintang Government in Canton—and such could be done by obtaining the officially approved notices in all parts of the city—declaration of war was the only alternative. He was positive that by fouting trade treaties Canton rendered herself liable to war.

headline: DYNAMITE IN CAR.
text:
CHINESE MOTHER AND SON. CONVICTED.

PRINCIPAL HEAVILY FINED.

An old Chinese woman and her son were charged at the Central Magistracy this morning for an offence under the Dangerous Goods Ordinance.

The accused were travelling in a motor vehicle to Aberdeen and were found to be carrying 400 sticks of dynamite (the contents of a full case of δ0 lb.) and 400 detonators.

The old woman, who was in the employment of the Tung.Wo Company, contractors, as stone-breaker, pleaded that she was engaged by her master to carry: the explosives to Aberdeen, where a man was to take delivery.

The Magistrate (Mr. McElderry) imposed a fine of $100 on each of the accensed, or two months' hard labour in default.

PRINCIPAL CHARGED. Following the conviction, the muster of the Tung Wo firm of contractors, was charged on two counts of causing the two accused in the previous case to carry the explosives and with having a quantity of gunpowder in his matshed at Shubs Road without a permit. Mr. L. D. Turner appeared for the defence.

Evidence, which was given at length, went to show that the exposures were removed without the knowledge of accused, who held a permit to carry dynamite for blasting purposes.

Mr. Turner submitted that there was no evidence to warrant conviction on the first charge. A plea of guilty was entered on the other charge of possession of gunpowder, which amounted to less than half a pound in weight. His Worship convicted on both counts, a fine of $100 being imposed for possession of gunpowder and $600 on the more serious charge.

headline: NO NOTICE.
text:
PRINTERS' COOLIE WHO LEFT.

ALLEGED. CRIMPING.

.

A Chinese youth was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning by Mr. Labrum, of Ye Olde Printerie for leaving without notice.

The complainant stated that the accused was employed as a printer's coddle on a wage of $12 a month, and left without giving any notice. A few days later the accused was found to be in the employment of Messrs. Der A. Wing. Complainant added that he was losing his men owing to other printing establishments offering more than the usual standard of wages.

The accused claimed to be only an apprentice and ignorant of the law regarding one month's notice. He said he was obliged to leave owing to insufficient wages, and added that he was now receiving $24 a month.

A fine of $25 was imposed, of which $12 was to go to the complainant.

headline: DRIVERS CONVICTED.
text:
A narrow escape was that of Mr. J. H. Simmons, Inspector of the Hongkong Tramway Company, according to the evidence given yesterday at the Central Magistracy against a taxi driver who was charged with negligent driving. As a result of the taxi running into his ricsha Mr. Simmons was thrown and the ricsha completely turned over. Ricsha puller and occupant both sustained minor injuries. In decision on the part of the taxi driver as to what direction to take was said to be the cause of the accident which occurred near the Tramway Shelter at Causeway Bay. Defendant was fined $10 and ordered to pay the ricsha coolie $10 compensation. Peckless driving also formed one of the items in the list of breaches of Traffic Regulations brought against Chinese motor driver who was yesterday charged at the Kowloon Magistracy. The evidence showed that he drove round a band at Kwai

Telegram upon telegram of the gravest possible nature has poured home from all sources, Government, public and private, stating the plain unvarnished truth: — manifestly they are either misunderstood or not believed—or else what is still more incredible nothing can be done.

The Theatre Royal has been booked for 5.15 next Tuesday, the 25th, and arrangements are in progress for a meeting at which the Colony will no doubt express its views in a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner.

I trust the promoters may count on the united support of the "entire Press" here and all who are convinced of the vital necessity for prompt action in making the meeting as widely known and as successful as the extreme gravity of the situation demands. It cannot be too clearly stated again that it is apparently still not realised at home that this is no question of a "Strike" but of an organised and inspired attack upon British trade and interests in all our Treaty Ports and Concessions and upon this Colony in particular.

Yours, etc., P. H. HOLYOAK. Hongkong, August 19, 1925.

headline: SHANGHAI CONDITIONS.
text:
DEFALCATION OF STRIKE

POSTAL OFFICIALS WAGES.

A secret meeting of a number of unions affiliated to the general union of labour, education and commerce, have passed a resolution seceding from the latter. The action is due to the alleged defalcation of strike funds on the part of general union officials.

The situation on the waterfront is improving gradually: Wharf coolies mostly have resumed.

The Ministry of Communications at Peking has authorised the local post office officials to offer strikers an increase of wages, but the strikers have rejected it. Junior clerks starting at $20 a month were offered $35, but demand $52.50. The officials have requested the public not to use pillar boxes and to call at the post office for their mails.

headline: KILLED.
text:
CANTON RED LEADER'S FATE.

REPORTED ASSASSINATION

According to a rumour which has yet to be confirmed, Mr. Liu Chung-oi (also spelt "Liao Chung-kai") the present "Canton Finance Minister, was assassinated in Canton this morning.

Liu has been head of the Labour Unions in Clinton and was one of the first of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen's party to encourage intercourse with Russia. He is very much opposed to foreigners and to the Chinese merchants as a class. Long before even the Shameen strike of last year he had been secretly working for Communistic ideals.

When the reorganisation in the Canton Government was put in effect about two months ago, he was appointed Finance Minister and is now one of the chief executives of the Kuomintang. The rumour current is that Liu

The rumour current is that Liu was fired at by an assassin and that he died almost instantly.

MACAO VESSEL TAKEN TO CANION

The Portuguese Naval ship Coloure arrived here from Málano on August 9, and tried to tow away the s.s. Foo Cheong, a vessel flying the Portuguese flag which has been tied up here since her crew deserted through intimidation.

The Colours did not succeed through, it is stated, the Labourers Corps preventing any help being given and the warship returned alone to Macao.

On August 14, the Foo Cheong was commandedered by strikers. Manned by her original crew who, according to one report, were made to work, the steamer was taken out of the port, it is believed, for Canton.

MERCHANDISE SEIZED. To-day a junk fully had so with groundnut oil, salt fish and other cargo, arriving from Macao, was seized by the Labourers Corps at Pakkai.

headline: The New Rules.
text:
The Chinese authorities have drawn up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.

All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union.

The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.

It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.

headline: RUSSIAN ARRESTED IN HONGKONG
text:
“UNDESIRABLE” PROSECUTED.

That he was found in the Colony without a valid passport wins the charge-framed against Joseph L. Teplitchi, an Ukrainian, before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning.

The accused was arrested by the Police on information received that he was a violent "Red" and had been seen taking an active part in directing the labour pickets during the strike at Sha-meen last year. His presence in Hongkong was therefore deemed undesirable, apart from the fact that he had no proper passport.

Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. (Captain Superintendent of Police) said that the accused was in Macao when the strike commenced. From there he answered an advertisement in a local paper calling for volunteers, secured a billet as fireman on the Empress of Asia, and was discharged after a trip to Vancouver and back.

The accused had in his possession a document which was stated to be a “certificate” in Rumanian, on which appeared the chop of the French Consul in Canton. His Worship said that he had an idea that the passport regulations were relaxed, and he was under the impression that a document with a vise by a French Consul was sufficient for landing in the Colony. After making enquiries, Mr. Wodehouse pointed out that there was an arrangement between the British and Japanese Governments and the British and French Governments under which a passport issued in favour of one of its nationals andvised by its own Consul was sufficient to entitle the holder to enter a country belonging to the other Government.

On being asked what he had to say to being found in the Colony without a proper passport or document authorised by the C.S.P., the accused stated that his passport was stolen while serving on the Empress of Asia. He made a report of the loss to the second engineer of the vessel, but not to the Police.

Addressing the accused, His Worship said that he was guilty of the charge, but before passing judgment he would remand him for two days in Police custody to enable him to produce any friends he may have to testify to his character. The accused said that he had many friends and could call them.

headline: BORDER FIRING.
text:
NIFERS USE PASSENGERS AS SCREENS.

THIS MORNING'S OUTRAGE.

Reports of two more shooting outrages at different points on the border were issued by Police Headquarters this morning.

A gang of Government coolies working on the road between Sheungshui and Ta Ku Ling were scared away from the scene by a shot fired at them from Chinese territory yesterday afternoon. This being apparently the object desired, a man crossed over into British territory and removed a bicycle belonging to the foreman of the coolie gang.

The other incident took place at 9 o'clock this morning at Lokma-chau. Below the Police Station here is a ferry, and. Sergeant Swan heard two shots being fired from that part of the river. Getting out of the station to investigate, he saw a man jump overboard from the ferry and swim to the other side.

The Sergeant sent a strong party of Police to the river, and on their way down they had several shots fired at them. They saw the pickets taking the passengers off from the ferry, and also observed two men in uniform, who did the firing. One of the men placed himself in the middle of a group of passengers, and, using the latter as a screen, fired at the British Police. The other man took cover behind a bank and sniped occasionally. After firing nearly a dozen shots, all of which, fortunately, missed their mark, the man behind the bank rejoined his comrade and all the people disappeared.

The Police did not return the fire for fear of hitting the passengers who were being used as a screen.

The shots heard by the European Sergeant in the first instance are believed to have been fired by the labour pickets to stop the attempts of some fruit sellers to cross the border.

headline: UP-COUNTRY NEWS.
text:
ENCOUNTER WITH PIRATES.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, August 17. The Hongkong steamers are still lying idle, without crews, at their respective berths.

One company (about a hundred strong) of Labourers' Corps-wearing blue shirts and khaki shorts—have arrived here. Their very first act was most unexpected; they drove away the strike pickets which had been keeping the domestic employees of Europeans out of employment. These new troops have orders to prevent strikers getting away, the export of foodstuffs, and the import of foreign goods. They are stationed at Kongmoon, Pakkai and Sanwui city.

Considerable damage has been done by gales to the sugar cane and orange crops. At this time in other years the river is flooded but now it is as dry as in winter. The price of rice has gone up again.

The Kongmoon-Fatshan towboat has had another encounter with pirates when off the Kamchuk lighthouse. The towboat escaped.

Fatshan and Kongmoon have been placed under municipal administration with mayors independent of the district magistrates.

The Chinese gunboats Kwong Ching and Kong Hon have arrived to drive away pirates who have assembled at Hoi Chau with the supposed intention of attacking Ngoi Hoi.

Foreigners resident here at present comprise six on the staff of the Customs, Dr. McBain of the Marion Barclay Hospital and the local manager of the A.P.C. One of H.M.s armed launches is always on duty here.

headline: China / HOW HE DIED.
source: (Photo by courtesy of the "Tsun Wan Yat Po.")
text:
ANTON RED MINISTER'S MURDER.

LATEST DETAILS.

The assassination of Liu Chung-oi, the notorious Canton Bolshevik —exclusively reported in yesterday's “China Mail”—has now been established beyond doubt.

.Nearly all the local vernacular papers came out with. "specials" yesterday afternoon but details were not available till this morning.

Some time before noon yesterday Liu left his private residence in Tungshan (the suburb to the East of Canton, in which are many foreign residents) to attend a meeting of the Kwangtung (Kuomintang) Government Commission which is established at the Waichow Association building, also in the east of Canton.

When about to enter the gate Liu was fired at by an unknown Chinese wearing the customary short jacket and trousers of black pongee silk, the fabric so much used by the lower and working class Chinese. The assassin drew a revolver and opened fire from almost point-blank range. One round entered the upper part of Liu's body and he expired almost immediately. In the subsequent confusion the assassin is believed to have escaped in the crowd nearby.

ONE OR TWO SHOTS? The "Tai Kwong Po" states that the fatal shot entered Liu's abdomen and that suspicions exist that the culprit was connected with a labour union opposed to the Communistic party.

The "Wah Tsz Yat Po" learns that one of Liu's relatives received a cable yesterday stating that the bullet entered Liu's chest and that he died shortly afterwards.

Another report, says the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," is that Liu had already been suffering from lung disease and was about to enter hospital for treatment in a few days when the murderer ended his life. Liu's relatives in Hongkong are leaving for Canton to-morrow. Yet another version reported in the same vernacular paper is that two shots were fired, one entering Liu's right side and that the assassin escaped before the police arrived.

Other rumours current were that Liu was shot by colleagues while actually attending a meeting of the Government Commission, that the murderer was one of Liu's personal bodyguards and that the assailant had been captured.

Several Chinese papers published in Hongkong say that a telegram has been received by the father of Liu's wife, definitely confirming the report but giving no detail.

A Reuter telegram from Canton reads:—Liu Chung-oi, one of the leading Bolshevik members of the Canton Government, was assassinated last night.

NOTABLE CAREER. As stated in yesterday's "China Mail," Liu is one of three executive members of the Kuomintang Government Commission which succeeded the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen as chief of the Bolsheviks party in Canton and which comprises about twenty members.

About forty-six years of age—although he appears to be not more than forty—Liu is a native of Waichow, the home of General Chan Kwing-ming, the Cantonese leader who so strenuously opposed Canton. Liu was born in America and returned to China when about ten years of age. He studied at Queen's College, says the "Toun Wan Yat Po" and subsequently entered a Japanese University.

After graduating in law and economics he entered the Government service under the Manchu regime. Since the Revolution of 1911 he has steadfastly followed Dr. Sun. He has been Finance Minister and Chief of the Finance Bureau at Canton and Civil Governor on one or two occasions. Several years ago there was a notorious Tse Ying-pat who missed so-called Labour backing. Life mined in the movement and Tse recaded into the background. Later he has been

advocates of dividing up private property in the province:

There is little doubt that a greater part of the recent trouble can be attributed to Liu Chung-oi (spelt Liao Chung-kai according to Mandarin pronunciation). Not over scrupulous, Liu has made many enemies since his recent rise to power. Those very bitter against him include some of Cantou's leading merchants, some bona fide workers who have not bent to his sweet will and rivals in the political camp.

headline: SHAMEEN AFFAIR. / CANTON AND PEKING DISAGREE.
text:
SUN FO RETURNS?

According to news reaching Chinese circles in this Colony, progress in the “Shameen incident” negotiations will be difficult owing to differences between Peking and Canton.

The "Wah Kiu lat Po" publishes a cable to the effect that Mr. Sun Fo, son of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen and recently Mayor of Canton, was to have left Peking yesterday.

It will be recalled that Mr. Sun Fo, accompanied by Mr. Fu Ping-sheung (Canton Commissioner for Foreign Affairs) went to Peking to discuss the Shameen incident.

The “Tsun Wan Yat Po” says that Peking has asked Canton for full details but Canton has failed to comply. Therefore, it is felt that as Peking has decided to negotiate itself, little will be accomplished.

headline: STRAWS IN THE WIND.
text:
That nine provinces of China are to unite in an armed movement against the Canton Bolsheviks is the purport of a report in this morning's vernacular papers.

General Hung Shui-lun of Chan Kwing-ming's army is stated to have come to Hongkong to embark for Shanghai where he will join his chief in a council embracing some of the most important leaders in the country.

Because of a feeling that the Bolshevik movement may spread from Canton, Wu Pei-fu (the former strong man of China) and several provincial rulers are, says the report, uniting to bring Canton under Ghana's central government.

headline: RIFFS ACTIVE. / DELAY FATAL
text:
The Canton-Hongkong problem is entirely separate and distinct from that in any other part of China owing to the fact that Canton does not recognise and is in rebellion against the Central Government at Peking and that no conference held at Peking on tariff or extra-territoriality or any other questions can possibly assist this Colony in the remotest degree, in its present most serious and urgent need; and any delay in dealing direct with Canton and on the South China situation can only result in daily losses to this Colony, of increasing and ruinous magnitude; moreover the British Government, if it delays decisive action now will most certainly have a far larger problem to face at Canton in the future than that confronting it at present. By prompt action now, the Naval and Military Forces, in this Colony could easily place alternative and friendly Chinese authorities in power at Canton.

headline: ULTIMATUM DEMAND
text:

AMENDED RESOLUTION.

TO-MOROW'S THEATRE ROYAL MASS MEETING.

The proposed draft of the telegram to the Prime Minister, to be unmitted at, to-morrow's public meeting, has been amended and as a result of deliberation over the week-end it has been decided to couch the demands to the Home Government in respect of their policy regarding the Canton authorities in very much stronger terms.

The original demands were that "immediate and decisive action" be taken with a view to maintaining treaty rights there but the amended ones call upon the British Government to deliver an ultimatum at once to the Canton authorities.

headline: FIGHTING SOON?
text:
CANTON SPLIT BECOMING INTENSE.

LOCAL INTEREST

Those who were in the Colony during the last seamen's strike may re-call Chan Ping-sang, who achieved notoriety as one of the men's leaders and who was alleged to have murdered his wife, for infidelity, at Canton, but was pardoned by the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen.

Chan, it is stated by a reliable source, is now at Namtau, a town just beyond Deep Bay and not far from the New Territory frontier. From this port Hongkong receives fish and other foods, and a ferry runs regularly to and fro. Recently there has been violent intimidation at Namtau and anti-British propaganda; and Chan is said to be the local head of the military-cum-labour self-established pickets.

headline: WHERE IS HSU?
text:
That General Hsu Shung-chi, who is considered the only man in the Kuomintang capable of offering armed resistance to the Reds, is moving away from Canton for fear of being enveloped, is the belief of those who are well-posted.

General Hsu is supposed to be leading a punitive expedition against one or two of Chan Kwingming's satellites on the upper reaches of the East River. Such was the gist of one of my former reports. I am now told that Hsu is really taking his army away from the capital as he believes that a Bolshevik v. Moderate crisis is imminent.

General Li Fook-lam, Governor of Honam, is gradually bending to the orders of General Cheung Kai-shek, commander of the Whampoa Cadets. He has abolished the opium monopoly in his territory, but he is still defying the Reds in that, so it is reported, he has declared he will continue the gambling monopoly until Canton pays him arrays of pay. The Red chieftain, Chaming, is mentioned as having retorted by thirstening to land his Gadgets in Honam if Li is adamant. Li, on the other hand, has driven out all strikers from his domain. The trouble at Shekki, the capital of Heungshan (Dr. Sun's birthplace and the proposed model), Communistic district), has not been settled. A body of Cadats are trying to ret in but the old garrison and local civil guards are strenuously opposing them. SQUARBLE OVER SQUEEZE

text:
VOLUNTARY SURRENDER.

The periodical raids on idlers' dens carried out by the Police on different areas almost every time have brought back to work a large number of those who would otherwise be numbered amongst the strikers.

That the effect of such action had, the desired result may be gauged from the fact that the idle hands in an area which was very much in the Police eye, and over which a raid was impending, voluntarily came out expressing a desire to work, according to a report furnished this morning. The returning workers included a large number of house servants and amahs.

BUT "NO BIAS" FINDS CHIEF JUSTICE.

The most serious and if it had substantiated, fatal, allegation respecting the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird's arbitration was that he had heard the parties separately, said Sir Henry Cowper Gollan, Chief Justice, in giving judgment this morning in the case in which application was made for a motion to set aside Mr. Bird's arbitration on the grounds of misconduct and by reason of interest that he was not competent to act as arbitrator.

His Lordship found against this application but said that the contention of the applicants with regard to the alleged separate hearing had been strengthened by a letter written to their solicitors by Mr. Bird himself. In view of Mr. Bird's evidence at the Court and the corroboration of Mr. Ogilvie he (His Lordship) was satisfied that the parties had in fact not been heard separately. At the same time His Lordship remarked that he thought this letter had a great deal to do with the initiation of the Court proceedings and after he had found against applicants he would not allow costs. In reply to the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster. (for the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird) His Lordship said that he had fully considered this question of costs and he could come to no other decision. Mr. Bird's letter had been “most unfortunate.”

The applicant in the case was Dong Toy and the defendants, Lam Tuck & Co., who had built houses in Kennedy Road to the order of the applicant. Owing to a landslide the houses were seven months late in being completed and applicant insisted that he was not entitled to pay the contractors extra for damage caused by typhoon: He also complained of bad workmanship and failure to construct a sullay drain mentioned in the specification. As arbitrator Mr. Bird wrote indicating that certain extras should be paid to the contractors and it was the contention in Court of the applicant that that by this letter Mr. Bird had shown that he had thus early made up his mind finally and conclusively against him. It would thus, claimed the applicant, amount to a miscarriage of justice to allow the award to stand.

His Lordship, however, found that there was nothing in the letter to show that Mr. Bird's mind was not open to argument. He also found against the applicant's claim that Mr. Bird had not referred to the whole of the terms of the agreement between the parties. Mr. Bird had told them that he had looked at all the clauses mentioned to him at the hearing with the exception of one with which he was acquainted. The parties had chosen their tribunal deliberately, said His Lordship, and the Court was not called upon to examine with meticulous care the methods adopted by that tribunal in coming to a decision provided there had been nothing radically wrong in his behaviour. There were no groups in His Lordship's opinion for the claim that Mr. Bird had showed bias and refused to admit evidence. It had been alleged, continued His Lordship that Mr. Bird had processed vastly and in such a manner that injustice might be done to one parties. The procedure had been informal and could certainly not be said, commented His Lordship that any line had been wasted but the relative clause of the specification providing for arbitration was in very wide form and gave large distribution to the arbitrator. headline: BLOCKADE MACAO?
text:
CANTON THREATENS NAVAL ISOLATION.

ABOYREMB ASK FOR HELP.

Reading very much like an inspired message is a report in a Canton vernacular paper, the "Kwok Wu Po," in which it is suggested that Macao be blockaded because "there are five steamers playing between that port and the Imperialistic Colony of Hongkong." Briefly, the article says that several butches of strike pickets and delegates have returned to Canton after making investigations in Macao and adjacent Chinese territory. The Executive of the National strike is satisfied that nothing can be done to cut off steamship communication between Macao and Hongkong. But Macao is only acting as a clearing house for its hinterland. Accordingly the Executive must take steps to prevail on the Kuomintang Government, says the "Kwok Wu Po," to send Canton's warships to the waters outside Macao. Those armed vessels could then blockade Macao and cut it off completely, as regards river traffic, with China. It is also suggested that the Canton Navy act in conjunction with the Strike Executive in maintaining the proposed blockade on Macao as the strikers are better able to carry out an embargo on passengers, foodstuffs, and any other merchandise. What will be the terms to be

What will eventuate remains to be seen.

headline: Shekki Cut Off.
text:
The tow-boat which runs to Macao daily from Shekki has been prevented from coming. Accordingly there are fewer passengers from that port who arrive here and re-embark for Hongkong. Most of these are real workers returning to their posts.

Recently the local commander at Shekki has gone out of his way to extend protection to people who want to sail from his port for Macao and to merchants importing cargo from Macao or exporting produce thereto. Unfortunately, he has been overcome by a batch of Whampoa Cadets sent there to obtain a footing for the first model of district government by Communism.

At first the commander forbade the Cadets to land in Shekki. Eventually he wavered and was soon overpowered. With the Cadets getting in, the local strike delegates—who had been in hiding from the former commander—came out into the open and held up the towboat. Previously the strike pickets had been kept away by threats of imprisonment for intimidation.

headline: WHICH IS TRUE?
text:
LOCAL MOTOR DRIVERS RIGHTS.

CONTRADICTORY NOTICES.

In one of today's vernacular papers appear advertisements by the local motor-drivers' union and the Captain Superintendent of Police, respectively, as follow:—

The Motor Drivers' Guild announce that members applying for new licences, must first obtain badges from the Guild; also that in case of accidents in which lives are involved, bail for members need not be by money but by the 'Guild's chop; and that the foregoing innovations are made with Police approval.

The C.S.P. notifies that there is no truth in the Guild's notice I

headline: LOCAL SCHOOLS.
text:
ALL TO RE OPENED AS USUAL.

AWATING A LEAD.

Enquiries made as to the position of local schools in relation to returning students show that without exception they will be re-opened as usual in September, although nothing is known as to the numbers

of those returning. The same applies to the University where, of course, there is a large number already in the Colony at the various Halls.

Some of the students who are due to take examinations, and whose parents are not willing for them to return, are making arrangements to take those examinations as external students.

Much surprise is expressed in local educational circles that the Government has given no lead in the matter of policy to be adopted toward students who are known to have been responsible for much of the trouble which resulted in the Easter term being prematurely ended.

headline: NEW LEADERS.
text:
MANY POLITICAL CHANGES IN CANTON. “The excessive charges made in respect of coal coolie hire is making thousands of dollars difference to us” was how he explained matters. “Whereas before the strike the average daily wage of a coal coolie was 80 or 90 cents, the coal coolie contractors inform us that their labour cannot now be obtained under $8.40 a day. The reason given is that, whereas

there were 7,000 coal coolies in the Colony before the strike, there are now only a few hundred; but this is ridiculous," said our informant. He gave as the reason for misbelieving these figures facts regarding coal coolie boarding houses in the Colony.

It would appear that coal coolie labour, as being one in connection with which there is always in normal times a very strong demand, is very highly organised in Hongkong. Shipping firms have to deal through contractors who in their turn pass on orders for labour to the No. 1 coolies in charge of large numbers of coal coolie boarding houses scattered throughout the Colony. He had made enquiries at these houses and was satisfied that the percentage of coal coolies who had left the Colony was nothing like so great as had been represented said the "China Mail" informant. "It is nothing but a ring to send up charges beyond all reason" was his comment.

Asked if ordinary coolie labour was not now plentiful and whether arrangements could not be made direct for the supply of such labour, our informant said that the work called for great stamina and a certain amount of skill. Orders had to be performed quickly in a stated time and the contractors and "No. 1 coolies" certainly seemed to be able to get work accomplished in half the time that ordinary street coolies were able to. There was not the slightest reason why they should be making such exorbitant charges, however, as the decrease in the number of coal steamers to be attended to was in proportion to the decreased number of coolies. The only shortage there might be was purely artificial in that a coolie who, before to day's exorbitant charges earned $7 a week by working all the week, was content to work for two days only for the same money. The matter was one calling for intervention, was the opinion of the shipping representative in question, who thought very strongly on the matter.

headline: RECOMMENDED BY REDS.
text:
(From Our Own Correspondent.

Recommended by M. Borodin, the Soviet emissary in Canton, Koo Ying-fan is mentioned as the most likely successor to Liu Chung-oi (the murdered Kuomin-tang Minister of Finance). Other names have been put forward for the post of chief of the labour unions.

Hu Han-min (Wu Hon-man) is stated as about to be despatched to Peking owing to the alleged failure of Sun Fo and Fu Ping-sheung to come to an understanding with Peking in connection with the Shakkee shooting incident.

Dr. C. C. Wu is rumoured as contemplating retirement, for the time being at least. The reason can only be guessed and the report has yet to be confirmed. Tuchun Wu, the chief of Police, is publicly stated to have aendered his resignation as the suspects arrested after the assassination of Liu Chung-oi are said to be connected with one of his departments.

Chan Chow-lam, the editor of the Hongkong "China News"—a vernacular paper which was closed by the Police—has died in the Kung Yee Hospital. After his release by the Hongkong authorities about two months ago, he came up to Canton when he was given an appointment. He was with Liu Chung-oi last Friday and mortally wounded.

headline: ABSURD DEMANDS.
text:
COAL COOLIES AND FOUR FOLD INCREASES.

Slight improvement as regards the clearances of ships and the movement of cargo locally has been reported from time to time but from the conversation which a "China M&H" reporter had this morning with a representative of a well-known 'local' shipping firm it would appear that the difficulties which are being faced in regard to coal steamers, at any rate, have become particularly acute of late.

"Mr. Frederick John William Focken, of Messrs. Alex. Ross and Company, with his assistant, Mr. Li Chi-kong, happened to be on the point of alighting from a motor 'bus outside the China Motor Bus Company's premises, when they heard police whistles being blown some distance down the road, where Mr. Focken's attention was drawn by a passer-by to a man who was attempting to board a 'bus going in the direction of Hunghom railway bridge. Mr. Focken seized this man, who attempted to escape, and handed him over to Mr. Li, who had at this time been joined by two other Chinese, who helped to hold the prisoner.

The revolver used by him was subsequently recovered by the Police in a side channel on the railway track about fifty yards from the railway sheds at Hungbom where he had dropped it during his flight."

The first and third defendants were each sentenced to five years' hard labour. The second defendant, who was too ill to appear, will take his trial at the coming Sessions. headline: BAMBOO BUNDLES. / DISPUTE OVER CONSIGNMENT.
text:
A consignment of over 800000 bundles of bamboo, which, in spite of disturbed conditions, had been brought to Hongkong for sale, formed the subject of Summary Court proceedings this morning, plaintiff and defendant both claiming to be dealers in the trade. It was the contention of the plaintiff that defendant had bought the consignment from him and not paid for it, whilst the defendant asserted that the plaintiff was his (the defendant's) agent and had been paid the money to go up country and get he bamboo.

After evidence had been heard Mr. Justice Wood found for the defendant with costs.

"His Honour the Chief Justice paid a tribute to the services rendered to the public by Mr. Focken on this occasion, and expressed his keen appreciation of his fine act."

Continuing, Mr. Wodehouse said that Mr. Focken's name has now been added to the long list of European civilians and service men who have from time to time given valuable assistance to the Police. "What we naturally expect of them," he said, "we always get."

The speaker expressed his pleasure at the part played by Mr. Li Chi-kong, especially as what he termed the Chinese national attitude—"each for himself, no b'long my pidgin"—was often encountered by the local Police Force, as every other Police Force in China, in the course of their duty. It was well known in the Colony that a crime of violence could be committed in a crowded thoroughfare without anyone lifting a finger, whereas in any other place in Europe or America a hue and cry would be raised. That being so, he considered that Mr. Li had set a good example to his fellow countrymen, which he (the speaker) hoped would be followed in future. (Applause). The presentations were then made, Mr. Focken receiving a silver cigarette case and a letter of commendation, and Mr. Li Chikong a cheque and a letter of commendation. The cigarette case was described. Presented to Mr. J. W. Pocken by the Hongkong Government in appreciation of public services, April 21, 1925. The recipients of the gifts or prezares their thanks and their ailements.

headline: Canton Troops Disarmed.
text:
Before this edition went to Press the "Wah Tsz Yat "Po" issued an extra to the effect that General Yeung Kwan-yu, a pro-Chan Kwing-ming, commander on the East River sector, had disarmed some Kuomintang troops this morning.

Those defeated were under Lam She-ngai, who, it is stated, is not in favour at Canton.

Macchi-guns were brought up into action when Lam's men refused to surrender and there were several casualties.

It is not supposed that the action has more than local significance.

headline: THE MORAL SCOURGE
text:
SINGAPORE AND VENESEAL JOSEASE.

110. Positions SERIOUS.

The Colonial Office's Advisory Committee on Social Hygiene, in its first report, deals with the Draft Ordinance on Veneral disease at Singapore prepared by the Government of the Statuts Settlements for submission to the Legislative Council.

The Committee says the position at Singapore is serious and must be bundled at the earliest moment, especially in view of the approaching enlargement of the Naval Base. It unanimously opnes that the Ordinance does not provide an effective remedy and strongly recommends it should not be passed into law. It recommends the Government of the Strata to take measures to improve social conditions in Singapore, especially as regards the immigration of female with male Chinese; housing, education and recreational facilities, and to appoint a mixed Commission of Europeans, Chinese, and Malays, to enquire into the social and economic conditions of the poor of Singapore, and to organise a medical service at Singapore with a view to the treatment of venereal disease as an integral part of preventive medicine, and prepare to a scheme of free facilities and diagnosis of treatment for the whole population, and frame a policy looking to the early suppression of brothers and an increase in the personnel of the powers of the Chinese Protectors, in order adequately to protect women and girls, not merely Chinese, but those of other races.

The report especially recommends that every effort should be made to enlist sympathy and goodwill of the Chinese community.

headline: KNOCKED DOWN.
text:
EUROPEAN INVOLVED IN TWO ACCIDENTS.

PORTOUERB LADY INJURID.

Four persons were injured in a series of motor accidents at Kowloon yesterday evening.

A small Chinese girl, who was alleged to have been crossing the road in front of a motor truck owned by the Lee Hang firm, was knocked down at Shanghai Street. She suffered injuries to the head and had to be taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital. At Coronation Road an earth coolie sustained bodily injuries by earning in the path of a motor car, which was reported to have been driven by a European.

A report was made later by Mr. Andrew Harper that he was involved in the accident, and he also informed the Police that the Portuguese lady and a child were knocked down by his car. Mr. Harper took the injured persons to Dr. Wong at Homutin, who had them conveyed to the Government Civil Hospital. This condition of the Portuguese lady is stated to be critical.

headline: Foodstuffs Seized.
text:
On Saturday morning a sampan proceeding from Macao to the Revenue Cruising Launch, Paktan at Chinsan with fresh beef, tinned foods and ice was stopped by troops who seized these goods. Later in the day, the beef was returned, but putrefaction had set in.

For weeks these troops have been impeding the importation of

fresh vegetables and eggs into Macao, but this is believed to be the first occasion locally in which they have opposed the supply of food to the men on board the Chinese Maritime Customs launches. Significant of the dire consequences which the strike is having on local Chinese is the fact that as many as twenty destraints (the selling up of the personal property of tenants who cannot pay their rent) are being enforced daily on behalf of lenders and in respect of arrenging.

headline: NOT TRUSTED?
text:
CANTON STRIKE LEADERS DISARMED.

ASSASSINATION SEQUEL

(From Our Own Correspondent.) 20 PESTRAINTS DAILY.

Because of suspicion spreading to labour guilds after the assassination of Liu Chung-oi, strikers are not allowed to carry weapons indiscriminately as heretofore: The defaults relate to shops, business houses and ordinary household tenants and an official with whom a "China Mail" representative conversed this morning said that such numbers had never been known before. In the ordinary course of events there might be one or perhaps two in the course of the day but very seldom any more.

Ever since the strike began everybody who bore a badge of the Strike Executive could carry arms. Now orders have been issued by the Kuomintang that only pickets, actually on duty and in uniform, can carry short or long firearms. It is understood that a few of the principal leaders still retain their revolvers. There is an under-current of

I here is an under-current of strong feeling.

headline: PRINCE GEORGE
text: H.R.H. Prince George, whose unobtrusive attendance at yesterday's public meeting was noticed by but a few, was present on Saturday last at a dance at the Seamen's Institute, arranged by the Lower deck men of the flagship. He participated in large number of the dances and entered with enthusiasm into the tug dances which were a feature of the programme.

headline: MONEY BEST.
text:
CHINESE MILITARY DEFY STRIKERS

FOODSTUFFS FOR MACAO.

Although it has been reported that Centon's Strike Executive has asked for the Chinese warships to cut Macao off-from communication—by water; with its hinterland, vessels are still reaching this port.

Now that the Shekki tow-boat has ceased running, armed launches bearing the standards of local military commanders are arriving at the vicinity of Macao. Such boats carry both passengers, and fruit and foodstuffs, and take merchandise back.

Apparently it is a case of the military making hay while the sun shines, irrespective of the labour professionals' desires.

headline: STUDENT STRIKERS.
text:
GOVERNMENT'S FIRM ATTITUDE. SENIORS EXPELLED

The lead which was promised over a month ago on behalf of the Government with regard to striking students will probably be made public at the next meeting of the Board of Education, for the main lines of the Government's attitude have now been decided.

These, the “China Mail” learns officially, are that “strikers” will not be taken back to Government schools, the definition being applied in respect of students who were absent on certain days. As a notice has already appeared in the Chinese Press notifying, on behalf of the Queen's College authorities, that students who were absent on June 17, 18, 19 and 20 need not present themselves for admission it may be deduced that these are the dates considered crucial in respect of other Government Schools.

The Government will "only enforce this expulsion in the case of students of 16 years of age and over, as it is considered that younger students may have absent themselves through intimidation; whereas senior students, after having the position fully explained to them, had no reason to act from motives of fear.

The co-operation among head masters which members of the Board of Education urged as necessary at the last meeting for any measures decided upon to prove effective is, in fact, in being, for a conference of head masters of all local schools was held yesterday at which, the “China Mail” understands, it was agreed that non-Government schools would co-operate in excluding any expelled striking students who might apply for admission. The action taken by such non-Government schools in regard to any of their own students who associated themselves with the strike must of course rest with the head masters of those schools.

The fees in respect of Government Schools are to be increased as from the next school year, although the "China Mail" was assured officially that this was not a direct outcome of the strike but merely revision which would be considered necessary in any case.

"Caution" money will also, it is understood, be required from parents and guardians in the future (also as from the commencement of the next school year). This will be to guarantee the Government against any loss from unwarranted interference with the normal course of study and will be returned after the course of study is complete, providing the conduct of the student in question has been satisfactory.

headline: DISHONESTY
text:
CHINESE VOLUNTEER SENT TO JAIL

In the early days of the strike a self-defence corps was formed at Tai Han village for the protection of the inhabitants, who, in addition to offering their services as volunteers, contributed to the cost of clothing and equipment. A Chinese member of the corps, who had been entrusted with the work of collecting subscriptions and placing orders for clothing, was brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning to answer a charge of misappropriation. It was stated that he collected a sum of $200, and bought a certain amount of clothing, leaving a balance in hand of $88. This sum, it was alleged the accused failed to return to the treasurer. The accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced to two months. As a sequel to the assassination of Liu Chung-oi, the Whumpou Cadets sent a detachment on Tuesday to surround the Foreign Ministry. Hu is stated to have been detained. His brother, Hu Sui-ching, is believed to have been forewarned and to have escaped. "Another detachment failed to arrest Ngai Bong-ping but a Mr. Lum, a former Superintendent of the Canton-Kowloon Railway (Chinese section) is believed to have been detained.

headline: REDS FALL OUT?
text:
An extra by the Wah Tsz Yat Po issued this afternoon, broadly translated, reads:

headline: COURT MARTIAL.
text:
ARMY DOCTOR'S EXPLANATION.

"Is gastritis the same as what is popularly known as 'pains in the stomach'?" asked Captain C.J. F. Bensley, R.A., when cross-examining Captain R.F. Walker, M.C., R.A.M.C., at a District Court Martial at Whitfield Barracks, Kowloon, this morning. Captain Walker was giving medical evidence as to the results of alcoholic poisoning. He explained that gastritis was in the stomach. People often spoke of stains in the stomach, he continued, when they actually referred to the abdomen and in this was the distinction.

Major W. P. A. Hattersley-Smith, D.S.O., R.A., was President, The other members of the Court were Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman, Surrey Regiment and Lieut. B. R. Wright-Neville, 2nd Punjabis.

Sergeant Samuel Robson, 38th Heavy Battery, R.A., pleaded “not guilty” to a charge of being drunk on August 8 at 10.45 p.m., and a second charge of being unfit for duty for nine days through indulgence in liquor.

Captain Bensley was the prosecutor and Lieut. H.L. C. Hall, R.A., acted as prisoner's counsel.

Battery Sergeant-Major Brice gave evidence that he saw accused helplessly drunk in the sergeants' mess. When accused complained of being ill, Battery Quarter-Master-Sergeant Moore and Lce/Bdr. Dunne helped to remove him to hospital.

B.Q.M.S. Moore gave cor- roborative evidence.

Major Pollard, R.A.M.C., of the Kowloon. Military Hospital said that accused was rather excited when he got to hospital, smelt of alcohol and had acute pains in the stomach.

The next day, accused was bent over to the Military Hospital at Bowen Road. There he was treated by Captain Walker who said that the pains complained of were due to alcoholic poisoning. When accused started to cross-examine Captain Walker's discussion, in which Major Hetersley-Smith participated, ensued as to what effect brandy would have on pains in the stomach and as to which specific part of the body was meant when the word "stomach" was used. The query by the prosecutor led to the answer which has already been mentioned.

On oath, accused told the Court that he suffered from chronic indigestion, that his depression was due to trouble at Home, that he had a severe attack of gastritis when coming out on the boat and that his health had been further impaired by the increased consumption of tinned foods since the strike began. On the day in question he felt ill and sent for some brandy. He had reason to believe that the brandy was of very inferior quality, thus causing his condition as he took very little. In reply to the President, accused mentioned the brand. Accused also emphasised his good conduct.
