si mercenaries were ejected about three months ago. These Northern mercenaries are now over running Canton and turning on their masters. A conservative estimate places their strength in the field, at 50,000 bayonets. All the other factions combined, in the province of Kwangtung, can hardly be a match for them with their superior munitions and strategic position.

As this edition went to press the "China Mail" received a message to the effect that the Whampoa Cadets are concentrating their main strength in the city of Canton. Practically all opposition to them has subaided and they are the undisputed masters at the moment of the situation. General LL. Fook-lam is reported to have fled from Honan, the island opposite Canton, for the village of Pal. Tode, where he is in hiding. The Cadets are momentarily expected to cross the River and take possession of Honan. The most serious of the several border incidents that have happened since the strike began took place yesterday when a decided scrap occurred between Chinese soldiers and the Taituling Police.

A strike picket commander from"Canton, who arrived here from Shekki late last night, has informed me that the Whampoa Cadets at their Canton headquarters have been firing indiscriminately in the city.

He believes that a campaign has been launched to disarm anybody who is not an out and out Bolshevik. This is a sequel to the assassination of Liu Chung-oi. There is no distinction maxix. The Cadets are attacking all who can't arms. Those who surrender are allowed to disperse.

However, resistance has been offered by military and gender-merie detachments who are suspected of favouring the anti-Bolshevik cause. One determined scrap witnessed by my informant was close to the City Police Headquarters. Everywhere in Canton, the Reds are guining the upper hand and they are making no attempt to hide their bid for power.

DETAILS OF THE COUP. Intelligence received in Hongkong has since borne out the report in yesterday's "China Mail" of a coup by the Red party in Canton. Several versions have come down as to what actually occurred and there are material divergences. The one given most credence is that Hu Han-min (formerly acting Generalissimo in the absence of Sun Yat-sen, Governor, and now Foreign Minister) has been denounced by the Bolsheviks; also that General Cheung Kai-shek, commander-in-chief of the Cadets, General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang's Cantonese troops and Wong Ching-wai (who made a sensational plot to assassinate the Prince Regent before the Manchus fell) are creating a triumph in the return of the war with which to rule Canton and to give full play to Communistic ideas.

The “Industrial and Commercial Daily Press” (“Kung Seung Yat Po”), a new Chinese paper published in Hongkong, hints that Hu's capture by the Reds may be attributable to alleged appropriations of funds from the sale of Soviet oil, such as oil having been imported to meet Canton's needs. A representative of this paper proceeded to Conduit Road last night to interview Hu Ching-sui, a brother of the arrested politician: Hu Han-min, it may be stated, has a house at Excelsior Terrace, which is between Conduit and Robinson Roads. The brother is supposed to have come down to Hongkong by train after an anxious time in custody.

Hu Han-min is said to have escaped, to be detained at the Whampoa Academy, and to have left for Shanghai by a vessel which did not put in at Hong-kong.

A very well-informed quarter in the Colony told a “China Mail” reporter, this morning that although it was assumed that the interests of Hu Han-min, Ngai Bong-ping (a former Canton general and chief of police), General Li Fook-lum of Honam and General Leung Hung-kai of Kong-moon, would unite against the Reds, their combined strength was small as contrasted with the armies of Generals Cheung and Hsu.

Hu Han-min's Capture. According to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," Hu Han-min escaped from the Foreign Ministry when the Reds surrounded him and proceeded to the house of Wong Ching-wai. Wong was out but Mrs. Wong assured him that a mistake must have been made and accompanied Hu to interview General Hsu. Once in the presence of Hsu, Hu Han-min was placed under arrest for removal to Whampoa. A military council comprising General Cheung, Techen Wu (chief of police) and Chu Pui-teh (a pro-Kuomintang yunnanese commander) and two others examined Hu Han-min's brother. Lam Chik-mien (formerly superintendent of the K.C. Railway, Chinese section) was bound in ropes until released on assurance

that he had nothing to do with the murder of Liu Chung-oi.

Ngai Bong-ping has fled either to Kongmoon or the West River. The "Wah Kiu Yat Po" says that Ngai's family escaped through the good graces of a German medical doctor and another paper states that Ngai's house was burned down by the Reds.

General Leung. Hung-kai's whereabouts are unknown. Some time before the present crisis came to a head, it had already been reported that he had disagreed with the Canton Reds although he was, nominally, a subordinate. On good authority, the "China Mail" is informed that he is still at his Kongmoon headquarters, and out of danger. Vernacular reports say that he has either been shot in fighting at his Canton quarters, or that he has been captured together with two of his leading subordinates who were among the first to dispute the authority of the Canton Commission of Government.

This morning's "Wab Tsz Yat Po" publishes a report from a correspondent to the effect that Sun Fo has been reconciled to Chan Kwing-ming and that these two have promised to co-operate in an offensive against the Canton Reds. It will be recalled that Sun Fo went to Peking where he, apparently, got no satisfaction. The supposition now is that he is dissatisfied with the present Canton rulers. The address (in Chinese) of the house in Shanghai, where Chan and Sun Fo are said to have sat down at dinner is actually given.

The Punjab's retaliated by firing four rounds, and one of the Chinese soldiers was seen to drop. headline: HABITUAL THIEF.
text:
YESTERDAY'S INCIDENT AT ICE HOUSE STREET. During

BASEBALLER'S FINE CATCH.

The street theft reported in yesterday's "China Mail" had its sequel at the Central Magistracy this morning when a Chinese youth was brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry on a charge of larceny.

The evidence disclosed that the accused snatched a sum of $12.60 from the pocket of an old Chinese message coolie of the International Bank as he was walking in Ice House Street at 2.45 p.m. yesterday on his way to pay a bill at Messrs. Kelly and Walsh. An alarm was raised, whereupon the accused threw the money away and ran along Des Vœux Road with two Europeans and an Indian constable in pursuit. The accused led his pursuers through a devious route extending through Statue Square, Chater Road, and the praya at Connaught Road, where he was eventually caught. Mr. B. A. Proulx, a local baseball player, who joined in the chase from the early stage, said that he lost sight of the runaway only for a few seconds when rounding Statue Square, and did not stop till he had caught him. The accused had three previous convictions; and a statement which he made denying the charge was disbelieved by His Worship, who imposed a sentence of six months hard labour.

Café Wiseman are now able to open credit accounts and deliver bread daily to Kowloon residents.

headline: CANTON MAILS.
text:
CARRIED BY TRAIN AND COOLIE

As will be seen from a Post Office announcement, correspondence for Canton specially superscribed "By Train". will be transmitted in the mail closed at 8.15 a.m. daily and forwarded by the morning train from Kowloon.

By an arrangement with the Chinese Postal authorities the mails are carried as far as Lo Wu, in British territory, and there transferred by coelite to Blumehun. On inquiry it was learned that the system appears to be working satisfactorily, similar arrangement being in force for letters from Canton to Hongkong.

headline: Strikers Disarmed.
text:
A presumption that, during the present upheaval, the “strike” movement in Canton has occupied little attention, seems to have been borne out. As is generally known, an exodus of the civil population usually follows a crisis in Canton city. At present there is no direct communication by steamer with either Macao or Hongkong. Nevertheless, in spite of strikers' pickets, quite a number of people have left for minor ports in the river delta and others have departed by the Canton-Kowloon Railway.

In their campaign of disarming everybody the Red, soldiers in Canton have also extended their activities to the strikers. Many of those doing picket duty and individuals carrying weapons have had such forcibly taken from them. In fact, some of the strikers seem to have incurred the suspicions of the Bolshevik leaders in connection with the death of Liu Chung-oi. A rumour is current, says a correspondent, that the Canton authorities suspect a member of the Hongkong-Wuchow (Steamer) Guild, a body previously in Hongkong but closed by the Police.

The “China Mail” is informed by the Chung Shing Benevolent Society that Captain Chan Kum (Chan Kwoon-hing), who is one of the members, has been released by the pirates which pirated the S.S. Kwong Hung on the West River. Captain Chan has been in command of the steamer for some years.

Pakkai, Kongmbon, Aug. 26. News has reached this port that the compradore of the

strikers claimed special privilege as... they were performing "patriotic service." The pirates stripped them of even their singlets and all they had and turned them loose.

A batch of Hongkong amahs who, after much pleading, obtained permits to travel to Macao, were turned back by strike pickets at Chinshan, which is just across the border here. Very few people, if any, are getting through by that route. Armed pickets are on duty at the large pavilion on the Shekki road, thus preventing people leaving. Meidourne, August 28. headline: WEMBLEY'S ASSETS.
text:
The Wembley authorities are appointing immediately a body to examine the question of realisation of the Exhibition.

Mr. J. H. Thomas, Secretary of State for the Colonies in the recent Labour Cabinet, has accepted the chairmanship of the Wembley realisation committee which will deal with the question of the assets and future of the Exhibition.

headline: ITALIAN AVIATOR
text:
DELAYED AT MANILA BY TYPHOONS

Major di Pinado has reimagined that he has been held up at Manila owing to vlock typeons. He is considering flying to Tokyo via Shanghai for the purpose of avoiding the storms. Melbourne, August 28. According to the “Herald,” the deportation proceedings are being taken only against the Labour leaders, Walsh and Johansen.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
SOUTH AFRICA BEING INVOLVED.

AUSTRALIA'S PREPAREDNESS.

The position as regards the seamen's strike is more serious. Meetings of British seamen are being held in favour of a strike unless the grievances are remedied. There seems to be a prospect that all South African ports will be rapidly affected. The steamship Ballarat and the mail boat Arundel Castle have been held up.

headline: STATE PREMIER CRITICISED.
text: In the House of Representatives, Mr. S. Bruce, moving the second reading of the Police Bill, condemned the attitude of new South Wales Labourite Premier, Mr. Lang, and said the Labourites could stop the trouble among overseas seamen if they had the courage to tell them that they were being dragged at the heels of extremists. The Bill was seconded.

headline: . CAPE DIEMMA.
text:
The day has been one of abortive conferences to settle the strike. Both the authorities and the shipping companies are in a dilemma as there does not appear any local way of dealing with the situation. The strike leaders admit that they signed the agreement in England, but say that they did so in order to get away from the Dominion ports where they have the whiphand to enforce a case-and-the-only way out was to pay the old rate until they reached England. The release without stain upon the character of two men sentenced at Durban is the only development of the situation. Stewards of the steamer Ballarat, persuaded the steward of the Arundel Castle to join the strike. The Premier, Mr. Hertszog, has cabled Mr. Havelock Wilson stating that British seamen are taking action on their own volition and are not incited by anyone in South Africa. EARLIER, EARLES Durban, August 28 The shipping strike has assumed serious proportions. The Continued at foot of next Column

crew of the Balmoral Castle have refused to work, and sailing has been postponed indefinitely.

The strike has occurred at a critical period because the ports are congested with steamers waiting to remove an unprecedented maize crop.

Two strikers of the Sandgate Castle who were sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment, have had their sentences suspended for a fortnight to enable them to reconsider their position and assist in getting the vessel away.

SITUATION IN AUSTRALIA. Melbourne August 09

There are further indications of the Seamen's strike ending. The Trades Council of Melbourne announces that it was in nowise in charge of the strike which is now in the hands of the British seamen themselves. The liner Chital has arrived and is being loaded with stevedores who intend to work all the British manned vessels.

There was an uproar in the House of Representatives when Mr. Bruce asked leave to introduce a bill to appoint special police in connection with the seamen's strike. Mr. Charlton, a labour leader, vigorously protested against "springing" such a bill in the House. The Senate after a vigorous debate, had adopted by a vote of 20 to 9 the ministerial motion that the Senate meet to borrow to consider special legislation and posting special police owing to the New South Wales Government's refusal to assist the Commonwealth to carry out the law in regard to possible deportations.

headline: CARGO OF BEER. / SCHOONER SEIZED BY DRY AGENTS.
text:
Key West, Florida, Aug. 28. The schooner "Fannie Prescott," bound from Havana to Nassau, with 750 cases of beer on board has been seized three miles from here. The crew of ten have been arrested and detained.

Philadelphia, August 28.—The Miners' Union has ordered a strike in the anthracite coalfields on September 1.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: BAD MAN.
text:
"Pardoned" by Dr. Sun Yat-sen for the alleged murder of his wife, subsequently deported from Hongkong as an undesirable, accused of having misappropriated public funds in this Colony, Canton and Shanghai, a notorious "labour boss" is now active once more in the strike against Hongkong.

Reported exclusively in the "China Mail" about a fortnight ago was the fact that Chinese coming to Hongkong from Nam-tau were being "squeezed" of various amounts. It was then stated that Chan Ping-sang, the notorious man whose career has been briefly given, was mainly responsible.

Namtau is a small port, in Chinese territory, just beyond Deep Bay. At least one big steam launch makes the journey to and fro each day. Fish and other foodstuffs, and passengers come to Hongkong from Namtau. With other routes temporarily closed up it was only natural that Hongkong strikers should make their way, overland or by native river craft, to Namtau to return to work. As soon as Canton heard of the port they opened up a strikers' branch office there. Pickets were sent out and soon Chan Ping-sang was the No. 1 man.

headline: $100 Per Head.
text:
For a time very few people got through and little or no fish was shipped here. Then the restrictions seem to relax. According to the vernacular papers Namtau's strike office is now letting cargo and trayellers through, on a consideration. Each person leaving Namtau for Hongkong, so the report goes, must pay a cash deposit of $100 which will be forfeited on failure to return the same day. In other words, those wishing to return to their old positions must pay $100 for the privilege. As many know, there are a good many domestic servants, coolies and seafaring Chinese from the hinterland of Namtau and the majority of market fish stall holders are also natives of that place.

It seems to be the same old story. Chan sprang into the limelight when the seamen's strike negotiations began. Then he was found guilty of murdering his wife at Canton but was released by Sun Yat-sen. He came back to Hongkong to be deported and returned to Canton where he fell into disgrace through alleged embezzlement of union funds. For a time he was in Shanghai till he got into trouble there. Since then he was not heard of until at Namtau, he cropped up again. It has also been rumoured that he has incurred the displeasure, by his actions, of the native garrison.

Troops Disarmed. In-coming passengers from Namtau have been able to throw some light on the recent Canton "war." Several hundred of General Hsu Shung-chi's Kuomin-tang (Cantonese) troops were seen to march on Namtau which was held by another band of Canton men who evidently did not satisfy the Bolsheviks.

The new-comers were far superior in numbers to the garrison and in a short while the defenders were disarmed.

It now means that the whole of the Chinese territory adjoining the British border is in the hands of Canton's trusted troops, including both the non-Cantonese "Cadets," and Cantonese regulars.

headline: WORLD'S BEST VIEW / HONGKONG SEEN BY NIGHT?
text:
Apropós of some discussion that seems to have been going on at Home, Mr. T. Simmons of Edinburgh writes the following letter to the Daily Mail:

In my opinion the world's best view is either the Firth of Fortb as seen from Edinburgh Castle, or Malta seen as one enters the port of Valette at daybreak.

For a night view one has to go a long way to see a more glorious sight than Hongkong viewed from the Kowloon ferry boat. Granted Hongkong, with all its fairly-like Lights leading up to the Peak but as for the other two we can imagine much controversy, remarks the "North China Daily News." In fact, the business is something like that which had two or three years ago almost as big a vogue in America as the cross-word puzzle, namely to decide who were the ten or dozen greatest men that the world had produced. The latter brought out some weird opinions, absolutely unheard of people being quoted, and nobody agreed on any of them. In the same way, that the Firth of Forth or Valetta should get away without a protest is too much to expect. There is no doubt about how impressive the great sweep of the Forth is, and the attraction of the terraced heights of Valetta, but on the other hand Naples Bay has an established reputation of its own and in many places the Rockies of Canada are magnificent in their uskers' splendour. In fact when we go into the question we have to admit that it is dangerous even to rest our belief on Hongkong at night for somebody may know of something very much better. On the whole it seems safer to allow Mr. Simmons of Edinburgh to bear the burden of his ruthness. headline: Wong Ching-wai—are very much in the background.
text:
West River Movement. Along the West River Red contingents are moving to attack a flank of the Cantonese garrison. Brigades of Cadets were thrown out in short time, occupying, without fighting, nearly all important points on the river, and railway. These troops, according to latest intelligence, are moving towards the Sze Yan. The Cadet/chief in is said to have refused the nomination of commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang Army, stating that he was satisfied to be President of the Whampoa Academy and garrison commander of Canton. He has appointed five army commanders, each with two divisions. In doing so he has named Hsu Shung-chi, hitherto the standby of the Cantonese Bolsheviks, as his subordinate. Li Fook-lam is also one of the chosen as are a Yunnanese and a Hunanese general, and Li Chai-sum whose sway extends along to Wuchow and parts of the West River.

In the excitement following the death of Lin Chung-oi, some of the strikers came in for rough treatment at the hands of Cadet patrols in Canton.

The position is that once having taken the guild leaders into confidence it will be necessary to provide for the rank and file. Liu Chung-oi's immediate subordinates are still officiating at the Finance Bureau and these are paying out the daily quota to maintain the strikers. Nominally, the Canton strike position has not changed. Actually, the possibility of a debacle is further removed and the outlook is not at all bright. With the pronounced Reds in the ascendant, it is only natural to presume that the politicians will maintain their policy.

headline: MAILS HELD UP.
text:
QUEENSLAND AND BOYCOTT PROTEST.

STRONG MEASURES NEEDED.

Following the action of the Queensland railway strikers in boycotting the malls, the Prime Minister, Mr. Bruce, has telegraphed the Premier of Queensland regarding the holding up of 26 mailbags at Rockhampton in consequence of the railway strikers' boycott of malls. Mr. Bruce points out the seriousness of such illegal action and requests an assurance of prompt measures to deal with the offenders. The Senate passed the third reading of the polled bill.

headline: CAUTION QUIET. / RESISTANCE TO REDS FADNS OUT.
text:
CADET COMMANDER RULES.

Having wiped out any possibility of resistance for the time being, the Bolsnevik party in Canton is now consolidating its position.

Not taking into consideration the Chan Kwin-ming forces now between the upper sources of the East River and the Fukien boundary, there is hardly any integrate force able to challenge the Reds. General Cheung Kai-shek, c.i.c. of the Whampoa Cadets, is the man of the hour. He only sprang into prominence earlier in the year in the campaign against Swatow but he is now the asocrat of Canton, ruling the city and other parts of the province with the aid of Bolshevik counsellors.

News from merchants indicates a feeling of unrest in apprehension of coming radical changes. Honam, like Canton, is also quiet but Li Foxk-lam's troops are still in the "provinces."

Strict vigilance is being maintained in the city and the comb out with which the coup began has no quite ended.

Otherwise there is little to report. Riserring to houses in Hongkong

headline: STOLEN FIREWOOD.
text:
GODOWN KEEPER HEAVILY FINED.

A Chinese employee of the Kwong Hung Cheong godown, Belcher Street, was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of a large quantity of wood cut from a plantation below the Infectious Diseases Hospital Kennedy Town

Sergeant T. O'Connell stated in evidence that he visited the godown armed with a search warrant yesterday morning. Some of the wood he said, were whole pine trees, freshly cut, and found hidden in the yard beneath a heap of bamboo. The accused claimed to be in charge of the premises and he was taken into custody.

Mr. H. Green, of the Botamical and Forestry Department, said that considerable damage had been done to the plantation by the removal of about 15 large trees. The accused denied that he had anything to do with the wood found on the premises, and said that the trees were brought in by a casual worker who lived there. He was, however, unable to point the coolie put as the latter was said to have suddenly left the godown. His Worship said he was not inclined to agree with the accused's story and imposed a fine of $100.

headline: DRUG EVIL.
text:
GENEVA COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

PERSIAN GULF OPIUM

The advisory committee on opium adopted the report to the Council containing seven resolutions dealing inter-alia with the illicit traffic in drugs and urging most energetic steps for the discovery of persons engaged therein.

The committee draws attention to the large illicit traffic in opium between the Persian Gulf and the Far East and suggested the adoption of certain measures.

The committee opposes any scheme of propaganda for the purpose of acquainting the general public with the consequences of the abuse of dangerous drugs. It recommends the conclusion of extradition treaties between the various Powers similar to the recent Canadian and American treaty.

Mr. Tsurumi in the course of the adoption of the minutes referred to a discrepancy in the statements of Sir Malcolm Delevigne and Mr. Campbell on the subject of drugs in Japan arising out of faulty translation of the record of the Japanese Diet. Mr. Campbell made an explanation with which Mr. Tsurumi expressed himself as satisfied.

In the course of closing the proceedings Mrs. Hamilton Wright attenuated her previous allegation by reading a telegram from General Wood, Governor-General of the Philippines, indicating that only small quantities of opium are imported into the Philippines from Borneo.

Mr. Pinkneytuck (United States) declared that his Government would continue to co-operate unofficially with the advisory Committee in the suppression of the illicit drug traffic on the basis of the Hague Convention of 1912.

headline: WEDDING AT HOME.
text:
INSPECTOR D. MACDONALD MARRIED.

PRETTY CEREMONY.

"Friends of Inspector D. Macdonald, of the Hongkong Police Police Force, who is spending his leave in Scotland and is due back next month, will be interested to hear that he was married on July 15 to Christina, elder daughter of ex-Baillie Norman Macrae and Mrs. Macrae, of Craig Road; Dingwall.

The ceremony was performed at the Castlehill United Free Church, Forres, by the Rev. Ronald Macdonald, M.A., of Dingwall Union Church, assisted by the Rev. R. G. Macdonald, M.A., and the guests were principally the relatives of the bride and bridegroom.

Beautiful wedding music was played by Mrs. Douglas, of Torres, the Second Paraphrase being sung at the close of the proceedings. The bride, who was given away by her father, was handsomely attired in a gown of broche crêpe de chine and silver brocade, caught at left side with large diamente ornament. Her long bridal veil was edged with rare lace and crowned with orange blossom, and she carried a bouquet of white roses. She wore a long string of pearls—the gift of the bridegroom—and silver shoes.

Miss Atta Macrae was principal bridesmaid. She wore a frock of shell pink crêpe de chine embroidered in mauve and gold, with cape of mauve georgette, and large hat.

There were four dainty attendants—the Misses Grace and Mary Mackay (niece of bridegroom), Miss Jessie Macdonald, U. F. Manse, Dingwall, and Miss Mary Black, of Edinburgh.

The bridegroom's brother, Mr. Duncan Macdonald, of New York was the best man.

Luncheon followed at the Royal Station Hotel, where the toast of the young couple and the bridesmaids, was drunk, and they had a hearty send-off on their departure for Cornwall for their honeymoon.

headline: PRISONER'S ESCAPE.
text:
CHINESE ELUDES INDIAN CONSTABLE

KOWLOON COURT INCIDENT

A mild sensation was caused at the Kowloon Magistracy at about noon yesterday when it was announced that a Chinese prisoner had escaped.

The man, who had several previous convictions against him, had just been sentenced by Mr. E. W. Hamilton to six months' hard labour on a larceny charge, and was being conducted to the cell by an Indian constable. Before being placed there the prisoner obtained permission from his guard to enter the lavatory, which is on the ground floor on a side of the building. The constable's attention being attracted elsewhere at the main entrance, the prisoner jumped over the short wall on the other side and escaped. Seeing that the prisoner was a long time in coming back, the constable went to investigate but he was nowhere to be found.

The constable is now in the custody of the Police for the negligence.

headline: NO GERMAN EXODUS.
text:
FACTS CONCERNING TUNG ON PASSENGERS.

RETURNING BUSINESS MEN.

The return from Canton to Hongkong aboard H.M.S. Tung On of passengers of German nationality who were not taken up by that vessel has led to the assumption that there has been an exodus of German business men from Shameen.

A “China Mail” representative who made enquiries this morning was informed that the numbers of Germans returning to Hongkong from Canton was but few, and that in nearly every case they had previously gone up from Hongkong, by train or other means as in view of the responsibility that the naval authorities had to assume for passengers on the Tung On, it was difficult to get a permit to go up unless one had exceptionally pressing business. It was less difficult to get a permit for return at Canton.

A German business man who returned to the Colony from Canton yesterday assured a "China Mail" representative that German residents' safety and their businesses were affected in the same degree as British, but there was no talk of an exodus.

As regards the general position in Canton, the “China Mail” informant could say little “apart from confirming the news that Li Fuk-lam's forces had submitted to the Red regime which appeared to be established as firmly as anything could be said to be in Canton. There was still no communication between Shameen and Canton, he stated.

headline: “HONAM” RETURNS.
text:
PASSENGERS LEAVE BUT FEW EMBARK.

CARGO BROUGHT BACK.

The s.s. "Honam" returned to Hongkong from Canton shortly after 4.30 p.m. yesterday.

Crowds of Chinese assembled on the Praya from the early afternoon at first in groups and then in crowds. Eventually, traffic being hindered somewhat, the crowd had to be cleared back to the pavement, the sight of a revenue officer with a broom proving quite sufficient enough for the purpose! The talk among these Chinese on the Praya, a "China Mail" representative was informed by one who spoke the language well was that the "Honam" had sunk with all hands aboard! On the wharf itself were a few Europeans who were expecting friends to arrive from Shameen, Mr. T. H. King, D.C.I., with police officers, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, the Hon. Mr. C. McI. Messer, Mr. J. Arnold, Mr. J. D. Lloyd, Superintendent, Imports and Exports Department, and revenue officers.

When the ship approached near enough for figures to be observed, it was noticed that there were not many aboard apart from officers and Indian guards. Actually, it transpired that there were about thirty Chinese, nearly all women and children and the rest were mostly "white" Russians who had helped to take up the "Sui An" and the "Sui Tai" and had remained in Canton looking for work.

The cargo which was taken up was brought back again, as there were no lighters available. The passengers who went up, however, managed to get off by sampan. The reason for so few boarding the ship was undoubtedly that pickets were busy intimidating the sampan people who had evidently been instructed that they might take anyone away from the ship, but none to it.

The skipper of the vessel told a "China Mail" representative that he did not see vessels which he could say with definite assurance contained pickets but other officers told the reporter that they had been assured by the Customs officials who came aboard that certain boats and launches were those of strike pickets. The only way in which the few passengers had managed to get aboard was that when these craft were on the other side of the ship the sampans in which were those desirous of boarding came nearer the ship and then occupants were hauled in, much to their triumph and satisfaction.

The following incident shows how keen the Chinese in Hongkong are to know more intimate details of events in Canton and the prospects of their friends there being able to get away. A Chinese woman who came off the "Honam" was questioned outside the wharf by representatives of the Trade Maintenance Association whose intentions were entirely friendly and who merely wished to obtain information as to how she had boarded the "Honam."

The woman, however, took fright, thinking that they were seeking to intimidate her. She took to her heels, being pursued by the Chinese seekers after information. She finally rid herself of them by jumping into a ricsha. The only hitch, and it hardly deserves to come under that head since those who were responsible for it acted on their own account, was the disappearance of two Press representatives who went up as passengers—Mr. F. Oliver, of the "South China Morning Post," and Mr. J. S. Cox, of the "Hongkong Daily Press." They went ashore in the Customs launch shortly after the boat arrived on Thursday afternoon and were seen to land on the Customs steps on the Bund. Their nonappearance was not reported to the Captain of the "Honam" until the ship was under way about 10 a.m. yesterday. He immediately caused a wireless message to be despatched to the Senior "naval officer" informing him that Mr. Oliver and Mr. Cox were saboreous. headline: BACK TO HONGKONG / HOW A STRIKER DODGED THE PICKETS.
text:
How a striker found his work on a long from Canton this week, in risk of his life, was related to a "China Mail" reporter this morning. After a stay of about two months in Canton he began to get tired of the inactivity. Some of his colleagues were earning money there by working at 20 cents a day — in addition to food provided by the Executive— on the road to Whampoa. This road was now as long as “the eye could see” but people whose property adjoined the highway were up in protest as their paddi fields had been ruthlessly cut up without compensation. Others, who had a few dollars, pitched stalls in the streets. They snipped off electric wires, took whatever current they wanted—also without payment— and made money by hawking. This man's batch was quartered in a block of new buildings but they got their meals in a disused Tantan house. Mosquito nets or even beds were absent. They slept on the hard floor. A trip to Shekki had proved abortive as the tow-boat carried about ten batches of new pickets for Chinshan. Taking the train at Qaishatau, the striker reached Samchan, the fare for a third-class ticket being $8. At Samchan Market, he passed the night in an improvised boarding house where he slept on the floor for 20 cents. Several "mushroom hotels" had spring up there to cope with the people always passing through. On being turned back at the point of the hayonet at the Chinese ridgehead on the Samchun River he striker paid $1.60 as a bribe and walked ten miles to a space where the river could be forged. When in knee-deep water some body opened fire at him and he ran for over three hours till he cached. Sheungahul station (in British territory) where a train took him to Yaumati for 35 cents. headline: China / "TELL THE KING."
text:
"I can tell the King", were words alleged by the prosecution at this morning's District Court Martial as having been used by the accused when the spoke to a military police men.

Private Henry Barber, East Surrey Regiment, was charged with striking a non-commissioned officer. Major E. S. Halford, R.A., presided and the other members of the Court were Captain Montamaro (Surrey, Regiment) and Lieut. Wright-Neville (Punjabi Regiment). Liout. A. E. Cottum prosecuted. Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman acted as prisoner's counsel.

Fra必Corporal Doubtfire, regimental police corporal, deposited that on the night of August 22, after roll-call he questioned accused at EVASIONOR COMPLICITY OF PICKETS?

Wellington Barracks and accused replied that he was going for a walk. Witness played accused under open arrest for attempting to break out of barracks. On the way back, accused—as alleged by witness—remarked that "it seems a pastime in the battalion, placing 'blokes' under arrest." Witness pointed out that this should be told to the company commander next morning whereupon accused rejoined "I can tell the King."

After another remark witness placed accused under close arrest. It was then that accused was supposed to have struck witness a blow in the face.

Private W. Moore, who was with the Lance-Corporal, gave similar evidence. He added that accused said something about looking for his dog.

Accused said that he was taking his dog for a final run before "lights out" when his pet chased another dog round the R. E. tennis courts. It was while following the dog that he was questioned by Lee. Cpl. Doubtfire. After being placed under open arrest and returning; as ordered, to his room, he said something to a friend. Lee.-Opl Doubtfire stood over him in a threatening manner, one hand on his hip and the other wagging a cane. He accused, was provoked and lost his temper. He made to strike with his fist; he nearly did so but realised his mistake and withdrew his hand in time.

Captain Drake-Brockman, who had taken great pains in cross-examining the witnesses for the prosecution, addressed the Court on behalf of accused. He submitted that the offence had provoking circumstances and suggested that the military police corporal had acted hastily. Subsequently Captain Drake-Brockman made a statement as company commander of accused. The speaker took over command on May 1, 1925, and had always found accused to be an efficient and clean soldier. On his recommendation accused was employed as an officer's servant. He had never had trouble with accused who was short-tempered and needed tactful handling. Lienk Colam then read out accused's record. In service of three years 71 days he had been charged once with neglect of duty and once with absence.

headline: BARON HAYASHI. COLONY'S DISTINGUISHEI VISITOR.
text:
Baron Hayashi, who is returning to Japan on the conclusion of his term of office as Japanese Ambassador in London, arrived in Hongkong yesterday by the s. "Fushimi Maru." He was met by the Japanese Consul (Mr. Takahashi) and other well-known Japanese members of the community. He launched at Government House and in the evening was present at a dinner given by the Japanese community in his honour at the Consul's residence. Prior to leaving London, Baron Hayashi had expressed in interviews, the valuable advice he had received from British statemen and to the "allace at heart" between Japan and Britain. In his opinion, he said, the greatest present menace to the world's peace were the questions regarding China and Russia owing to the efforts of the Soviet Government to create disturbance. There was no doubt, he said, that this interests of the Powers were being increasingly centred in the Pacific but he did not think that the Singapore base was a solution of the problem for Britain. He thought the scheme would be a waste of millions of pounds. The Colony's distinguished visitor left this morning by the "Foshima Maru" Error a brief holiday in Japan at his intention to return to England at any rate until Prince Ghichiku has completed his studies. text:
LOCAL PRESSMEN'S CANTON EXPERIENCE.

SHACKLED AND JAILLED.

Mr. E. Oliver, of the "South China Morning Post," and Mr. J. S. Cox, of the "Hongkong Daily Press," returned to Hongkong by the 8.5. "Honum" yesterday after having been captured by strikers in Cinton, by whom they were subjected to indignity and imprisonment. After being protected by armed Chinese soldiers from an angry mob to whom the mere fact that they were foreign and in their power was sufficient for them to demand their death, they two journalists had chalms clamped on their necks and were incarcerated for 17 hours in a filthy cell with 14 Chinese prisoners. The reason for their venturing into Canton at a time when affairs may well be described as critical was that they wished to despatch a cable to their respective newspapers announcing the safe arrival of the 8.5. "Honum" upon which they had travelled from Hongkong. It was 6:30 p.m. on Thursday, when they went and still light when they returned to the Customs wharf with their object achieved. Nothing unleavied had occurred and the reception they had had from officials and passers-by had been cordial. Their troubles began when arriving late, they found that the boat they were expecting to be waiting them at the wharf was not there.

The English bridge to Shamean at Shu Xi, not far from where they were, was barricaded with buried wire. Passage by boat also was impossible because the sampan people would not take aboard foreigners. The only course open to the two pressmen there for was to on the 11th of March. The crowd of Chinese had collected. Hostility, later to be replaced by funateak hatred, was not forthcoming until, under the pretext of finding them passes from the Government which would enable them to get a motor boat to Shamean, in Chinese in European dress persuaded them to accompany him to what must have been in the nature of a gathering place for strikers.

From then onwards the pressmen were virtually captives and there followed what Mr. Oliver terms a "ghustly" ride to further headquarters with the hostile and fanatical mob surging around. Only the armed Chinese guards with which they had been provided seems to have saved them from probable death and these same guards, reinforced, were called upon later to repel the mob which attacked the building when Mr. Oliver and Mr. Cox were undergoing cross-examination.

headline: WHEN THE STRIKE WILL END.
text:
Giving ample reasons for such an attitude, a letter from an agent in Canton to the principal of a Hongkong Chinese business house with extensive interests in both places, states that both the "strike" and the "boycott" will shortly be over.

Translated broadly, one paragraph in the message reads:—General Cheung Kui-shek is not naturally inclined towards an anti-foreign, or even an anti-British, policy. His civil subordinates feel that the present plan of isolation will soon be discarded. With the most hostile agitators out of the way I feel that in a few weeks' time Canton will be restored to normal. It is now safe foreigners to go about in daylight. Vigilance against British goods is also decreasing and there are amply grounds that the strike leaders are losing ground. But as the new rulers have a little more to do to accomplish their position they will not risk things just at the moment by ignoring the labour agitators.

The political outlook is not so promising. I am informed that General Cheung is only a figurehead and that one or two behind the scenes are the real masters. But whoever may constitute the leaders they will not rest till their authority is absolutely assured and there can be no dispensing their power. General Hsu (Shung-chi) is not secure as the time must come when the Bolshevik element consider him a hindrance.

You will remember that in my last letter I stated that the "Honam" would not be molested if she came up here as you advised. The Strike Executive issued circulars to the effect that on each side of the ship were forty British gunners who would bombard anybody that threatened them. Accordingly pickets were warned to give the vessel a wide berth, to refrain from open agitation and/or intimidation if she came alongside the wharf for fear of being fired at, but to warn all friends against the danger of travelling to Hongkong by her.

When the "Honam" first came up there was little or no trouble but the captain was arrested at the wharf for being in possession of a loaded revolver without a permit and he was confined in a saltfish shop.

[Note:—The writer obviously mistook Messrs. Oliver and Cox for the “Honam’s” captain!]

headline: A TREASURE SHIP.
text:
REPORTED SEIZED BY BOLSHEVIks

FOODSTUFF FOR HONGKONG.

Treasure and foodstuffs, bound for Hongkong on board a Chinese coasting steamer, are alleged to have been seized by Chinese troops, said to be under the Canton Government:

This morning's vernacular papers state that a meeting was convened last night to discuss means to protect the interests of shipowners whose boats run along the coast of Kwangtung.

It transpired that the s.s. "Wah Shan," which is under the Chinese hug, but which was registered as Chinese a few months ago, left the French port of Kwong Chow Wan about two days ago. Her cargo included over $30,000 in Canton subsidiary coins, also pigs, cattle, poultry, native sugar and mats. The report is that when this small ship was near the port of Yeungkong she was stopped by soldiers from Canton, who took away all the cargo and money.

[According to recent reports Youngkong is in the hands of Commander Chan Cheung-po who still flies the Chan Kwing-ming standard. Commander Chan is allied to General Tang Pun-yan of the southern peninsula and Hainan Island. His troops cannot be classified as “under the Canton Government” as the reverse is the case. Nor has anything been heard of Canton troops capturing Youngkong and district.]

Strike pickets at Kongmoon, brandishing Mausers and other firearms, boarded a Hongkong enrgo-boat and took away two of the crew for entering that port without a permit, but the junk was “resued” by an anti-Red commander.

Such is the gist of a report made to the Hongkong authorities by the boat owner. He sailed from Hongkong to Kongmoon with about 2,000 piculs of coal (over 100 tons). On arrival there the strike pickets forcibly took away his lience, although he had informed that the coal was for Commander Li Yat-ngok, erst while garrison commander of Kongmoon and one of General Leung Hung-kai's assistants.

Commander Li fled from Kong-moon on the approach of the Red vanguard from Canton, but he did not lose his coal. With the junk lying in the strikers' hands he sent and took the junk away by force. After the coal had been landed he sent the junk back to Hongkong.

headline: S.S. "HONAM."
text:
CARRIES OVER 1,000 PEOPLE TO-DAY.

On her return to Hongkong from Canton yesterday, the a.s. "Honam" brought back 10 passengers, including 15 Europeans. The efforts of the strike pickets to prevent anyone boarding the vessel from Canton who has not a permit have been redoubled and strong action is reported to have been taken in respect of sumpian owners who have not observed "orders." No difficulty is experienced in passengers getting ashore other than in benting down the sumpian owners who are reported to have demanded at first $10 for passage and eventually to have come down by competition to the regulation 20 cents. This morning the "Honam" left with over 1,000 passengers.

"Honum" for Canton have informed the "China Mail" that a proportion of the passengers were obviously students who had been refused re-admission to Hongkong schools and were, praumably, making their way to Canton. headline: STRIKE ECHO.
text: RUNAWAY STOKER CHARGED BY FIRE BRIGADE A Chinese stoker of the fire float who ran away in the early days of the strike was arrested in the New Territories and charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with desertion. Not being a sworn servant, the charge could not be maintained and, an amended charge, that of leaving without notice, is now being framed against the man.

headline: SLIGHTLY IMPROVED.
text:
LATEST COASTAL SHIPPING POSITION.

CERTAIN WAGE DECREASES.

The shipping situation as reflected in the record of entrances and clearances from the harbour remains practically unchanged. As it affects coastal trade more particularly, a representative of one of the best known firms in Hongkong who was approached by a “China Mail” representative this morning, said that there certainly appeared to be fewer ships laid up than at any time since the strike, but the freight being carried amounted to comparatively little. Things generally showed signs of a slight improvement but nothing like a return to normal yet.

Asked if it was not a fact that the 10 per cent. decreases in wages of seamen which had been enforced in certain cases was resulting in the better men leaving the coastal service and accepting more remunerative pay in other shipping concerns, the "China Mail" informant said that the decreases were not in any way representative of a vindictive attitude but were due to the force of economic circumstances. With little money coming in it was imperative that there should be economy. He could not speak for others, but his firm were getting all the men they wanted at the reduced rates,—in fact the men were very glad to get the jobs. As regards the situation generally as it affects shipping he was afraid that he could see no definite signs of vital improvement, although as the present state of affairs was affecting the merchants more and more considerably as time went on there might be hope of some move on their part. He thought they were genuinely doing their best to restore trade.

headline: WHAT NEWS IS GOOD.
text:
Interesting developments have followed, in quick succession, the acts of violence on the Chinese s.s. "Wah Shan" which was bringing treasure, livestock and a general cargo from Kwong Chow Wan to Hongkong.

Seen this morning, a representative of the Sui Lee "Co., owners, told a "China Mail" man that he had received "good news" regarding the "Wah Shan." On learning that the steamer had been taken to Shekki, his master had proceeded to Macao, en route for Chinshan, where negotiations had been opened with agents of the authorities directing the strike. The speaker was not in a position to say whether the cargo would be returned—and he gave the impression that beyond being interested in the safety of the ship, the cargo being, perhaps, more a matter for the shippers and/or consignees—but his information was that there was little anxiety as to the ultimate fate of the "Wah Shan."

headline: ILLICIT SMOKING.
text:
CHINESE CONSTABLES AS CUSTOMERS.

EQUIPMENT UNDER A BED.

A raid on an opium den at Stone Nullah Lane was described by Senior Revenue Officer G. Watt when five Chinese were charged before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Three of the inmates were Chinese constables who were indulging in a smoke when the officers entered. The equipment of one constable, who should have been on duty at the time, was found hidden under a bed. He was charged with misconduct and fined $25, or one month's hard labour in default. The others were fined $1 each for smoking.

The fourth accused was discharged and the other man was fined $50 for unlawfully keeping an opium divan.

This gentleman also informed the “China Mail” that the “Hok Canton”—whose fate was described in yesterday’s issue—was converted into a Kuomintang transport, later sinking near Swatow. Nobody has accounted for the shipload of opium taken from her by the “Wing Fung.”

headline: “HONAM'S” TRIPS.
text:
PASSENGERS NOT ALLOWED TO LAND.

PICKETS' STRONG CORDGN.

A surprise awaited the 700 odd Chinese passengers who travelled to Canton by the fourth trip of the s.s. "Honam" on Wednesday morning.

On the three previous trips rampans were allowed to come alongside the ship off Shameen and take the passengers' ashore, but on Thursday afternoon it was seen that the strike pickets had determined to prevent any of the passengers landing in Canton. Sampans were kept back at a distance from the ship and a strict watch was kept by the pickets to carry out their purpose. That the sampan crews had been threatened of the consequences was apparent from the fact that the few that came near the boat. disregarded the appeals of the passengers to take them away. A strike picket on a motor boat was overheard to say that if they wanted to return to Canton they must come by train.

headline: STRIKE EPISODE.
text:
CHIVALROUS PICKET AND CORPSE.

HONGKONG WOMAN'S STORY.

That Canton strike agents are openly working in Macao is one of the allegations made by a woman who has just returned to Hongkong from an up-country village.

Taking her children with her, she left Hongkong by ordinary steamer at the beginning of the strike. This week she decided that trouble would break out in Canton and that, after all, Hongkong was the best place. One reason for her thinking that disorder would break out in Canton was the fact that several imposing bridges of boats had been thrown across her part of the Canton River delta—this being one of the Bolshevik preparations to take Honam. These bridges were not taken down after the danger to Honam blew over, but Li Fook-lam's troops still remained in her village and their proximity was threatening.

headline: IMMENSE CLEARING HOUSE.
text:
She went by the regular tow-boat to Canton. From Canton she proceeded by other tow-boats to Heungshan, to Shekki and then to Chinshan which is outside the Macao border. Here the strike pickets have established an immense clearing house. People arriving there, to get into Macao, are closely scrutinised and questioned. If it is admitted that Hongkong is the ultimate destination the person is immediately sent back. Those who have the appearance of workers—of either sex—are also frustrated, being detained in large boats until passage is secured.

People wishing to go on to Macao must give an address in that Colony from which a (shop's) chopped guarantee will be forthcoming to the effect that the person concerned is a bona fide resident of Macao. This woman did not know a soul there, but she concocted an address on the spur of the moment. "In vestigators' left that same evening for Macao to look up the place mentioned as all others given by travellers on the same tow-boat. Some of the pickets were, so she told a "China Mail" reporter, chivalrous to the extreme. They pointed out that she had two very young children and that accommodation could not be found for them nor provision made for them. Some wanted to let her go as she did not look like an amah but others were adamant, and she had to pay 14 cents per head for a meal.

headline: BOUND WITH ROPES.
text:
Next morning the “investigators” returned. Those who were lucky enough to have had guarantees found for them were released. The address she gave could not be found and she had to stay another day.

Later in the morning she saw a country woman sneak up close to the pickets' headquarters where she turned over a man's corpse to see if it was that of her husband. Four villagers had run the gauntlet in getting vegetables down to Macao that morning. They carried firearms and one striker was killed. The smugglers' casualties were not known. This country woman had turned over the striker's dead body by mistake and she was instantly bound with ropes and imprisoned for being a spy.

The next morning it was decided to let the Hongkong woman go. Her money had been taken from her—she knew not where—and so a sampan was ordered to give her a free passage to Macao, whence she came over to Hongkong.

headline: LIKE WILD WEST.
text:
ENSATIONAL FRONTIER SHOOTING.

RAILWAYMEN KIDNAPPED.

Reading like an episode from a Wild West story is the report of how two European Police sergeants set out yesterday over the hills and dales along the New Territories frontier to cut off Chinese pickets who had carried off a number of men employed on the Kowloon-Canton Railway.

As telephoned in the most important feature of the report is that the police officers were sighted and fired at. They returned the fire and as far as they know, two or three of their adversaries were shot down. However, up to the time of the report, the kidnapped railwaymen had not been rescued.

The engine driver, stokers and possibly other employees on the branch line from Fanling to Shautukok have, for some considerable time, made it a practice of entering Chinese territory for a meal in the late afternoon. Shautukok, it should be explained, is the name given to a small township, at the almost extreme North-East corner of the Territories. It is such that there is a street of which one side is Chinese soil and the other British. Practically, it is possible to cross over from either side in a few yaces. During some fighting last year, some defeated troops hovered on the line and jumped into British ground when pressed, to be disarmed and sent on to Hongkong.

Entering an eating-house on the Chinese part of the street, the railwaymen were “arrested” by strike pickets. Perhaps they had no right to go there. At any rate, two or three were marched off, ostensibly by road to headquarters at Samchun Market but one stoker escaped.

Sergeant Knowles happened to be not far away and he set off with Sergeant Clark to intercept the prisoners. Along the frontier is a road which, according to the Convention by which the New Territories were leased to Britain, is accessible to both nations. Taking a route which would serve the purpose, the sergeants arrived at Lim Ma Hang where they took up a position. They then saw about twelve armed men approaching from the direction expected and the latter were escorting several prisoners who were in bonds.

Apparently the armed men spotted the sergeants and opened fire at them. Sergeants Knowles and Clark returned the fire and saw a number of their shots find the mark. But the remainder of the posse got away with their prisoners and the chase proved fruitless.

All steamers bound from Kwong Chow Wan to Macao must pass through the water between the two major Ladrone Islands, Le, Man Shan and Pu Toi, to enter the Great West Channel and then take the same route as the steamers from Hongkong. In the Ladrone group — famous for pirates in the days of the Portuguese settlers — outlaws found shelter there and the Bolsheviks will do so if the prey is worth while. These islands can be seen by the naked eye when nearing Macao.

headline: “NEAR” SWATOW.
text:
REPORTED ANTI-RED MOVES.

CHAN COMING BACK?

Reports are current in the Colony that there is considerable activity in such districts as Wai Loi, which form the hinterland of Swatow, generally known as the East River region.

Scattered here and there are different armies — varying in strength—under General Chan Kwing-ming's banner. United, they would be a formidable force. At present they are, according to a staff officer seen this morning by a "China Mnil" reporter, reorganising and resting.

It was even stated that the Bolshevik hold on Swatow had been checked but this may be premature. However, there seems little doubt that troops have been on the move, and to the advantage of the anti-Red forces.

The staff officer interviewed also told the "China Mail" that General Chan Kwing-ming was expected to sail from Shanghai very shortly, for Hongkong, to go up-country.

Certain significance is also attached to a number of very high military officers having passed through recently.

headline: MATE'S WAGES.
text:
ORDER 1N RESPECT OF S.S. "ANJOUT"

On the grounds that it had been impossible for the ship to do any business, the manager of the company owning the s.s. "Anjon," applied for a stay of execution in respect of an order made against him in the Supreme Court this morning. This was for the payment to the Chief Officer of the ship of wages amounting to $492.

Mr. T. Addis, instructed by Mr. W. B. Hind, was for the "plaintiff and the claim was not contested.

Chief Officer John Suiter Wilson formally proved the claim, stating that he joined the ship on July 11, and left on August 24, during which time he had been paid nothing. His study was $290 a month.

The Chief Justice refused the application for a stay of execution.

headline: THE WEATHER. / BALINTANG CHANNEL TYPHOON. / "FINE" FORECAST.
text:
First reported almost stationary and now stated to be inclining slowly Northward, a typhoon is near the Balintang Channel, which is the southern of the two passages which separate the Philippines from Formosa. It is through these channels, the Balintang and the Bashi, that most of the big typhoons that strike Hongkong, enter the South China Sea from the outer Pacific.

The position indicated is a good distance from the 300 miles radius. As the depression is going towards the North, the danger is not apparent.

At any rate, the forecast for the 24 hours ending at noon tomorrow reads: — North winds, moderate; fine.

For the Formosa Channel, the forecast is: — North winds, strong.

It is interesting to note that near Amoy yesterday the wind force registered about 7 (Beaufort scale) which is fairly strong blowing.

headline: TRAFFIC ACCIDENTS. / TRAMS AND LORRIES COLLIDE.
text:
In the report of week-end accidents appear two collisions between motor lorries and tram carsyone at Shaukiwan Road and the other at Wong Nel Chong Road near the race course. In each case the hand rails of the tram cars were damaged. A fracture of the right leg was sustained by an old Chinese woman when she was knocked down by a taxi at Poldulam Road. At Bulkeley Street, Hunghom, a Chinese woman emerged from the rear of a stationary motor bus and walked into a moving vehicle. She was knocked down and sustained slight injuries.

For throwing coal into the barbour with ulterior motives, a Chinese was sentenced to a month's hard labour at the Maine Court this morning.

headline: HONAM” BLINDED / CURIOUS SIDELIGHT ON CHINESE MENTALITY.
text:
VOYAGE 1 N°IDENTS.

Jinks and boats with eyes painted on the bows are by no means uncommon in Chinese waters. That the superstition which caused them to be placed there when the vessels were built so that they could see their way to port is still firmly implanted in the minds of some Chinese, is demonstrated by the trouble which has been taken to perform an optical operation on the s.s. "Honam."

Since the "Honam" was built some forty-five, years ago, two eyes, placed there in conformity with the old custom, have embellished the port and starboard sides, but during Saturday night the one on the port paddling box was removed. That this was done deliberately presumably in the hope that minus one eye the "Honam" would not be able to continue her runs to Canton is obvious from the thoroughness of the "operation," a panel nine feet by six and of considerable thickness, having been removed.

The "Honam" at the time was living at the local wharf of the Steambout Company after her latest voyage to Canton. The strike picketing experienced at Canton was more strict than ever, and not a Chinese passenger of the forty taken up was able to land. A special motor boat accompanied by an armed escort took off a number of missionaries returning to the Canton Christian College, and launches sent for other. European passengers wishing to land on Shumeen were not interfered with. The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyonk was one of the European passengers. His trip was undertaken in connection with the business of the steamboat company, but he could not say anything regarding the policy of the Company in connection with the future running of the "Honam" until he had discussed the matter at a meeting of the Board of Directors. For the present the "Honam" will continue her Hongkong-Canton service as usual.

Whilst in Shameen, Mr. Holyook and Mr. McI. Messer discussed the present situation with Sir James Jamieson, the British Consul-General.

headline: UNCHANGED. / CANTON'S TREATMENT OF FOREIGNERS
text:
NEED FOR TRENTINA.

What reads like a chapter from the early history of Canton in the days when foreign ships first appeared off the coast of the southern city and their crews went ashore to see the strange new land; is the news from Hongkong detailing the treatment of two British journalists who arrived at Canton on the British river steamer "Honum" on its first trip since the boycott was imposed. There on peaceful pursuits, the two men were quickly made the target of an ugly demonstration, surrounded by Whampoa endets with fixed bayonets, a heavy chain tightly clumped round their necks and were then imprisoned with fourteen Chinese strike-breakers. In the meanwhile crowds had gathered who clumored "Kill the foreigners," so incensed were they to find that two during Britons had entered the city. It was only with difficulty that the captors were persuaded to release the men and permit them to return to Shameen. The captives returned to safe territory to the accompaniment of profuse apologises on the part of the Chinese who excused themselves on the grounds that an ignorant, undisciplined mob was responsible.

This incident is but one of many proving conclusively (says the Shanghai Times") that Canton hasn't changed much in sentiment towards foreigners during the past hundred years or more. British pioneers in the latter part of the eighteenth century met with identical treatment as did the two British journalists, and the pages of history dealing with the early landing of foreigners in Canton are filled with the same type of incidents. It was this type of thing that made treaties with China absolutely necessary if China was to trade with other nations and if other nationals were to be guaranteed the slightest modicum of protection. At that time treaties guaranteeing such protection were necessary, and a necessary precaution which the years have in no way tended to destroy. Today they are as essential to the safe conduct of trade and legitimate business intercourse as they were in the eighteenth century. Those idealists who deny this do so simply because they are in complete ignorance of the facts, and are unable to appreciate the fact that Canton in 1925 is little removed from the Canton of Lord Macartney's day. What is true of Canton is true in somewhat lesser extent of other sections of China where anti-foreignism has been permitted to breed. A careful reading of the so-called 'inequal' travel will reveal that they are founded upon a basis of just protection for foreigners.

headline: FURIOUS DRIVING.
text:
EUROPEAN MOTORIST'S OFFENCES.

JATL WITHOUT OPTION.

Charges of furious driving of a motor car and falling to report an accident in which two Chinese pedestrians were injured at Queen's Road Central at 11.30 p.m. on September 7, were preferred against Mr. C. W. Mckenzie before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning.

At the previous hearing when the case was adjourned for developments in the condition of the injured persons who were taken to the Government Civil Hospital. Chief Inspector W. Kent stated that the injured persons were husband and wife and belonged to the working class. The woman had since been discharged from the hospital, but the man was still there and might be able to attend Court next week. There were other occupants in the car who insisted to the defendant on the desirability of stopping after the accident, but he asked them to mind their business as he was the driver of the car. One of the occupants then turned the steering wheel and brought the car back to the scene of the accident, but the defendant again drove away. His Worship informed Mr. F. G. Vaux, who appeared for the defendant, that a plea of guilty had already been tendered, and asked if he had anything to say.

Mr. Vaux said that he had been asked by the defendant to express extreme regret for the accident and his willingness to compensate the injured persons to the best of his ability. He considered that the defendant suffered from nervousness and was not possessed of that sense of the road which he ought to have in driving a car. The car was not a valuable one, but the defendant was prepared to sell it and use the money as compensation. Counsel asked for leniency by bringing to His Worship's notice that the defendant was a married man with two children.

The defendant bore out the pleadings of his counsel, and said that words failed to express his sorrow at the unfortunate accident. "I completely lost my nerves," he added, "and have since found out that I am not a fit person to drive a car." The records of the Traffic Department showed that the defendant had been fined $100 on two occasions last year for similar offences when he was riding a motor cycle and there was another conviction early this year. Under the circumstances His Worship said that he could not give the defendant the option of a fine in the present instance. The sentence was six weeks' hard labour and payment of $25 as compensation to the injured persons.

headline: PICKET'S LAXITY.
text:
NAMTAU'S FIVE DAYS' HOLIDAY.

Although only a temporary phase it is interesting to note reports of laxity in the work of strike pickets at two places giving access to Hongkong. People coming to Hongkong from Canton, via Shekki, Chinshan and Macao, report that when the tow-boat reached Chinshan (near the Macao border) no picket was to be seen on duty and everybody took sampans or ricshas to Macao without interference.

Yesterday it was reported in the vernacular papers that passengers were again coming by the steam-launch ferry direct from Namtau, where the notorious Chan Ping-sang is said to have declared five days' holiday!

headline: $10,000 START.
text:
MONEY

RETURNED CHINESE SUBSCRIBE

That even the uneducated class of Chinese is awakening to the danger of Bolshevism is evident from the action of certain overseas men who are now in Hongkong.

On such who made a fortune, estimated at a million dollars, in the F.M.S., is a native of the Wai Chow prefecture. He is over 60 years of age and dresses in the ordinary garb of black pongee silk. When a youth he went to Singapore to seek his fortune, and there, under the protection of the British flag, he became wealthy.

He is now convening a meeting of clansmen and other emigrants returned from the South, to raise a loan for the anti-Red cause. In an informal chat with several he opened the list with a fixed deposit receipt for $10,000.

Pointing out that the people who have the upper hand in Canton to-day are aliens—Russians or mercenary, invaders from other provinces—the old man urged the necessity of overthrowing “the traitors who are the running dogs of the Russians.”

Unless the Cantonese who have the real interests of their province and city at heart united, they would never get rid of the unscrupulous people who are trying to ruin China to serve their own selfish ends. He was too old to fight, but he would do what he could. Hence his gift of $10,000.

headline: MORE THAN 50,000.
text:
HOW MANY STRIKERS IN CANTON?

EXACT FIGURES GIVEN.

How many strikers are there still in Canton? Information obtained by the "Kung Sheung Yat Po" (a Hongkong vernacular paper) from Canton gives the total as 50,836 exclusive of 2,618, who worked for foreigners, whatever that may mean.

Details are given of each police district. Where there is a falling off of any considerable number, the deficit is put down to "returned to native villages." There is nothing about those who have come to Hongkong at the risk of their lives.

headline: GOING TO DOCK.
text:
“HONAM” TIMPORARILY CHASES SAILINGS.

PADDLE BOX DAMAGE

The s.s. "Homem," which for nearly a fortnight has maintained communication between Hongkong and Canton, being the only ship during that time to have carried the red ensign into the latter port, will have temporarily to cease sailings on account of damage done to the ship's paddle box as she lay at the buoy off Shameen in the course of the last trip. It was found as the ship was about to have that the buoy had fouled the paddle box and the assistance of a tug had to be obtained before it could be engaged.

The s.s. "Honam" was still at the wheel this morning but it was learned upon enquiry that she was about to proceed to dock. The Superintendent of the Stembont Company has made an examination, but the extent of the damage is not known. The arrangements as conceived at present are that she will still again us soon as repairs are effected.

The long arm of coincidence is seen at work in that the "eye" on the ship's paddle box, as already reported, was removed by presumably hopefully superstitious persons on Saturday night.

The passengers taken by the "Honum" on her last trip all left the ship, the foreigners by launches and motor bons, whilst a Chinese passenger jumped into the water and was not seen again. Chinese members of the crew state that in their opinion the strong current was too much for him and that he was drowned.

The "Homem brought to Hongkong 46 passengers, including 17 Chinese who either had passed or eluded pickets; also 43 bags of small and similar number of pockets of cargo.

headline: MORE FLOODS
text:
SHANTUNG CONDITIONS

(Reuter's Service.

Deking; Sept. 15.

In connection with the reported floods in Shantang, the Famine Relief Committee at Tsinonfu recently telegraphed to Peking stating that a dyke had broken, but reports regarding the damage and casualties are conflicting. It is known, however, that conditions are bad and relief work will be started soon.

headline: MAY 30 RIOT. / JUDICIAL INQUIRY NOTE
text:
POLICE CHIEF'S POSITION

The Senior Minister has happened the Foreign Office a note on behalf of the interested Powers stating that the Powers decided to request the British, American, and Japanese Governments to designate a jurist for the commission of enquiry in order definitely to clear up the unfortunate incidents of May 30 in Shanghai and expressing a hope that the Chinese Government will see fit to appoint a Chinese jurist to sit on the commission.

The note adds that the Shanghai Municipal Council have bound themselves to abide by the findings of the commission, and the Commissioner of Police, Mr. McEuen, will be suspended without prejudice until the completion of the inquiry.

The American Commissioner is Mr. Justice E. Finley Johnson, of the Philippine Supreme Court, and the British, Sir Henry Gollan, Chief Justice of Hongkong.

headline: Latest Reports
text:
A message from Casablanca states that General Lyautey has arrived there.

According to a Fez telegram evidently the reported capture of the Bibane heights was premature. The French artillery and aircraft bombarded this position yesterday. Otherwise all is calm. A message from Casablanca says that two Communists named Calvano and Brebant have been arrested on a charge of inciting the troops to mutiny. They will be tried by court martial.

headline: PRISONER'S FRIEND.
text:
ONE DOLLAR COSTS FIFTY

OFFENDING PRISON RUIES.

For extending his sympathies in the wrong direction a Chinese coolie found himself in the dock at the Central Magistracy this morning, the official charge reading “attempting to convey $1 to a prisoner.”

The accused visited the prison yesterday afternoon to see a man who was held on remand. He was observed by an Indian warder to throw something into the enclosure where the prisoners were kept, but it failed to get through the wire netting. On investigation it proved to be a one dollar note.

Captain Bloxham informed His Worship (Mr. R. A. D. Forrest) that unauthorised articles were often smuggled into the prison and it had been difficult to detect the carriers. He pressed for punishment which would serve as a warning to other offenders.

The accused, who pleaded guilty, was fined $50, or in the alternative two months' hard labour, the one dollar note going to the poor box.

headline: STUDENTS RETURN
text:
NEW UNIVERSITY TERM COMMENCES.

GOOD ATTENDANCE

As the day on which the University of Hongkong opens, to-day has held a certain amount of significance and there has been speculation as to the probable attendance at the various Halls. It was not anticipated officially that there would be a large number of absentees for statistics given recently respecting scholars at Government schools show that where it has been possible students have returned and in other cases they are desirous of doing so.

There anticipations were fulfilled this morning and a large percentage of students have enrolled for the winter term. Others who are prevented temporarily from getting to Hongkong have written expressing their intention of returning as soon as possible. It will be remembered that the University was in vacation during the trouble experienced in certain of the local schools and colleges and that the University is not called upon to prevent the return of any student, the only provision of the Government's policy affecting them being co-operation in the exclusion of "strikers."

Work in preparation for the orthocoming examination will process usual.

headline: RATHER STRANGE.
text:
RESTRICTIONS RELAXING

Surprise has been expressed at the manner in which people are once more being allowed to come to Hongkong from Namtau, the small port in Chinese territory, just beyond Deep Bay.

Two ferries ply between Nam-tau and Hongkong and they have been fairly well supported during the last two days, the first indication of this having been noted in yesterday's "China Mail."

Some think that the notorious Chan Ping-sang has a grievance against Canton and has relaxed the restrictions on travellers wishing to get to Hongkong, but other believe that the amount needed as "squeeze" for a passport has been reduced and this has tended to an increased turnover. It has been reported that at some times the strike pickets are not even functioning.

headline: PASSING THE TIME.
text:
RAID BY POLICE SPOILS FEAST.

GAMBLERS IN COURT.

A gambling den at Bowrington Canal Road was raided by Sergeant O'Donovan and a party of detectives last night when 21 persons were secured.

When charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning, only three of those arrested were present. The others had their bail money estreated.

It was stated in evidence by a district watchman that the raid was not put into execution until he had been a few minutes in the house and had observed one of the three men collecting the winnings, a part of which he dropped into a box.

The defendants claimed that they were employees of the Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Company, and having nothing to do until 10 p.m. they passed the time by playing "Pai Kau." The man who was charged with being the keeper of the gambling house explained that the few ten-cent pieces he dropped into the box was for the purpose of providing a feast after the game.

This story was disbelieved by His Worship, who imposed a fine of $75 on the keeper and $2 on the others. The money seized, amounting to $22, was confiscated.

headline: LINERS TO BE WITHHELD?
text:
Though two maize steamers have sailed and the Dutch vessel "Rietfontein" is taking mails and gold bullion from the Rand, the strike situation is becoming worse.

There are now 2,000 seamen ashore at South Africa. Hundreds are enjoying the beautiful environment of Table Mountain, playing football and cricket. Local Labour leaders are making public appeals for more playing outfits.

The fruit congestion at the docks, is very serious and the egg exporting season has just arrived. The captain, of the steamer "Athel Foam" has committed suicide at Durban, allegedly through being worried by the strike.

It appears that the “Port Curno,” mentioned earlier, was taken out by the officers, but the firemen refused to work, except back to Durban, where the strikers have now been accommodated in public halls and at the police station.

headline: OWNERS' BURDEN.
text:
Thirty-three overseas vessels of a tonnage of a third of a million are idle at Australian ports.

The liner "Trafford Hall" has sailed for England with a Lascar crew carrying a full complement of 86 passengers and £800,000 in specie.

Acting on official instructions the police have informed the captains of vessels that it is illegal to refuse to feed strikers and the Government holds the shipowners responsible for expenditure incurred to feed men forced ashore.

Fifty-one striking seamen have been arrested.

The Australian Labour Congress has issued a manifesto urging the workers in nowise to assist in carrying out deportation sentences in connection with the seamen's strike.

Brisbane, Sept. 16. The crew of the “Port Hobart” walked ashore, but the vessel has been manned by officers, fifteen engineers, three boys and four apprentices.

When the vessel sailed the crew standing on the wharf cheered lustily. The captain acknowledged this by raising his cap. SEVENTY BRITISH VESSELS IDLE.

London. Sent. 16.
