headline: “MORE SERIOUS.” / CANTON REPORT ON THE STRIKE.
text:
NOT "ANTI-FOREIGN."

Highly lauded by the "Canton Gazette" is a long survey on the recent situation in Canton by the correspondent of "an important news agency in North China."

The strike, strange to say, is becoming more serious owing to the strengthening of the strike organisation. It is hoped, however, that with the departure of the delegation, new developments in the strike situation may be expected. Very much depends on the nature attitude of Hongkong. Unfortunately she still demands intervention in Canton instead of pursuing a policy of reconciliation and mutual understanding. There is not the slightest trace of anti-foreignism in Canton. I learn from reliable sources that the Whampoa incident in which a Japanese launch was shot at with casualties already reported, has been settled in an amicable manner by both parties. Evidently neither side cared to give prominence to the incident. The blockade seems to have affected Canton very little. The import-export business is deeply affected, while the silk of this season has found a way out directly to Shanghai, it cannot be said that the problem of the export of silk from Kwangtung has been completely solved.

headline: BRITISH CARGO.
text:
UNAFFECTED BY WHAMPOA SERVICE.

HUROPE TARIFF RATES.

Enquiries made regarding the movement of cargo between Whampoa and Shanghai, to which reference has already been made, go to show that there has been no relaxing of the boycott against the import or export of British goods even where direct loading or unloading is done at Whampoa. So long as the present state of affairs continues at Canton the institution of indirect communication between Whampoa and Hongkong by way of Shanghai can therefore help but little, if at all, in the clearance of British cargo at present in godown in Hongkong. In so far as direct trade between Whampoa and Europe is concerned the purely British boycott is as rigid in its application, and two German boats are thought to have been the only ones to have loaded there for Europe since the present trouble. As, however, there was no direct loading by ocean steamers at Whampoa prior to the strike and boycott, some tariff rate was considered necessary by the shipping companies concerned in the event of there being any considerable movement of cargo between Europe and Whampoa direct.

headline: SNUB TO REDS
text:
LABOUR CONFERENCE DEFEAT.

COMMUNISTS NOT WANTED.

The Labour Conference adopted the Executive's recommendations against affiliation with the Communists by 2,600,000 against 480,000 votes rejecting the third Communist attempt to refer the matter back.

Complaints of the Communists that the Standing Orders were invoked to burke discussion, evoked an emphatic denial from Mr. Arthur Henderson, the Secretary who said the Executive considered it was not desirable to waste further time on a question which the Labour movement had already decided.

Mr. Harry Pollitt, Communist, declared that whatever the Conference did it could not keep the Communists out, adding that the Labour Party should be wide enough to include not merely those who dined at Balmoral, like Mr. Ramsay MacDonald or stayed on a yacht at Cowes with Lord Inchcape, like Mr. J. H. Thomas.

Mr. T. Bromley, of the locomotive Union, said the decision of the conference meant the beginning of a heresy hunt in the ranks of Trade Unions.

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald was ringingly cheered when he told the Communists to come out of the Trade Unions and propagate their opinions honestly outside.

headline: SEIZED SHIP.
text:
PORTUGUESE BOAT AT CANTON.

NOW IN STRIKERS' HANDS.

In the early days of the strike the s.s. "Foo Chebng" was "abandoned" at Pakkai, the port of Kongmoon, through the native crew deserting.

Subsequently a report went round that the ship had been seized by the strikers. A Portuguese naval vessel from Macao was stated to have failed to bring the boat back and the "Foo Cheong" was last heard of in Kongmoon.

Saturday's "Canton Gazette" says:—Owing to the transportation of "undesirable" goods the s.s. "Foo Cheong" was detained recently by the pickets at Canton and for various reasons, the case has not been settled.

The same report says that the Ning Hoi Co. wishes to charter the steamer from the strikers, for the Canton-Wuchow run, promising $1,200 a month as charter hire, and stipulating the services of 20 pickets on board "for protection." The “Foo Cheong” was well-known on the Canton-Macao run prior to being superseded by the s.s. “Hang Cheong!” It is under Portuguese registry and when the strike started, was put on the Kongmoon-Macao run till it was forced to tie up through the crew going ashore on being intimidated at Pakkai.

"Wah Shan" Sequel.

Negotiations are continuing for the release of the Chinese s.s. "Wah Shan" which was seized by Canton while conveying livestock from Kwong Chow Wan to Hongkong. According to one report the owners may be willing to pay a few thousand dollars as a "fine" and it is likely that an amount may be named by the strikers holding the ship.

NEWS WANTED OF MISSING SHIP. "YUE YING WA" MYSTERY. "Upright and honourable men are requested to take note of an advertisement in the vernacular papers, asking for news of the missing son. "Yue Ying Wa" which has been posted missing for over a month. The vessel was on a voyage from Hohhot to Houtong and has not been heard of after Contacting from the same port early in November. The vessel said to have perished by the sea in the same hand.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE / SHANGHAI TRADE.
text:
The result of the year's trade at Shanghai came as a surprise to the mercantile community in general, says Mr. L. de Lana. Statistical Secretary of the Maritime Customs, in his 1924 report. Throughout the year there had been a feeling of depression, trade was reported as dull and featureless, profits as unsatisfactory, and yet the Shanghai Customs Returns show, in round numbers, a revenue collection of Hk. Tls. 27,500,000, an increase on the 1923 collection of no less than Hk. Tls. 3,640,000, the bulk of which—Hk. Tls. 3,470,000—was derived from import duties alone. Furthermore the gross value of the import trade was Hk. Tls. 488,000,000, an increase on the preceding year of Hk. Tls. 65,000,000. It should be noted also that the greater portion of the increase in revenues—Hk. Tls. 2,800,000—was reached during the first six months of the year, which represented a period of comparative peace and freedom from political disturbances. Trade during the September and December quarters was much less satisfactory, in consequence of political complication and fighting in and around the port.

To enter into a minute study of the causes which contributed to the expansion more especially of the import trade and to the discrepancy existing between the good results achieved—from the point of view of Customs revenue—and the general fdeling of dissatisfaction prevailing in the mercantile community would be beyond the limits and scope of this report; never-the-less, a brief enumeration of some of the causes which may be taken as an explanation of the situation will not be amiss.

In the first place, it should be remembered that Shanghai is the principal entrepot of China and that not all the trade that comes to it is for the local market; a good share of it is destined from the outset for other trade centres, principally the northern and Yangtze ports. In fact, the total value of foreign imports re-exported to Chinese ports was Hk. Tls. 174,000,000 which, when the value of foreign re-exports to Hongkong and foreign countries—Hk. Tls. 12,700,000—is added, leaves a net value of foreign imports into Shanghai of about 301 million tnels, and increase on the 1923 figures of about 57 millions.

Secondly, German competition, which had been practically extinguished during the European War and for some time afterwards is now reviving: thirdly, the Chinese are said to be doing more direct trade, instead of through the intermediary of foreigners, and several large Chinese firms have their own buyers in Europe and America; and, lastly, the cessation of the anti-Japanese boycott on the Yangtze and at some of the coast ports has enabled Japan to take a more active part in the import trade of China, which, in her case, was favoured also by the low value of the yen.

The report and accounts having been in your hands, for some days, with your permission I will take them as read. In spite of the continued depression in shipping and shipbuilding during the years under review the net profits is just over Tls. 100,000 more than the previous year. An interim dividend of 5 per cent. was paid and it is now proposed to pay a final dividend of 9 per cent. and carry forward Tls. 172,444,50. It was considered unnecessary to increase the reserve account which now stands at Tls. 1,250,000 or the depreciation account standing at Tls. 750,000, but it is felt that a somewhat larger carry forward is necessary owing to the present strike, which has now been in force amongst the dock company's Chinese staff for over six weeks. With regard to the land belonging to the company, your directors have come to the conclusion, after very careful consideration, that we have a greater area than required and that the land between the International Dock and Cosmopolitan Dock can best be spared. The Cosmopolitan Dock requires lengthening and repairing and two schemes have been considered:

-Lengthening and repairing the Cosmopolitan Dock, leaving for sale an area of 110 mow between the Dock and International Dock with a river frontage of 1,300 feet.

2.—Making a new Cosmopolitan Dock alongside the International Dock, leaving for sale an area of 140 mow with 1,800 feet river frontage.

Both these plots of land have a deep water frontage, in fact as deep as any in the harbour, and we are now prepared to consider offers for either; plans being obtainable from the manager, Mr. Burns. We are not in any immediate hurry to dispose of this land but the decision as to whether we shall remove or merely repair Cosmopolitan Dock will be dependent, to a certain extent, upon the offers received. If necessary we are prepared to consider part of the purchase price being covered by a mortgage. In order to increase our ability to handle every class of work, improve the quarters for employees, and generally improve the value of your property, we have authorized the expenditure of about Tls. 500,000 spread over a year or 18 months; this will considerably reduce our cash on deposit and in current account, and as we do not consider a return of capital under Tls. 25 per share worth while, the matter of reducing the capital will have to be left in abeyance until the land near the Cosmopolitan Dock is sold. On behalf of the directors, and I feel sure I may say the shareholders as well, I should like to thank Mr. Burns and the staff for the able and loyal manner in which they have carried out their work during the year under review and I trust the bonus and the provident fund, which is at last in proper working order, will be appreciated. In this connection we have decided to appoint Mr. W. S. Burns, who has been with the company 26 years, managing director, a step which I am sure will be appreciated both by our clients and staff. Before closing I consider it advisable to say a few words regarding the strike and prospects of future business. That the former is caused by agitators is beyond question and the fact that we have received numerous letters from Chinese employees who have been with us for 40 or 50 years, stating that they are perfectly satisfied with their pay and the treatment they have received, is sufficient testimony to the fair manner in which the company has dealt with them in the past, and the fact that but for these agitators they would never have ceased work. It is difficult to deal with the prospects for the future but a good deal of work is waiting to be done directly the strike is over and our strong financial position enables us, even at the present time, to look forward to the future with equanimity if not with optimism.

headline: السلام عليهم السلام عليهم
text:
CAPITAL AND THE EAST.

Mr. Smillie, M.P., speaking at a Cumberland L.L.P. rally at Keswick on August 3, said he sincerely hoped that a Labour Government would never again take office without power. He did all he could to prevent the Party doing so last time. They were told they should be Constitutionalists, and not go outside the Constitution or be rebels, but when they came into their own and the country returned to the House of Commons sufficient men and women to form a Labour Government with a majority of 20 or 30, and they began to touch the real issues, to take the first step, the taking over of the hand, and began to nationalise mines and railways, the talk about Constitutionalism would fall through, and the other side would throw Constitutionalism to the winds in favour of raising the Army against them. He believed in trying to get some of the palliatives--improved old-age pensions, widows' pensions, protection for life and limb, and a minimum wage--as long as capitalism continued, but they wanted to wipe out capitalism.

A prominent mineowner had said that so long as British coal had to complete with coal produced in other countries, it would have to be produced under similar conditions to those under which it was produced in other countries. That was the owners' idea with regard to coal in the mointime, but it applied to every other commodity produced in the country. In India coal was being developed with British money, for some amount of which was invested by British coal owners, and there were and children were working under the conditions they were working under in Britain 80, 90, or 100 years ago. The little children were carried into the Indian mines, and they and their mothers worked for twopence and the price a day, and for ten hours a day, and aground. India might be a competitor with British coal some day, as it was further developed by British-money and ealdowners' money, and the outlook for the British miner, his wife and children, was that they would have to bring themselves down to the conditions under which coal could be produced elsewhere, to the standard of good labour. That was the outlook under capitalism, not merely in coal-mining, but also in every other industry. Capital had lost all nationality, and went wherever it could go the cheapest labour to harness to its machine, and it was now beginning to exploit the East.

headline: GFRMAN CREDIT
text:
Hamburg: July 1.—Moscow reports that Krupps Germain Werft at Kiel, and the Deutsche Werft at Hamburg have offered to the shipping department of the Soviet Government to build ships for Russia on a basis of allowing 90 per cent. of the contract price to be paid out of profits for the ensuing 10 and, if necessary, 15 years.

The full reconstruction programme of the Soviet shipping department is said to provide for the construction of 208 new units, with a total capacity of 733,000 tons.

According to the Russian press it was stúbed at a meeting in Moscow that the present Russian mercantile fleet has inherited from its predecessor, the State Mercantile Fleet, a deficit of 4,242,000 rubles, in addition to which it is notorious that the present working capital has for some time past been quite inadequate. The Soviet administration with its usual optimism hopes to do a great deal with the promise of 1,800,000 rubles placed at the disposal of the shipping board by the council of labour and defence.

headline: Other Credit Inclinations.
text: This inclination on the part of Germany to give credit to Russian customers is also seen in the case of German exports to Russia. According to the Fremdenblatt, practically all the goods bought in Germany for Russia either through the medium of the Commercial Mission in Berlin or by the agents of the various Soviet States trusts and syndicates are purchased on the credit system. The German exporting firms are as a rule content with a cash payment of 50 per cent or in some cases of only 25 per cent of the sum due, the remainder being payable on short term credits. The reality is that the German export trade in Russia rises and falls according to the willingness of the seller to with for his money. It is estimated that on an average goods to the value of 2,000,000 gold marks are as present being exported each working day from Germany.

headline: CHINA MISSIONS.
text:
FACTORS LEADING TO PRESENT UNREST

ARCHIDEACON BARNETT'S COMMENT.

No-one is better qualified to write on the present and past situation in South China as it affects missionary work than the late Archidencon, the Ven. E. J. Barnett, who devoted over 20 years of his life to such service. The extent to which mission work is affected by recent disorders in China has already been referred to, also the decision of missionary bodies to hand over supervision, temporarily at any rate, to Chinese, and it is interesting to note that Archidecon Barnett has contributed to the August number of the "Church Missionary Outlook" an illuminating article on the factors leading up to the present unrest. The author of Church Notes and News in the "Telegraph" comments as follows on this article:—

Archdeacon Burnett takes the view that the present serious crisis is more deep-seated than the Boxer outbreak, and more dangerous, because there is recognised reasonableness in certain of the demands. The chaotic condition of robber-ridden China, under so many independent military rulers, doubtless favours the anti-foreign agitator. But the root cause, he points out, is a hideous sense of humiliation which, if it is to be removed, demands (so they are taught) desperate measures. Neither economic nor industrial conditions alone would have produced the present upheaval. It is an attempt to wipe out what is regarded as an intolerable national reproach. The means being used to that end are improper and illegal, but they are prompted by a new and sinister influence which has of late worked its way into Chinese politics.

headline: account for much.
text:
In judging the Chinese today the archdeacon warns us not to forget that they can boast an historic past which is millennium older than that of the Western peoples whom they regard as their oppressors. They are conscious of capabilities and intellectual powers which will well compare with those of others. It is therefore mental agony to the later educated generation to realise that their great country, with all its immeasurable possibilities, hags so far behind Japan and the Western peoples in their forward march. For their backward position they blame (not altogether justly) the Great Powers, who in the past have imposed upon them trenties which they now demand shall be revised. The archdeacon concludes his review of the position by saying that it is not all evil is certain, for the motive is one which all fair-minded Christians must respect. During the past decade we ourselves learned anew what patriotism means. Patriotism is now the dynamic of Chinese discontent. Without belittling the students' serious mistakes, it is through the exercise of Christian virtues—love, sympathy, patience—that we, with unfailing prayer, can best set forward God's own remedy for China's present troubles.

Writing from Shaolisingfu, Chekingu, under date June 30, the Rev. T. Grant ends an account of local conditions by saying: "Our Chinese Christian fellow-workers and friends remain friendly to us; though taking the Chinese point of view in the Shanghai affair. I think they are beginning to see our point of view more clearly now, as the truth comes out. I believe that none of the Chinese newspapers has published, true accounts, with all the facts, of the troubles, and, consequently, a great many lies have been believed by the Chinese, much to the detriment of the good names of the foreign sojourners in the country."

London, July 25.—Figures just published by Lloyds Register of Shipping show that whereens British shipbuilding output has declined, more work is in hand on the Continent.

The total world tonnage under construction, viz., 2,369,831 tons, shows a decrease of 27,000 tons as compared with the previous quarter, and is over 1,000,000 tons below the pre-war record.

The motorship is steadily gaining headway, equalling 98 per cent. of the steam tonnage, although British yards have only 58 per cent. motorships on hand. On the other hand some countries, like Denmark, Germany, Holland, Italy and Sweden, are going in largely for motorships, the combined totals for these five countries being 216,257 tons of steamers, as against 645,600 tons of motorships.

The horsepower of the marine oil engines building in Denmark, for example, amounts to 125,950, compared with 2,100 horsepower of steam engines. Out of 294,800 horsepower of marine engines building in Germany no less than 227,000 is for Diesel engines, there being 57 sets of Diesels building in that country. Italy shows only 10 sets building; the enormous powers of the large motorships ordered there recently having evidently not yet been started.

Eight sets of 14,790 horsepower are under construction in the United States, and as only two motorships are building in that country they evidently represent some advance work, and possibly interesting research.

Sweden has more Diesel engines building than any other country in the world, there being 89 of 57,000-horsepower, but the average size is rather lower than that of other countries.

There is, however, general stagnation in the shipbuilding countries, with a few exceptions and recent statistics such as the freight index number of the Chamber of Shipping, the laid-up tonnage returns and the import

and export figures show that there is little likelihood of any immediate improvement.

headline: SILVER AND ELECTRO-PLATE
text:
Sheffield, July 29. — The Sheffield silver and electro-plate trades are passing through dull times again. The usual summer lethargy has been accentuated by a scarcity of big business from the colonies, which have been good buyers for some years. In the case of Australia the falling-off is most marked, especially in the better qualities of plated ware. Some firms who cater for buyers of cheaper qualities have booked some business with Australia, but from the point of view of value the trade has fallen off considerably. One of the striking features of the trade, both in electro-plate and nickel silver is the collapse at last of the phenomenal demand for spoons and forks. For over three years the resources of the factories have been taxed to meet the huge demand both for the home trade and export. Makers could not account for the extraordinarily heavy demand, and now they are at a loss to understand why it has collapsed. It had been sustained so long that they believed it had come to stay. Sterling silver sells extremely slowly. Best quality: electroplate, because of the relatively high price of nickel, is prohibitive in price to the average buyer, while electro-plate. Britannia metalware seems to meet the demands of the majority in these days of cutting down expenses. Stainless nickel has come to stay although progress with the sale of best qualities is slow. headline: ATTRIBUTED TO OWL8.
text:
"At last they died away—those awful cries—in one long inearthly wait, I rolled out more dead than alive, got home and went to bed. I did not then know there was such a thing as a devil-bird in the Island. I certainly thought some wretched girl was being killed. I never slept a wink, but got up before the sun, and went down to the next village to rout the villains out, and there got to know all about it. " "You see," said the headman, "lift night one of our women died in labour, and her spirit went at once into a devil-bird, which must have been sitting handy. So when your Majesty hears a devil-bird again, lie still, for it is always the soul of a woman in panga, and it's best to give it a wide berth."

What then is the Devil Bird? So far, the consensus of recorded opinion seems to be that it is an Owl—the Brown Wood Owl ("strix indrancee"), Tennant, Layard, Kelaart, Legge, Neville and many others accepted this view; and today if you ask at our museum to be shown the Devil Bird, starix indrancee will be the bird pointed out to you.

Tegge is very unconvincing in his attempts at proving the bird's identity; and Neville seems to be tied up rather in knots, seriously giving as possible solutions of the cry. "The dreadful shrieks, like those of a young child, or those made by frogs in the jaws of rat-makes or in the cruel talons of a night hawk."

headline: GRIM SEUGGESTIVENESS.
text:
It is the human note in these series that is their appalling feature; the one that of a lost soul, the other that of a person being garotted. What wonder the villagers in the localities the bird accustomed to hunt, hold it in holy terror, and its cry as of ill omen. So much so that if it be heard when a person is seriously ill, his relations will not bother much about him, but leave him to his fate, saying intervention is useless. They will run away from the sound, if it be heard close and stay hushed indoors.

There are scores of people in Ceylon who have shot the Devil Bird while it cried: only they are not the people who write about such things. I myself know half a dozen of them and the descriptions of every one were in agreement.

Only four days ago I asked a man who had spent a great part of his life in the forests whether he knew what the Devil Bird was like.

"It is an Engle with a crested head," he promptly replied.

"How do you know?" I asked. "I shot one while it was "hooting" and ogling on a large dead tree one moonlight night by my camp," he said. "I not only shot it, but ate its flesh to prov to my terror-stricken coolies, who ran away when they first heard the cry, that it was no demion but a bird." That is the kind of evidence I have repeatedly elicited from reliable informants.

Now the question is: Are the two cries—the long drawn hoo-oo, and the guttural chortle, so unitative of a person being strangled—made by the same bird or by different species?

The cry of the Devil Bird is generally heard early in the night, at midnight, and towards dawn. The boo cry can be heard far the

guttural. gurgle-only-op-close-que- cers.

Two Devil Birds are seldom or never seen in company. While foraging singly during the day, they apparently roost together at night, but often perhaps wander away startled by what power who knows, waking the forest with their unearthly cries.

headline: LOCAL STRIKE.
text:
SHANGHAI PAPER'S COMMENT.

WHY WE MUST WIN.

in some respects, are really separate and apart, remarks "Shipping and Engineering" (Shanghai). While the peg on which the excuse for the Shanghai strike was hung was the Nanking Road shooting affair, there has been no such excuse for the walk-out at Hongkong, and the affair has been from the beginning; an openly anti-British movement, engineered and financed by the Bolshevist element which is so powerful in the Province of Kwangtung, and in Canton particularly. With the foreigners in China—and the British and Japanese particularly—already experiencing great trouble in regard to the Shanghai strike and the general stoppage of shipping, the Bolshevists at Canton were not slow in utilising the opportunity of striking another blow at Great Britain through, the medium of the great port of Hongkong. It will be remembered that on June 12 the Yunnanese troops who had been in charge of Canton for so long were overwhelmingly routed by the Bolshevist forces, under the wing and guidance of Soviet emissaries, and that as a result of that victory a horrible revolting massacre of the defeated Yunnanese took place in Canton. It is well known that the Seamen's Union (of Chinese) which has a branch in Shanghai has its headquarters at Canton, and that the leaders of that Union are frankly and avowedly Bolshevist-inclined. It is perhaps hardly to be wondered at, therefore, that when the Bolsheviks assumed full and unfittered control of the Kwangtung capital they should take the first opportunity of adding to the trouble in those parts by engineering a general strike of all kinds of workers in Hongkong. The machinery for such a move was, apparently, all ready, and the strike commenced to take serious effect in Hongkong on June 19/20, and quickly embraced all of the essential and non-essential services affecting the Colony, including the most important of all, shipping. In a short few days the commerce of the port was practically tied up; all manner of Chinese employees, from workers in Government departments to houseboys, dockyard workers and seamen walked out, or, rather, went out under the duress of intimidation; and at the end of the month Hongkong, as Shanghai, was carrying on as best it could—and a very good best, be it understood—with foreigners (including Americans and other nationalities), doing their utmost and taking part in all manner of services, protectional, governmental and commercial, in order to keep things going. And so the situation is at the end of June: Strikers in all departments of activity in the Colony, trade disorganised and every foreigner doing his best to help to carry on. The Hongkong strike is wholly one where the forces of intimidation have been supreme. It is certain that not one per cent. of the men out have wanted to go on strike, or that they have any serious grievance against their employers, or the Hongkong Government, or the British people generally. It is simply a move in the gigantic Bolshevist scheme to get China under domination, to ruin foreign trade with the country and to abrogate foreign influence. To the ends of such a scheme, the paralyzation of the commercial activity of Hongkong is essential, and there is no doubt that, were the present strike to realise the

and there is no doubt that, were the present strike to realise the hopes of the Bolsheviks who have engineered it, it would constitute a real, a definite and a valuable step in the ruination of foreign influence in, and foreign trade with China. The Government of Hongkong, however, is living up to its trust, and the foreign inhabitants of the Colony are supporting that trust with every means at their disposal. The struggle may be a long-drawn-out one, but that the forces of law, order and sanity will eventually prevail, and that the strikers will return to their employment chastened and disillusioned, and thankful once more to work under British protection, is inevitable. Let us hope that that time will not be too long in coming.

headline: NATIVE DANCES.
text:
BASIS OF A NEW HEALTH SYSTEM.

Native dances as done by native men and women in North and South America, Australia, Africa, and other parts of the world form the basis of a new health system which a New Zealander, Mr. F. A. Hornibrook, and his wife are urging the civilised world to adopt.

Forty-six doctors and a number of eminent scientists attended as demonstration in London, when, after a paper read by Mrs. Hornibrook on the scientific side of the theory, a Maori from New Zealand gave examples of the original dances, and Mr. Hornibrook demonstrated exercises based on them and adapted for civilised men and women with little time to spare.

The strengthening of the abdominal wall is the end to which the system is adapted, and it is claimed to have exceptional results in the treatment of intestinal troubles.

"These native dances are really a system of physical education which, judged by its material results or judged by its hygienic effects, is far in advance of anything which the Europeans now have." Mrs. Hornibrook told a "Daily News" representative: "Yet we Europeans in our insolent conceit, suppose such dance exercises were merely grotesque antics, un-becoming gestures, without any survival-value-of-hygienic-useful-ness."

Modern civilised dancing is not enough." Mr. Hornbrook added. "It moves the shoulders and the legs, but the middle part of the body, the all-important part, no-missing rigid."

headline: MORE COME OUT.
text:
STUDENTS PAY WAGES

Slightly over a hundred servants are now on strike at the British Legation, including some of the clerks as well as domestics.

The students are picketing the North and West gates to prevent servants entering the Legation Quarter and are also intimidating the families of servants living in the Legation Quarter with the object of compelling the latter to quit.

The strike has evidently been planned for a long time, and a considerable sum has been collected for the purpose. All strikers have been paid a month's wages by the students.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs so far outwardly appears to have done very little to end the strike, but the British Legation is hopeful of an early settlement. Up to the present there is no sign of the strike spreading to the employees of other British residents in Peking.

It is understood that at a meeting of students, this afternoon, it was decided to attempt to induce all Chinese, in foreign employ in Peking, to go on strike.

headline: Number Increased.
text:
The number of Legation strikers increased yesterday and the employees of the Legation Electric Power House walked out early this morning, bringing the number of strikers to over 200.

The strikers' committee has passed a resolution, stating that their object is to make the British Charge d'Affaires and the British Government realise their mistaken policy in China and arouse the patriotic sentiments of the Chinese people.

A Bureau has been opened at the National University, where employees of any foreigners in Peking, desirous of striking, may register and receive a month's wages. But, hitherto, practically there has been no response. The Legation officials are still optimistic that a settlement will be reached very shortly.

headline: TO FIRE. / MANY KILLED AND WOUNDED.
text:
The Chinese police and military yesterday were compelled to fire on striking millworkers, wounding eight, mostly in the legs.

Many were killed and wounded and three hundred arrested to-day when Chinese guards were compelled to fire on a very large crowd on the scene of yesterday's shooting. No details are at present available.

The "Peking and Tientsin Times" reports that it is was believed that a settlement had been reached in the strike of the mill-workers, and the police were accordingly withdrawn. However, trouble broke out again yesterday, following the efforts of agitators from the native city, who were sent to the mills and the Russian Bund to endeavour to cause a strike among the workers of the British-American Tobacco Company.

Some of the millworkers were very reluctant to strike but were intimidated by strikers armed with sticks and stones. Strong police guards were sent to the mills, and were later reinforced by a hundred Fengtien soldiers.

All the afternoon the strikers formed processions, making threats. Shortly after six o'clock the temper of the crowds became uglier and stones were thrown at the police. Attempts were made to rush the mills, culminating in an attempt to rush the police and military cordon at the mill outside the Belgian Concession. The guards then fired, wounding eight. A Foreign eye-witness states that about two hundred shots were fired into the crowd which dispersed immediately. The situation is at present quiet.

headline: COTTON MILLS. / SHANGHAI STRIKERS NOT SATISFIED:
text:
The chairman at a meeting today of the General Labour Union stated that the agreement reached on August 12 by which the workers of the Japanese cotton mills were to return to work had not satisfied the labourers.

After discussion it was decided that operatives would not resume work unless, inter alia, one-third strike pay was granted them and their wages increased by ten per cent.

headline: A PLANNMD THEFT.
text:
The thieves penetrated into the Treasury from one of the rooms just above. Masons and painters had been working here, and their implements were scattered about. In one part of the room a large wooden box seemed placed negligently, and it appears that here one of the robbers had been working for days making a hole large enough for a man to pass. They probably remained inside the Sacristy on Friday evening, and during the night left the rope ladder through the opening, and rapidly carried off what they could. They must have been two or three in number, and seem to have been suddenly disturbed by some alarm, as they left without carrying away other objects they had already prepared to steal, and one monstrance was found broken up. Luckily, they seem to have had little artistic discrimination, as, apart from the ring of St. Peter, they overlooked many other far more precious objects and things of great historical value. As suspicion falls strongly on the workmen, several masons and painters who had been working in the room just above the Treasury have been arrested and are being examined by the police.

The Robbery has caused a paid impression in Rome, and especially in the Vatican. At nine o'clock the Pope was informed, just before he was about to receive the Cardinal-Secretary, and when Cardinal Gasparri appeared his Holiness spoke to him in bitter terms on this sacrilege committed. He requested Cardinal Gasparri to go and see what had been stolen and inform him. At noon Cardinal Mairy del Val appeared and made an inspection of the Sacristy and Treasury, when the police were on the spot, and conversed for a long time with them. The masonry through which the robbers broke is nearly 8ft. thick, and it is supposed they took at least five or six days to open the hole. In the evening the police stated that seven workmen had been arrested.

headline: STRIKE NEEDS: / HONGKONG'S FLOGGING ORDINANCE. / COMMONS QUESTIONS.
text:
In the House of Commons, on July 21, Mr. R. Morrison (Co-op), Tottenham, N.) asked the Secretary for the Colonies whether he was aware that the Hongkong Legislative Council had recently passed an Ordinance authorising the Governor to put into practice the method of flogging in the case of Chinese pickets and others who were attempting to intimidate would-be workers in connection with the present shipping strike; and, in view of the effect which such authority, if used, would have upon anti-British feeling in China, would he say what instructions he had given to the Governor upon this matter.

Major Ormsby-Gore (Under-Secretary for the Colonies) replied that the Governor of Hongkong had reported that the Legislative Council of Hongkong had recently passed an Ordinance validating an emergency regulation which permitted flogging for intimidation. No such punishment had been inmited, the existence of Ordinance having proved a sufficient deterrent. Previously to that there had been two murders and a case of bomb-throwing.

Mr. Morrison: Does not the right hon. gentleman think the promulgation of this order may have an effect on anti-British feeling?

Major Ormsby-Gore: I am quite sure the first intention of the Governor of Hongkong is to protect the lives of innocent people. The Governor is supported by the Chinese members of the Legislative Council.

Mr. W. Thorne: Would not another kind of punishment serve?

Major Ormsby-Gore: In a time of emergency we ought not to interfere with the discretion of the Governor and of the Legislative Council.

Lieut.-Commander Kenworthy (L. Hull, Central): Do not these Ordinances have to be approved by the Secretary of State?

Major Ormsby-Gore: No, not in an emergency of this kind. This was done entirely on local responsibility. We have telegraphed to the Governor that we would support him in any measure necessary to protect the lives of the people.

Colonel Appln (U., Enfield): Is the Governor not merely following the example of General Gordon? Mr. Beckett (Lab.-Soc., Gateshead): In every industrial dispute

there is the allegation of intimidation. Where is this to end? Major Ormsby-Gore: This is a case of people coming in from outside, some armed, and endeavouring to interfere with people trying to follow their lawful vocations.

Sir William said that he was quite cravined that the modern idea of working seven or eight hours a day would do nothing more than keep men in the middle rut of life, and they would never get out of it. He urged the boys not to slouch through the last two or three years of school life, wondering in a vague sort of way what they were going to do, and imagining that the "Governor" or the "Old Bean", would decide for them, and do what was best. Boys should think for themselves what they were best capable of, and what line of life would be best for themselves and for the country. He warned them against shifting and drifting from one profession to another.

There are more vacancies for a ten-thousand-a-year man than there are for a two-pound-a-week man, because there are practically no vacancies for the latter. But the big jobs were not for the man who would only work the ordinary hours and was content with the ordinary trade union wages. Business people wanted the young man who was not hide-bound, the man who would devote his whole soul to his work, and that was the man it was so difficult to get.

Emphasising the necessity for character, Sir William remarked: "It is no use having a first-class brain if there is a second-class character behind it. Speaking as a business man, I think a first-class character and a second-class brain will carry you a good deal further than a first-class brain and a second-class character." (Cheers).

headline: BRITISH IN CHINA.
text:
HORNE'S CONFIDIN OUR POLICY.

Sir Robert Horne, M.P., speaking at an East Lothian Unionist Fête at Gosford Grounds, Haddingtonshire, said the uprisings in Shanghai were due to the persistent and assiduous efforts made by the Soviet Government of Russia against, etabl Government in every part of the world. The Soviet recognised that the chief opponent and the greatest obstruction to the theory of Communistic Government was Great Britain. If they could get rid of the influence of Great Britain in the world, they would have done more than by any other effort to establish their hateful disastrous theories throughout the whole world.

"They have been striving now," said Sir Robert, "for the last four years in the face of very solemn obligations under a Treaty, which I made with them myself to upset our Government in India, and to set the whole of the East aflame. Happily, they have entirely failed, but in China they have found elements which are more easy to work upon, and to-day you find the ministers of this great Soviet Republic of Russia boasting of the attack which they are making against our interests in China, and asserting that the disturbances that we have already seen are only a poor rehearsal of the massacres which they hope to see in the future.

It is for us to see that the defence of our citizens there is made secure. We can thank Godt o-day that we have a Government in power with a proper appreciation of the situation and we can thank Heaven, too, for our knowledge that whatever happens, no prejudice in favour of this disastrous system which has destroyed Russia will prevent the Government taking all the adequate means in their power for the safety of our British fellow subjects. Urging the need for trade development, Sir Robert said he welcomed the chance of peace in Europe which had been brought nearer by the great Pact which Mr. Austen Chamberlain had been endeavouring to make with other countries. The greatest hope of the country for the future was in the great Dominions and possessions which they enjoyed in other parts of the world. It was for them to encourage the union of Great Britain in political and commercial matters.

headline: VIENNA RIOTS.
text:
FOLIOEN QUEEL ZIONIST DISORDER

Then fourteenth Zionist Congress was opened last evening by Herr Weizmann in the presence of representatives of the Austrian Government, the League of Nations and diplomats from Britain, America; France, Germany and elsewhere. The initial sitting of the Congress passed off without incident but previously there had been serious riding owing to bad blood caused by the Austrian Nationalists' anti-Semitic propaganda. The entire police force of six

'The entire police force of six thousand was mustered to cope with disorders in which forty persons were injured and over a hundred arrested. Much damage was done to property. Sentences of from eight to fourteen days' imprisonment were imposed on those arrested. Vienna' is now quiet.

headline: SHOTS AT BUS. / ATTEMPT ON BULGARIAN OFFICIALS
text: An outrage was attempted on the Champs Elysees last night by a band of forty Bulgarian communists who attacked MM. Theodore Koulieff and Boris Vasoff, the President and Vice-President, respectively, of the Bulgarian Sobranje, who are visiting Paris in connection with the Decorative Arts Exhibition. The parliamentarians managed to take refuge in a motor bus which the assailants rushed. The police were compelled to draw revolvers when the situation became threatening. When police reinforcements arrived they dispersed the demonstrators, two of whom were arrested.

headline: EXCURSION DEATHS.
text:
MILLHANDS INJURED BY EXPLOSION.

Seventeen persons were killed and seventy-five injured in the explosion of a boiler aboard an excursion steamer. The majority of the victims were employees of Messrs. Coat's thread mill at Pawtucket.

Later

The deathroll is now twenty-three. Doctors say that ten more are likely to die. The explosion occurred suddenly while the steamer was in front of the naval station on her return from Pawtucket after a day's outing of millhands. Naval launches and destroyers hurried to her assistance and took off the injured, and conveyed them to the naval hospital.

headline: RUBBER WANTED.
text:
FIRESTONE COMPANY'S BIG PROJECT.

Negotiations for the lease of a million acres of land in Liberia for rubber growing have virtually been concluded between the Firestone Tyre Company and Mr. Edwin Barclay, Liberian Secretary of State. It is learned from an authoritative source that a $100,000,000 corporation will be formed to operate the plantation on a scale ensuring American rubber manufacturers an adequate supply.

Now that it has appeared, this thort book, entitled "I Seek the Truth" (Verlag Cotta, Stuttgart and Berlin), contains very little that is new for the public to be curious about. There are two points about it, likely to provoke adverse criticism at the outset. One is the fact that the author signs "Wilhelm, Crowthprince," on the cover and title page, which is likely to prejudice Republicans as patriotic in spirit as himself. The other and far more important one, if the book is to rank as the serious contribution to the question of Germany's war guilt that its measured tone suggests, is that the author should have confined himself to more events as far as Germany is concerned, ignoring all personalities save that of the Kaiser in the attempt to prove the entire absence of any idea of war in German heads before 1914.

The object of the book is highly interesting in itself, as it represents the standpoint of thousands of German Nationalists at the present moment. It is not written to promote the rescinding of the Treaty of Versailles, "whose crown of thorns is the Dawes plan," but its immediate aim is to bring about the solemn refutation of the Note signed by Clemenceau on June 16, 1919, elucidating Article 231 of the Versailles Treaty, which deals with Germany's war guilt. With this moral victory the ex-Crown Prince thinks Germany would have to be satisfied for a time, for, though recognition of the fact that Germany was not alone in causing the war, is gaining ground, a public admission of the fact has yet to be made. This admission, he considers, should be the condition of Germany's entering the League: One is not socially possible with brand on one's brow. He does not think there is any possibility of altering the Treaty for many years to come. Though he has no hesitation, after what appears to have been a very close study of all the documents and memoirs published in every country, in roundly calling Isvolski, Russian Ambassador at Paris in 1914, "the father of the Great War." The Entente, the ex-Crown Prince considera, "was concluded from the same conception of Germany as a potential danger, as the witty director of the Lardin des Plantes in Paris chorothermed when he said of one of his wild beasts: 'Cet animal est très moissur.' If Germany had not pursued a policy of peace during the Boer War and resisted all tempting offers, the ex-Crown Prince believes that the European combination that led to the Great War would have been formed many years earlier. As to the belief that the German strength of arms was the secret of her will to strike, several arguments are used to prove that German arma- ments were the effects, and not the causes, of her neighbours' efforts. Of these the strongest is the evidence of General Buat. French delegate at Washington for Briand's Government, who stated that the German Army was not at its full power in 1913; when 3,800 healthy young men were refused, while France had taken every recruit. The weakest spot in his evidence here is the contention that "the numerical superiority of the Allies on August 1, 1914, was such that a German victory could only be hoped for if a leader of genius arose."

The book is curious, unconscious contribution to the father-and-son problem which has exercised German literature during the past few years. Serpulous attention is paid not only to every utterance or rawled remark before the Great War broke out, but to every fear the Kaiser ever expressed that the Central Powers might be dragged into Balkan struggles. An occasional note or message that was too temperamental the son excuses from the purely human point of view of momentary and perfectly natural exasperation. The whole rings very true, and for foreign readers at least has the merit of summing up under one head accessible to all who care to read them all the arguments lying buried in a beap of political memoirs on the vast subject of "Who began the war."

headline: DR. WILLIAMS' PINK PILLS. / REDS TO GO.
text:
SHANGHAI MEN ATTACK BOLSHEVIKS.

Ill-feeling against the Bolshevik section of local labour leaders culminated this evening in an attack on the headquarters of the Shanghai Labour Association in the Chinese city by a large crowd of strikers, armed with miscellaneous weapons, including sticks, and knives.

Both sides had casualties and it is reported that one or two Reds were killed.

The demonstrators complained that they had been deceived and robbed by the Bolsheviks.

headline: CALL FOR ACTION.
text:
(Continued from Page 2.)

Swatow Volce.

The next official speaker from the platform was Mr. Macgown of Swatow who said he had been specially requested by the members of the British Chamber of Commerce in Swatow to represent them and to associate the British community in Swatow with any resolutions sent to the Home Government by Hongkong. He quoted articles of treaties with China which, he said, had been completely and absolutely violated not only in the spirit and letter but in the practice of them.

The illegal Bolshevist Government of Canton had put into force a very effective embargo on all trade to and from Hongkong, and in Swatow all British and Japanese interests are boycotted. "What about it?" asked Mr. Macgown. Are we to accept these conditions without protest? (Cries of "No.") The trouble started in Canton and must be settled with Canton, Canton is quite separate and independent of the Central Government of Peking.

"Swatow has been badly treated and unless the Reds are kicked out there is no possible chance of the resumption of trade as before. The loss of this trade will hit the Colony of Hongkong very hard, harder than many realise. British shipping interests are very large in Swatow, while large quantities of British goods are imported yearly. All trade has now stopped. I have much pleasure in supporting this telegram to the Prime Minister, and I hope prompt action will be taken by the Home authorities to stop this reign of terror in South China. I should like to say that if any attack is made on Canton, a similar attack should be made on Swatow because unfortunately, Swatow is in Kwangtung and just now entirely under Red rule. (Applause).

Shameen And Foochow. Mr. C. E. Peacock, from Shameen, said that all he could tell the meeting, so far as the situation there was concerned was that "we are still cooking our own food, doing our own washing, cleaning our own house, and doing no business." He also referred to the article with reference to Sir James Jamieson and termed as "grudging" a retraction of some points which had afterwards been published. A letter from a Shameen merchant pointing out the Shameen point of view and stating that they were not looking for a scapegoat had not been published.

The speaker said that the article in question had been referred to by Mr. C. C. Wu, "probably one of the ablest men in the Canton administration." In a situation of this kind he thought the greatest care should be exercised by the Hongkong newspapers in regard to what they published (hear, hear). "Indications of disunion, as these, merely give confidence to the other side and make our battle all the harder."

The Chairman then read a telegram from the Chairman of the Foochow Chamber of Commerce, in which it was stated that the residents of Foochow desired to be associated with the telegram to be sent Home. The telegram also stated the Foochow residents were prepared to share expenses.

At this point a gentleman moved to the centre of the platform from the rear who, although he slurred his words, must have been inaudible except to those in the immediate vicinity, was very much in earnest and was applauded when he retired. He had just come from Shameen, he said, and he could say that it was with difficulty provisions could be obtained. He had been all-round the world and found that Britain was the most hated nation in the world. That was because she was too lenient with the people with whom she had to deal. This was the richest Colony Britain had got, he continued, and why should they not give it protection. We all knew that the British lion was slow to act but why could it not put out its paw and protect Hongkong?

Coast Officers' Voice. Mr. T. T. Laurenson, of the China Coast Officers' Guild, was the next speaker. On behalf of the mercantile marine of the China Coast, masters and officers, on Thursday afternoon last, a telegram had been sent, he said, to Secretaries at Home, urging them to make every effort with the Imperial Merchant Service, the Marine Engineers' Association; and the Navigators and General Insurance Company to persuade the Imperial Government to take immediate action with regard to Canton and China generally. Further delay, it was pointed out, might be ruinous, and have disastrous effect on the mercantile marine. That telegram was sent by the mercantile marine who he would venture to say, were never behind, and were the first line of defence, after the Royal Navy. (Loud cheers).

Mr. H. Somerset Fitzroy, a local barrister, then took the platform. He rose, he said, to express his disagreement with the latter part of the telegram.

When we get down to what this meeting proposes to send to the Home Government what does it amount to? It demands that the British Government deliver an ultimatum at once to the Canton authorities. (Applause). Have you stopped for one moment to think what that means? A Voice: "No time to stop." (Laughter and applause). You are recognising a belligerent. Can you point out any time in the history of the British nation when it has recognised a two-penny halfpenny belligerent? Take your thoughts back to the civil war when the South was fighting against the North, when the whole of that Continent was in the great throes of war. Did the British Government recognise them? Not a bit of it. You have a small community, whom you say are acting contrary to Peking. You have your treaties with China. Where is the proper place to go? The place where the Foreign Office is going at the present moment. There is one, and only one channel through which we can deal and that is through the diplomatic channel of Peking. A voice: “Go up the West River and see what Peking can do.” (Loud cheers).

Mr. Fitzroy: The next thing you ask the Home Government to do is to turn out the Bolsheviks. I do not know the exact meaning of that. Perhaps some of you mean the Chinese Bolsheviks, but at any rate what you are asking is that the whole of these people shall be turned out. I think I can hear in that an echo of the ultimatum which was delivered to Serbia in 1914 by Austria. (A Voice: "Nonsense"). It is the same sort of thing that you want to destroy—the sovereignty of a nation and take it by force. Very well, how do you propose to do this when you have sent your ultimatum? (A Voice: "Send a telegram.") (Laughter). Exactly, but that is not what we are discussing at the present moment. We are sending a telegram in which we are usurping the functions of the Home Government, in which we say the Home Government are totally incapable of doing their job despite the fact that we are told they are trusted by everybody. We propose to do it by establishing a blockade by naval forces of Canton. (Hear, hear). Does it ever occur to you that somebody else has something to say besides Great Britain? Europe would be ablaze in 20 minutes after this went through. "Then let us have a blaze." "You are not discussing the matter but asking a series of questions" were the only intelligible of many remarks from the audience at this point.

Mr. Fitzroy, continuing, referred to incidents transpiring in the South American republic of Venezuela in 1902 when measures similar to those advocated, at the meeting were instituted. What was the result? Theodore Roosevelt was the President of America at the time and within three or four days the American fleet was sent to Venezuela. The British ambassador at Washington had to state that the developments there were unauthorised.

In conclusion, the speaker said that he thought they should leave whatever action was considered necessary to the Home Government who had a far greater knowledge of the situation than Hongkong had (Dissent).

The Chairman remarked that the last speaker had entirely overlooked the explanation he had made that while they made some suggestions with regard to the form intervention should take, they, of course, fully realised that the form of such intervention was solely a matter for the decision of His Majesty's Government. (Applausion). That meeting was not presuming to dictate to the Home Government what they should do, but was simply venturing to voice the feeling of the Colony that something must be done and done quickly. (Applause). The diplomacy of Peking had so far absolutely and entirely failed and it was not realised that there was a problem in the south.

Mr. Best, then mounted the platform from the body of the hall and alleged inaccuracies in Mr Fitzroy's statements regarding the Venezuela trouble. Cleveland was President, he said, not Roosevelt and the trouble had been over a gold field and boundary problems.

Old Residents' Views Mr. S. Boulton, speaking as a resident of 27 years, said he could not understand how it was that a Government with such tremen, dous interests as Britain has in Hongkong to day should remain passive and seemingly indifferent. headline: QUAINT. CURIOS.
text:
SOME EIGHTEENTH CEN. TURY EXTRACTS.

Let us for a few moments see what quaint items can be gathered from an early issue of the "Morning Post," writes a correspondent of that newspaper.

Here is a coach for sale, "little worse than new." In the same column we find Mr. Hay, opposite Burlington House, in Piccadilly, offering "glass Bee-hives" with a curious Obelisk worked by the bees to be seen, and contrived as such, that a lady may have them at her dressing table without the least danger of being stung.

Complaints of the idleness and inefficiency of servants are very common in Eighteenth Century writings, but a treasure was occasionally to be met with:—

"Wants a Place, where a lad is kept, a clean, diligent man, between 30 and 40 years of age, can dress hair or wigs, brew, understands the management of a family, can bear confinement, wages is no object." Brewing would be by no means regarded as the least important of this man's accomplishments. In the country, beer still held its own against tea as a beverage at all meals, even breakfast.

The simple contract creditors of the late Bishop of Exeter, are desired to meet his administrators at the Devil Tavern (1) on Friday next, the 22nd instant, at 6 o'clock in the evening on special affairs."

Mr. Joshua Long, No. 73, Cheapside, has for sale a quantity of "real red and white French Vinegar, Chilly ditto, and ditto of the 4 thieves." Lord Chesterfield, who began by being a render of The Tatter and The Spectator, of Steel and Addison, published in Queen Anne's reign, lived to see the first hundred issues or so of the "Morning Post." The famous "Letters" omnamently met with a better reception in some quarters than they got from Dr. Johnson. For in an issue of this "Morning Post," published some time after his Lordship's deaths, we find the following announcement.

"Lord Chesterfield's Plan of a foreign and domestic Education is now being carried out for six young gentlemen, but so improved as to form the Gentleman and the Scholar without endangering their morals or religious principles. A vacancy now offers, and the success, terms, etes, may be known by applying to Mr. Bird; Jeweller, No. 7, Cornhill."

The "Morning Post" did not like the Public Ledger, an organ which supported Charles James Fox and the so-called "Patriots," who were accused of sowing "seeds of noise and discluindre" against the King's Majesty and his Government, as may be gathered from the following "obituary":—

"On Saturday last March 18, 1780] died of a political decay; Brewman's Public Ledger, an offspring of a modern Patriotism, a brother to Friction, and nearly related to Rebellion. The infamous principles of this disgrace to Literature are bequeathed by testament to a fellow-lubourer in Sedition, the "General Advertiser," and yesterday the will was published by the infamous legates."

Poulters, the gamekeeper, was faced by a new problem. He understands the habits of birds and the ways of most of the sportsmen with whom he had to deal, but now a Bishop was one of the party of guns. How to address him was the question that troubled him, as he confessed to a friend whose sympathy led him to ask later how he had fared.

"B-badly," was the answer. "The very first thin' a rabbit run right past 'is legs an' I said 'Shoot the d——d thin', your Holiness.' An' I saw at once from 'is face that 'holiness' was the wrong word!"

headline: RAN AMOK. / CHINESE ATTACKS EUROPEANS.
text:
REPULSE BAY INCIDENT.

A Tientsin Chinese "boy" occasioned much excitement at Repulse Bay Hotel on Tuesday afternoon by running amok with a pair of scissors and injuring his employers, Mr. Osland Hill, Postal Commissioner, Canton, and Mrs. Hill. The boy, whose behaviour at the time and subsequently (he attempted to commit suicide by beating his head upon the ground when arrested) indicates his having lost his reason, "seized the scissors and made a murderous attack on the baby," Mrs. Hill, who got to the spot first, was injured in the face by the point of the scissors and Mr. Hill, in a subsequent struggle, was wounded in the leg, and had his thumb dislocated. Members of the Hotel staff and police officers placed the boy under restraint until arrangements were made for his removal in custody.

headline: HIGH POLITICS.
text:
(Reuter's Service.) London, Sept.

During a lull in the proceedings at Geneva, Mr. Chamberlain, M. Painleve and M. Briand motored to Aix-les-Bains where Mr. Baldwin is spending a holiday. Mr. Chamberlain interviewed on his return to Geneva said that they talked about art and crossword puzzles, but a long inspired message from Paris declares that the conversation appreciably advanced the Allied agreement on European questions, notably the French desire to adapt the general principles of the protocol to particular treaties like the Rhineland Security Pact. It admits, as regards the latter, that the negotiations are dead-locked and will remain so until Germany definitely declares her position. It concludes saying that future conversations will be either through Diplomatic channels or at a conference of Allied and German Foreign Ministers, which will be held at Lausanne and will turn on the question of Germany's former occupation of her eastern frontiers.

headline: ANOTHER SLANDER.
text:
WNRTHAND RUSSELL'S "PALSEN CHARGES"

STRONO SHANGHAI COMMENT

The weary task of trying to overtake the shanders on Shanghai and its British community published abroad brings us into conflict with an article by Mr. Bertrand Russell in the "Nation and Athenæum" of July 18, says the "North China Daily News." No sensible person in China wastes time, under ordinary conditions, in replying to Mr. Russell, whose views of this country would appear to be formed entirely by what confirmation he could get for his own prejudices out of the least trustworthy elements in the student body. But when the "Nation and Athenæum" publishes an article by him, it cannot go unnoticed. In passing, it is much to be regretted that a paper of such standing should have opened its columns to a contributor so equivocal. This is what we find Mr. Russell saying:—

With regard to the Shanghai shooting, some of the facts are still in debate, others are now generally admitted. The following facts are not in dispute: the crowd outside the police station was unarmed; no notice was given of the intention to fire upon them; the order to fire was given in English, and therefore not understood by most of the crowd; the firing began ten seconds after the order was given; many of those who were hit were shot in the back, showing that they were trying to disperse, "but were not giving time to do so. Other crowds were fired upon during the next six days. Altogether about seventy people were killed, with a proportionate number of wounded. Every non-British person, and almost every British missionary, who has spoken about the affair has pronounced that the British authorities were not justified in their action. Dr. J. W. Cline's formerly head of the missionary college at Soochow, who saw the whole thing, says: "I was not expecting to see the police fire, was shocked when they did fire, and have been sorry about it ever since."

headline: AN ABOMIX ABLE LIE
text:
Who started the abominable lie that “about seventy people were killed”? We met it in Mr. Sherwood Eddy's slanderous article with which we dealt last week and naturally, as it was in the air, Mr. Bertrand Russell, with his peculiar preclivity for saving everything that he can to the detriment of his own country—one imagines, with some idea of enchancing his own self-importance—has sniffed it out with ghoulish delight. The facts are given in the police report published in the Municipal Gazette of August 6, and, as we said before, the police would be very careful not to give anyone a chance of tripping them up in such a matter. Here they are:

Attacks by the strikers or their sympathizers resulted in the death of two Chinese and one foreigner. The Police in the suppression of the riots killed 22 Chinese and wounded 36. These figures include rioters who lost their lives on May 30, on Nanking Road. Further efforts of the Police to suppress lawlessness led to the arrest of 92 persons for rioting or assault, the apprehension of 22 others for tearing down Municipal Proclamations, and the prosecution of 35 persons for disseminating inflammatory strike and anti-foreign literature. All of these, with a few exceptions, and 34 other persons charged for other offences arising out of the strike, were extremely leniently dealt with, either by being cautioned, fined or imprisoned for short periods.

headline: VISITORS AT HOTELS.
text: Yet Mr. Westridge was unquestionably the most important witness of all. He was nearest to the actual shooting; fifteen years' residence in the interior of China for the China Inland Mission had brought him more than once into contact with Chinese mobs and taught him what Chinese mob psychology is; and with all this to give weight to his words, he said emphatically, in the Mixed Court trial of the students, that he considered the police could have done nothing but what they did and that, in their place, he would have felt compelled to do the like. But testimony of this kind does not suit the purpose of men like Mr. Bertrand Russell and Mr. Sherwood Kiddy.

headline: COLOURED STATRMENT8
text: In another part of the article Mr. Russell recommends his renders to obtain a little pamphlet called "China's Case," if they "wish to see how the matter appears to eminent Chinese intellectuals." We have seen it; and we deeply regret that men of the standing of Mr. V. K. Ting and Mr. Lo Wen-kan should have been among those who put their names to it. The internal evidence of the pamphlet shows that the writers must have had before them the full versions of both sides, including the verbatim report of the Mixed Court trial mentioned above and they have carefully suppressed every scrap of evidence which told against the students' version. When "eminent Chinese intellectuals" are capable of such dishonesty, what can be expected of the uneniment? What reliance can be placed on any Chinese testimony?

headline: Late Sir John Jordan.
text:
You have found it impossible, as it is impossible for me, to meet on such an occasion and in such an audience and not try to express something of the debt which we and China alike owe to the great figure which passed from among us actually at one of your meetings the other day. It is nearly fifty years since Sir John Jordan entered the Chinese Consular Service. After many years of useful and distinguished labour, he became His Majesty's Minister at Peking in 1906, and for fourteen years represented our King and country in the capital of China. Even when he retired in 1920 from that position, his public services did not cease. He accompanied Lord Balfour to the Washington Conference and continued to the last moment to place his ripe experience and intimate knowledge on Chinese conditions and his deep sympathy with the Chinese at the disposal of the British Government and give us the benefit of his lifelong labours and service.

He was in truth a type of that great race of public servants who work quietly, caring little for personal fame, for the honour of their own country and at the same time penetrated with sympathy for the country and people among whom his lot was cast. I think of Sir John Jordan as a great Englishman who loved China only second to his own country and who served his own country well in the important posts he held because he was never lacking in sympathy for the people among whom he worked and sought to reconcile them as they are and can be reconciled to the interests of his own country with the interests, liberties and developments of China.

headline: “Unequal” Treaties.
text:
After all you cannot deal wisely with a few domestic problems unless you have regard to the traditions of the country with which you are dealing, and you can deal wisely with no foreign problem unless you can enter, to some extent at any rate, into the aspirations of people with whom you are dealing and unless you can feel sympathy with their grievances and their hardships and realise their long history, and in case of China almost im- memorial civilisation, to which modern China is heir. These events of yesterday and to-day stand out against the long historic background. During the whole of the eighteenth century our relations with China as traders—and we are not unwilling to recall Napoleon's gibe, which may be our glory, that we are a nation of shopkeepers and as anxious for peace as any shopkeeper—our trade relations were subject to two great monopolies namely, the East India Company on the one side and the Cohong of Canton on the other.

Their passing was one stage in the development of relations between the East and the West and in the growth of our common concerns. The bonds of monopoly were too narrow to serve the purpose of the new times and in 1833 the monopoly of the East India Company was abolished and trade was thrown open. What followed? China could not adjust herself to the new conditions. Seven years of constantly increasing the strain of constant friction and complaints and failure to secure any satisfaction led, as these events must lead a country, to the so-called Opium War of 1840. But there were much more important things at stake in the Opium War than any question of Opium. The boycott of British shipping and confiscation of traders' goods, restriction of liberties and imprisonment of British citizens and finally the expulsion of the merchants from Canton—these were questions which led to war and which found their solution in the Treaty of Nanking in 1842, the first of those unequal treaties whereof China complains to-day.

headline: Policy of the Powers.
text:
We agreed that that conference should prepare the way for the abolition of Likin as contemplated in our old treaty of 1902 and to an interim imposition of a surtax-of-2½-centum-on-general tariff with five centum on certain objects of luxury with a view to increasing the freedom of China, to strengthening the authority of the Central Government and to providing means for the development of China's trade and prosperity. We agreed further, and again in accord with the other Powers, to appoint a commission to go into the question of extraterritoriality to see what progress could be made in that question and what measures were needed to prepare for the eventual surrender of all extraterritoriality rights.

Finally we and the Japanese agreed that the Japanese were to hand back Shantung to China and we to surrender our lease of Weihai-wei and, though the subject was not mentioned at Washington, to surrender the claim on our taxpayer to the relief which the payment of the Boxer Indemnity was intended to give to him for charges incurred in consequence of, shall I say, weakness of the Chinese Government and to devote money so received to purposes which were not merely of interest but of direct benefit to China alone. On those lines we were ready to act at once.

It is not our fault if in the interval since the Washington conference greater progress has not been made. We were inspired by nothing but goodwill to the Chinese people.

Sympathetic Attitude. I have had no personal connection in my life except as member of the Government with the Far East but as a member of various Governments I have talked with many men whose active lives have lain in the Far East. I have never yet met an Englishman who had been in China and passed at any rate a reasonable part of his working life there or who was intimately connected with British trade with China who had not imbibed a great sympathy with the Chinese, (Cheers), a great trust in the honour of their pledged word and I would add, almost a personal affection for the characteristic features of Chinese nationality (Cheers). can assure him in your name and in the name of all our country that our hand will go out to meet his with the same memory of old friendships and with same desire to restore cordiality and confidence. (Cheers). I do not conceal from myself that in many respects the circumstances are not those which I would have wished for an international conference of this kind.

Our representatives will go there to the new conference fortified by those old friendships and inspired by a sympathy for China that they drink in at every gathering of Englishmen who have passed their lives there, ready to take full account of China's aspirations, conscious that we have no interest that can conflict with the real and abiding interests of China itself, and fortified by the knowledge that in serving their own country they need do nothing and ask nothing which will not equally avail to the advantage of China and the Chinese people. (Cheers) I read the other day in a newspaper.
