His greatest exploit was the taking of a recalcitant chief single-handed, armed only with a knob-kerrie and a concealed revolver.

Leaving many hundreds of his own armed soldiers at a distance, he marched straight into the hostile chief's village, right to where the dusky potentate was sitting surrounded by warriors, and promptly clubbed him senseless.

With hand on revolver he then awaited the onrush, but his extraordinary pluck had paralysed the savages, who were already aware that he was reputed to possess supernatural powers. One and all threw down their weapons, and Boyes experienced no further trouble from that quarter.

But at the apex of his power his reign came to a sudden end. Two British officials arrived on the scene and ordered his arrest on charges of having waged war, personated government without authority, taken part in six punitive expeditions, and committed dacoity.

Conviction on any one of these charges meant death. For several weeks this King Crusoe languished in an evil-smelling gaol, but when, finally, he was brought to trial he was honourably acquitted.

After these experiences Boyes returned to England, A rover all his life, however, he found it impossible to settle down, and once again he set sail for Africa. This time he tried farming, but it was not long before he was once more seized by the wanderlust, and, leaving his land in responsible hands, he started out on a hazardous elephant-hunting trip to Abyssinia and the Belgian Congo.

For nearly fourteen years little or nothing has been heard of him in England. How he fared after he plunged into the jungle—the thrilling adventures and hairbreadth escapes he had—is now made public for the first time in the exclusive story he told me at the home of his father-in-law at Hull.

"In order to reach the Congo from Nairobi," he said, "I had to trek through Kenya, cross Lake Victoria Nyanza, and then strike right through Uganda to the Blue Nile. I had heard that gold had been found in the district, and I determined to have a go at that if the elephant hunting did not come up to expectations. But the prospects of one soon receded into the background when I arrived at my destination. There was no doubt about the elephant hunt being a success, for the must have been thousands of them. Herd after herd I saw and the sight fairly made my fingers itch round the trigger." "Pitching my camp on the British side of Lake Albert Edward, I started in to do some fancy shooting." At best it was a dangerous job, and to make matters worse most of the native there about were candidates and particularly hostile towards white male. In each I was told what it was a hunter's luck to escape being gored by the elephants, he was almost certain to jump out of the frying pan, so to speak, into the stew pan. The climate was about the worst you can imagine, and blackwater fever, tick fever, and sleeping sickness were about as common as influenza in England.

headline: WALKED OVER HIM.
text:
“I had even a narrower escape than this from an elephant when I was trekking up to. Abyssinia on another expedition. I was the last man of my party when, suddenly, the elephant broke cover and made straight at me. My mule, startled, threw me off, and by the time I had picked myself up, the elephant was not more than three yards away. Quick as a flash I threw my hat at his face and took a header in the bush, thinking he would not follow. But he came on, trumpeting madly, and I thought I was doomed. And then he seemed to step right on top of me, and I closed my eyes....But nothing happened. The great brute had walked clean over me without noticing that I was there.

“As I scrambled up, however, he saw me and charged again, and I was thrown into the air like a stone from a catapult. Fortunately, a tree broke my flight, and I hung on to one of the branches and waited until the animal went away.

"On this journey I had considerable trouble with the Abyssinians, who frequently were very hostile. At a native village they decided on a lightning strike for double rations.

"They were stubborn and said that if they did not get what they wanted they were going to leave me in the lurch. 'Very well,' I said, 'you can clear

'Very well,' I said, 'you can clear out straight away.'

"All this time angry native from the village were surging about me. Suddenly the Abyssinian guide who started the trouble walked away with one of my mules. I could not shoot him because he was careful to take cover behind the animal, but I made a big display of my guns, and let it be clear that if there was going to be a fight I intended to give a good account of myself."

Scared by my bold front, but still spoiling for a scrap, the natives made a dash at my deserting servants. For a few seconds there was a wild melee, and then my boys broke away and rushed back to me for protection. They got it, and that finished the trouble as far as they were concerned.

headline: THE MOSCOW METHOD
text:
A remarkable narrative of imprisonment in a Bolshevik dungeon and a trial before the "Proletarian Court of Justice" at Vladivostok is told by Mr. Sydney C. Suter, chief officer of the Glen Line steamer "Carnarvonshire," who has just returned home.

Mr. Suter was liberated from prison, in which he suffered the vilest possible torture, through the efforts of the Navigators and General Insurance Co.

At the time of his illegal arrest and imprisonment the riots at Shanghai were in progress, and, according to Mr. Suter, he was made the medium of propaganda by the Bolsheviks to show that they were protecting Chinese against "British tyranny."

As the “Carnarvonshire” approached Vladivostock a Chinese sailor was discovered pilfering the quarters of the Chinese crew. This man was ordered by Mr. Suter to be handcuffed to a rail, mainly to save him from the violence of the other Chinese, while a Bolshevik policeman was found to take the man in charge. When the policeman appeared he apparently took the word of the Chinese thief before that of Mr. Suter, with the result that the later was charged "under Paragraph 160 of the Penal Code—forcible deprivation of liberty by a painful method which endangered the life or health of the person detained."

headline: SHIPS WANTED. / CANTON ASKS RUSSIA FOR MORE.
text:
Since the participation in the general strike by the seamen, inferrupting communication with Hongkong, the sailing of steamers between Canton, Swatow and Shanghai has been less frequent, remarks the "Canton Gazette," Communication between these places has been, however, maintained with vessels despatched by the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Co. At present, although there are vessels sailing between Canton and Swatow, the sailing time is so irregular, it is most inconvenient to the merchants. In view of this, the Soviet Steamship Co., telegraphed some time ago to Russia requesting the despatched of more steamers to sail between Canton, Swatow and Shanghai so as to facilitate communication and the transporting of cargo.

It is learned that several of these vessels will sail to Canton regularly, and will take passengers and cargo to Swatow and Shanghai. Besides these vessels, there are other vessels, American, Norwegian and German, which will arrive in Canton shortly.

A later issue of the same paper said:—

A German firm has written to the Strike Committee reporting that by the steam's "Hang Fung" of which they are the agents, they have imported a large shipment of food stalls and other candries from Shanghai, on Canton and the steamer is now lying off the Macao Passage.

headline: BOME PEOT
text:
JARDINE STEAMER'S ESCAPE.

When the Indo-China Steam Navigation Company's steamer "Tuckwo," which arrived at Hankow this afternoon from Shanghai, was about two miles above Wuhu on the evening of the 25th inst. a violent explosion, accompanied by smoke, occurred in the Chinese third-class accommodation. Anti-fire measures were taken and no fire resulted, the ship continuing on her voyage.

An enquiry into the cause of the explosion resulted in the finding of a, cunningly-contrived bomb, the cover of which was the outside container of a Thermos flask, which had been placed in an innocent-looking "box. According to the story of the passenger coolie concerned, the box was brought aboard at Chinkiang by a Chinese who left the ship at Nanking and did not return.

Only slight damage was done by the explosion, two Chinese passengers being slightly injured and two bunks wrecked. There had obviously been a determined and well-planned attempt to wreck the ship, which might have had most serious results had the bomb exploded elsewhere than under the wide airshaft, which gave the flame access to the open air and dissipated the force of the explosion. This combined with the excellent behaviour of the officers and crew, tended to allay any tendency to panic on the part of the passengers.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
While Washington despatches are optimistic in regard to the prospect of the Franco-American debt settlement, Paris is doubtful and some papers even anticipate the failure of the negotiations. The despatches from French correspondents at Washington, however, speak of the new French proposals as possibly providing for initial annual payments of thirty instead of twenty-five million dollars, increasing in a decade to a maximum of approximately a hundred million, payable in fifty-two years instead of ninety. The Americans are now said to be ready to agree to maximum annuities of 120 million dollars. M. Caillaux is said to have assured Mr. Mellon that no payment would be made to Britain and no Franco-British arrangement will be concluded without identical payment and arrangement with America. The incident of the loan to the Bank of France is reported to be settled.

headline: BETTER BUSINESS.
text:
HONGKONG AT WEMBLEY.

Scores of letter- and verbal requests are being received daily by the Wembley officials asking whether the Wembley exhibition will go on next year in spite of the definite official statement that the gates will close for good at the end of October, states the "China Express and Telegraph." Malaya and Hongkong have never looked more animated than during the last few weeks. A Hongkong official declared that much better business had been done lately and that every hope is entertained for a continuance of the same until the pavilion closes. As was the case last year, the Hongkong section closes a month earlier than the general Exhibition, this step having been decided on principally in order that the Chinese employees may leave for home before the cold weather sets in. The Commissioner and Mrs. Flallifax were "at home" at the Pavilion on September 22.

headline: CHINA SUGAR."
text:
EFFECT OF TEMPORARY STOP PAGE.

From a letter appearing in the “Times” from a Robe reader it would appear that the stoppage of the British sugar refineries in China has created a demand for the Japanese product in Manchuria in the boxcott, and in other Eastern countries.

The increased export trade in Japanese goods such as cottons and manufactured foodstuffs is also reported to have reacted favourably on the value of the yen. Japanese grey shootings, again, are reported to have made considerable inroads into the trade with East African ports.

Commenting on the statement with regard to sugar, the "China Express" and Telegraph" thinks that the Taikoo and Jardine concerns in Hongkong are those particularly referred to: The news from Japan certainly indicates activity, of which British interests, seriously affected by the deadlock in China, should take note, it states. Hongkong is not afraid of Japan as far as sugar is concerned. The market lost is not easy to regain. The remark applies equally to shirting and shipping.

Vera Cruz, September 28.—One person was killed and fifty wounded in rioting the municipal elections. It is alleged that Lopez, the Red candidate, abstracted ballotting papers from one booth and that the followers of Galvez, the opposing candidate, began the shooting which became indiscriminate. Troops restored order. Numbers of Reds have been arrested on a charge of inciting revolt.—Reuter's American Service.

Notwithstanding police supervision, an unidentified anti-Fascist shot and slightly injured two Fascist-symptholders, and escaped. Reuter's American Service DRIVER CHARGED WITH MANSLAUGHTER.

headline: BLOOD GIVEN.
text:
MAN WHO FELT PAIN WHEN PATIENT DIED.

Nearly three years ago Frederick George Lee, an ex-regimental sergeant-major, now 34, was asked at a labour bureau if he would allow some of his blood to be transfused to a girl of 10 at the Middlesex Hospital, Mortimer Street, W.

“I’ve kiddies of my own,” he replied, promptly agreeing to the request.

The subsequent operation was the first of 25 of a similar nature to which Mr. Lee has submitted since November 1922, there being a chance in every case of saving the patient's life.

He has given 36 pints of his life-blood to others, and at least 17 persons owe their lives to him and to the Middlesex Hospital surgeons in whose care he has placed himself.

In cases where transfusion has not been successful in saving the life of a patient Mr. Lee has had a curious knowledge of the fact. "Should my patient die," he said, "I know at once, for I feel a severe pain in my arm."

Mr. Lee has been ordered a rest, and for two months is not to be allowed to give his blood to patients.

“We want at least 20 volunteers of equal fitness,” a horse surgeon stated.

"They must not have had malaria or serious blood diseases; otherwise, any fit man or woman up to 50 is capable of acting as a donor. Volunteers should write to the secretary of the Middlesex Hospital."

Genoa, September 28: — The Council of the League of Nations has appointed an Estonian, General Leidoner as commissioner to investigate the Mosul deportations. He will be assisted by a Czechoslovakian Lieutenant Colonel. Later: General Leidoner will have two assistants, chosen by the League Council's Mosul committee: — Reuter.

Mar del Plata, September 28.— On the eve of the departure of the Prince of Wales he banquetted President Alvear on board H.M.S. "Repulse," which was brilliantly illuminated. The function was very splendid and attended by the Argentine Cabinet Ministers, officials and society leaders, who affectionately bade freewell to the Prince. The newspapers cordially pay tribute to the royal visit.—Renter.

headline: LABOUR QUESTIONS.
text:
The statement in the House of Commons by the Labour Socialist, Mr. Ponsonby, that he thought it was farcical to attribute the trouble of China to Communistic agencies drew from the Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, Mr. R. McNeil, the comment that he did not think any proof of propaganda could be so positive as to convince that right honourable gentleman.

In the course of discussion Major-General Knox insisted that the anti-British propaganda in China was engineered from Moscow. Their agent, whose name was Tomski, was now known as Livinski. (Laughter). Mr. J. Jones (Labour-Socialist, Silvertown): Is it in order for a member of this House to refer to the member of another Government as if he had changed his name for some disreputable reason? (Ministerial laughter). The King of this country had changed his name, and they thought none the worse of him for that.

A Labour-Socialist: And so has the President of the Board of Trade. (Labour-Socialist cheers).

A. Knox had referred in any dis- respectful terms to the gentleman he had mentioned. (Ministerial cheers).

Sir A. Knox regretted that he had ruffled hon. members opposite. (Laughter and cheers). In the course of his speech, Mr. Ponsonby asked the Government to give the House some information in regard to China. The problem was one that might smoulder until it blazed up into something extremely dangerous. His Majesty's Government were showing a sort of spineless inertia, and were taking no action. They seemed to have an incorrigible habit of allowing situations, whether at home or abroad, to come to a head before they could be persuaded to move at all. He thought that the suggestion that the disturbances in China were due to Bolshevik propaganda had been disproved. To say that the movement was due to Communist agitation was far critical in the extreme. It was the culmination of events that had been growing in China ever since the Western exploitation of that country in 1840. The breaking point had been reached in the way the Chinese had been treated as inferior people and exploited by the Western peoples. If the Western Powers wanted to deal honestly by China; it would not be long before a strong Government arose in that country. We were throwing Russia into the arms of Asia; we were entranging the whole of the vast population of China; and were raising up a sort of suspicious feeling against Japan. The unfortunate action of to-day might culminate in great catastrophes years hence. In reply to Mr. Ponsonby, Mr. R. McNeil said that Russian intrigue was creating great difficulties and making much missionary and unhelpful, however, believe that in the long run it would do any material damage to the British Empire. (Ministerial cheers).

As regarded the attitude of the British Government there was not the slightest foundation for Mr. Ponsonby's charge that the Government were showing supine inertia. From the first moment the troubles developed, the Government had been very active in trying to bring about a wise settlement of the existing troubles, and to devise and encourage and initiate as far as they could a wise policy dealing with the subject of our relations with China and the internal conditions of that country. He agreed that the condition of affairs in China was not due to Bolshevik propaganda, but he did think that Bolshevik propaganda had been fishing in troubled waters. It had been exasperating tempers and making more mischief where there was mischief to work on at the beginning, and he had very little doubt that it was very largely due to Bolshevik propaganda that, anti-foreign hostility had largely concentrated its animosity upon this country rather than upon others. Chinese interests and British interests there were identical. Trade could only flourish in an atmosphere of peace and confidence, and it was obviously to our interest that China should enjoy those blessings. In spite of all the existing difficulties, he did not think we should be pessimistic with regard to the future of China, and as to what we could do there. He hoped that the coming conference would improve the whole of the foreign relations with China. He did not believe that the present Chinese feeling of animosity against this country would continue.

headline: "TAKE MEN AND MONEY."
text: The idea of conscripting both men and money in the event of war, is gaining ground. The world war saw the almost universal adoption of conscription, as it related to man-power, by countries concerned, but not that of wealth. An approach to such a state of affairs was made when, as in the case of Britain, certain industries were temporarily nationalised and prompt and effective use was made of them to speed on the war to a successful conclusion. The extension of this idea is summed up in the words: "The whole power of national service, lives and property, for the defence of the nation." Those who seek to promote the adoption of the suggestion, and are urging legislation on it, hail principally from America and Canada. They argue that war can only be effectively, and economically, carried on, and quickly brought to a conclusion, if conscription of wealth and man-power is the rule and not the exception. In this way rich and poor, old and young, contribute to a common cause. The pacifist with the individual with a pronounced belief in the force of arms, is, so to speak thrown into the common melting pot. The profiteer is automatically obliterated, whilst the arm-chair critic, the dispenser of white feathers and the conscientious objector, by a machine-like process become as one in an effort that, because it is a piece of law on a statute book, may go a long way to prevent the outbreak of war, and in the event of war is likely to finish it in a very short space of time. The idea has about it a considerable amount of commonsense. We are inclined to suggest that the Colony should have a similar piece of legislation in mind to guard against the possibilities of strikes which are nothing less than attacks on the stability of a friendly place and people..... The suggestion is thrown out as a suitable and profitable week-end discussion that should be the cause of some interesting thought. Thrice armed is he who hath his quarrel just, but the getting in of the first blow is also part of a piece of uncontradicted wisdom. We know nothing better to meet such unjust quarrels than the one forced upon us, than a solid wall of conscriptive effort as has been indicated.

By 1894 Japan had so reformed her judicial system and internal administration that Great Britain — this alleged wicked, Imperialist power — voluntarily surrendered her extraterritorial rights and Japan became an independent, sovereign State after a lapse of 36 years. Similarly, Siam in 1907, after a lapse of 54 years, secured a revision of her treaties of 1855, thereby obtaining rights of jurisdiction over foreigners. In 1925, after a lapse of 67 years, China stands where she did; although in 1902 at Shanghai and twenty years later at Washington she was offered political autonomy on conditions well within her powers of fulfilment, but which, so far, she has not fulfilled. Granted that the extent of the country is considerably greater than that of Japan or Siam, surely for a highly intellectual race, as the Chinese rightly claim to be, and one which historically and traditionally has always affected to"despise the other" two, to moan that they are still under foreign tutelage is a lamentable confession of weakness and incompetence. The truth is that China has not attempted to raise her own international status. It must be admitted that there are many difficulties in her path, but they are of her own making — difficulties created by personal ambitions, the purloining of fiduciary funds, the predominating rivalry between North and South, the idiosyncrasies of revolting troops and, latterly, subservience to the Bolsheviks. These difficulties, not foreign—particularly British—Imperialism, constantly impede all sincere efforts to establish a stable central government and secure administrative and political progress.

"The image maker does not worship the gods: he knows what they are made of," says an old Chinese proverb. The naval patrols are few: they guard Chinese and foreigners alike from the attacks of pirates who infest the rivers.

THE SLIGHTEST PROTEST ON THE PART OF OUR PEOPLE WHO ARE TOILING TO AMASS WEALTH, NOT FOR CHINA BUT FOR FOREIGN CAPITAL, ARE BEING SHOT DOWN IN COLD BLOOD AS FOREIGN SLAVES WERE BY THE PATRICIANS IN ANCIENT ROME, — FROM THE TREMENDOUS RESERVOIRS OF OUR AGRICULTURAL POPULATION, THESE CONCESSIONS DRAW HUNDREDS OF CHEAP LABOURERS INTO SHOPS AND FACTORIES IN THE CONCESSIONS, WHERE THEY BECOME DEFENCELESS SLAVES TO BE EXPLOITED IN MEDIAEVAL FASHION, BEATEN INTO DUMB SUBMISSION AND SHOT DOWN WITHOUT MERCY BY HIRED SOLDIERS AND POLICE FROM THE MOST BACKWARD PORTIONS OF THE WORLD. These horrors are so graphically descriptive of actual conditions and evyents in Soviet Russia that one is tempted to see the red hand wielding the red-hot pen. But let the credit be given to Mr. Wu Hon-man. After all we do live in the 20th century; and mediaeval barbarism now finds favour only in Russia. I said only in Russia; sometimes it is practised in Canton. In June 1925 we had a mediaeval outburst there; when the Yunnanese soldiers whom the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen brought in to help him were ousted by the redoubtable Whampoa Cadets, the flower of the Cantonese army, not so much in open fight as by "strategy." Leaflets were dropped into the city, where the Yunnanese had retired, promising them life and liberty if they surrendered. When the Yunnanese laid down their arms they were slaughtered; the hooligans of the town lending a hand.

headline: COOLIE HIRE
text: Exceptionally high rates of wages were paid in respect of coolie hire at the beginning of the strike and these have been gradually reduced with the continued return to more normal conditions until the figure now stands at 60 cents a day. The Government have now circularised all departments that from August 1 no casual labour must be employed and that all about must be paid for at the usual monthly rates.

headline: THE POWERS AND CHINA. / FOREIGNERS' SAFETY DEPENDENT ON / RIGHTS
text:
WU HON-MAN'S CLAIMS ANALYSED.

The key-note of the following analysis of a statement made by Mr. Wu Hon-man, prominent member of the Canton Government, may be said to be the claim that extraterritoriality cannot be abandoned until the growing strength of China enables her to maintain the right of administering protection and impartial justice within her borders.

Mr. Wu Hon-man, the “Minister” of Foreign Affairs of the self-appointed “Nationalist” government of Canton, has indited, or caused to be indited, a Manifesto addressed to the peoples of the world. It specifies the tribulations of China through her contact with foreign Imperialism. Whatever we may think of the Canton government as a “Government,” we must concede the prize to its Fabrication Bureau. This manifesto, is a remarkable document: it uses words so skilfully in a Pickwickian sense that the questions resulting are not those of veracity but of method. And in places it wipes out the frontier between reality and dreams. It was published in the “Canton Gazette” of the 9th July, and we may be sure that copies have been supplied to various revolutionary leaders and organisations, and to others who are sufficiently unacquainted with the true facts to be deceived by plausible insinuations.

Mr. Wu Hon-man makes himself the spokesman of the "nationally minded people of China." Before examining his statements it is desirable to examine his status. Who is Mr. Wu Hon-man? He is an official of an unrecognised, revolutionary party at present in power in Canton, the fountain-head and focus of China's unrest. This government is attempting, with generous assistance from its Bolshevik sponsors, to throttle the unfortunate people under its sway. It rules nominally over the Kwangtung province, which represents about five per cent. of the area and eight per cent. of the population of China. It is no more representative of true Chinese thought and aspirations than, say, Cuba is of America. I lay no stress on the opening hyperbole of Mr. Wu Hon-man's diatribe. It is merely a rhetorical exaggeration of Dame Partington's historic attempt to sweep the Atlantic from her doorstep. He predicts that unless the peoples of the world give urgent attention to his warning, "a new universal tragedy will be enacted in the Pacific Ocean. It will then be too late for you to help to extinguish the conflagration." But in quoting his serious statements I lend them the conspicuity of capitals.

Foreigners' Protection. The document states that all the confusion in China is due to her unequal international status. The key to China's internal trouble is extraterritoriality. Mr. Wu Hon-man says the agitation is not due to alien and subversive influences. CHINA HAS AWAKENED TO THE PAINFUL REALISATION THAT SHE IS NOT AN INDEPENDENT COUNTRY LIKE JAPAN, RUSSIA, ENGLAND, FRANCE, ITALY OR THE UNITED STATES. Apart from the ethics of this vexed question of extraterritoriality, the necessity for the measure remains. It is perfectly obvious. It is one of right, of fact rather than of principle. In earliest times the Tyrian voyager along the coasts of the Mediterranean secured only such rights as he could buy or enforce. With the extension of the Roman dominion the paa Romana spread, and every citizen travelling was under the segis of the Jus Romanum. The idea, like many other Roman legal ideas, came to stay, Chinese in Europe enjoy the security and justice of well-considered and properly enforced laws, which include the rights of extraterritoriality for their Ministries and Consulates. Have conditions in China ever encouraged us to believe that Europeans would be secure in person and property without the defence of their nations? Extraterritoriality in China is a remedy for the intolerable situation of the first half of the 10th century. It was designed for the protection of certain juridical rights. There are laws in China—interniable codes of Regulations for civil criminal and judicial procedure. But they are generally abortive. It would seem that in their efforts to deter crime the local Justinians overreached themselves and the severity of their laws like the laws of Levantics have fulfilled their application. Leaving Europe and America out of consideration if China is not an independent country like Japan, the fault is entirely her own China.

headline: Labour Conditions.
parent_headline: THE POWERS AND CHINA. / FOREIGNERS' SAFETY DEPENDENT ON / RIGHTS
text: Let us consider Mr. Wu Rongman's fanciful statement about the exploitation of the labouring classes. The conditions of labour in China, bad as they are, have not been introduced into the Far East by foreign capitalism. They are indigenous in China. Yet in the concessions and foreign-owned factories and mills the wages are higher, the task lighter and the working hours shorter than anywhere outside. The "slaves" go there voluntarily and eagerly because the conditions are much better than in the surrounding country. For examples of the cruel way in which workers are being exploited by Chinese outside the Concessions, I quote from the letter of the Rev. G. T. Warren, which was published in the "Times" of June 12, 1925. Mr. Warren lived in Changsha and Hankow for forty years. In both these places, he says, hundreds of children under ten work eighteen hours a day for seven days a week for food only—and an insufficient supply of that—at tailoring, weaving and even as apprentices to tin-smiths and blacksmiths. And Mr. Warren relates a case of cold-blooded murder by the Chinese authorities. An incident occurred in a Chinese-owned mill at Changsha over a trifling question of a small allowance. This led to a slight demonstration without violence or damage to property. Within twenty-four fours two men who were supposed, perhaps rightly, to have been leaders were arrested in the street at dusk and taken to the Governor's headquarters. The next morning their decapitated bodies were lying outside the city gates. No legal help could have been obtained at the trial, if they had one, and no witnesses or documents could have been produced. There was a sequel to this affair. In the same jurisdiction four lads under twenty had been imprisoned for four months, not only without trial but without any kind of formal accusation. The Chinese Governor urgently needed someone to translate into English a letter to the People in which he defended his查訪 in executing the two labour ladders.

We know that the industrial conditions in foreign mills in China are undoubtedly superior to anything prevailing in the native mills; we know that the failure to secure the attendance of the two thirds majority of the Shanghai ratepayers which was necessary before reforms in all mills could be instituted was due to the deliberate abstention of a section of the ratepayers who were not British and who had been influenced to that course by owners whose mills would be most affected by the proposed reforms; we know, too, that the British Government proposed to take further steps to legislate in the event of the deadlock resulting from the absence of a quorum continuing. Unfortunately, the proportion of informed to uninformed would be at its lowest amongst those readers of a journal which has come to be regarded as the organ of the "working man" and whilst in many cases the allegations of "British oppression" will conflict with the innate good sense and reason of the "working man" and lead him to a true appraisement of their value, there will be many homes in which credence will be placed in such statements through lack of information to the contrary and the equally untrue statements of members of a certain political party which have redounded in the Far East to their everlasting discredit. It was to counteract the influence at Home of such gross misrepresentations that the Hongkong resolutions (now supported by Amoy and likely to be further supported in the near future by Shanghai) were despatched Home for publication, but if the "champions of the working class" have descended to such depths in their efforts to prove the Government in the wrong and to weaken its hands,

It is doubtful if they will allow to be published in their organs what amounts to a grave censure on themselves. As a result there will still be many at Home who will not have a chance of being able to judge for themselves the falseness even of such statements as the following:—“At the bottom of the trouble is the exploitation of the Chinese people by the foreign industrialists in whose interests these costly warships are being despatched to China.” In a previous article we gave it as our considered opinion that at “the bottom of the trouble” was Bolshevik activity and almost it would seem that certain British organs and politicians are going out of their way to encourage it.

headline: SCHOOLBOYS.
text: If striking or absenting servants are to be punished, it follows that schoolboys who set such a bad example must also be punished. It seems simple logic and simple justice. And if the former did so because of fear—craven or otherwise—then the punishment in the case of schoolboys must be doubly severe; for schoolboys are in the first line of intelligent thought, and of course, know no fear! But, Mrs. Beeton again—first catch your schoolboy striker. And this, in addition to the facts in connection with this particular matter suggests the thought that heads of schools would be far better engaged in considering the effect of their past teaching and influence, and taking steps to make it more perfect than it is. It is possible to write and speak a considerable amount of rubbish on education in Hongkong, and on this subject very few angels step in where fools do not fear to tread. The fact is that a number of Europeans are set in the midst of hordes of boys and young men and expected to give them the essence of Western education. The teachers are European and the young people are Chinese. The hours of tuition bear no comparison with the hours that boys are either in the home or the street. A boy may not even be under direct parental control but under the somewhat hazy guidance of a person known as a guardian. In addition it has to be remembered that just as there are what is known as "rice-christians," there are also those who may be termed "rice-educationists"—the many who desire a smattering—for time and money does not allow of anything else—of that which may possibly help to get them some sort of office positions. This somewhat sketchily states the position; it is designed to show the difficulties attached to local education, which must be the despair of the idealists in a singularly important profession. In addition, it has to be remembered that the schoolboy comes into a contact with masters and superiors, that has hitherto been unknown to him, and, being treated as a supposedly intelligent entity, is prone to lose a sense of proportion, and, in homely phase, being offered an inch, takes a mile. Above all there is the universal schoolboy spirit—not unknown in Britain—which is quickly roused, passionate, idealistic, and at heart intensely patriotic. Who will deny that the Chinese schoolboy has not been moved with a sense of wrongly inspired patriotism which has moved him to acts of foolishness? If this is agreed, shall we blame the boy or the system or influence which has had no effect upon him in a great crisis, and shall we stoop to punishment where it can be inflicted without any possibility of injustice being done? We are certainly in favour of a measure of punishment, leaving the declaration of that punishment to those in a position best to decree and administer it. In this way, it is likely that youthful culprits will see the error of their ways, and be inclined to use a little thought in future actions. For it is thought that needs to be insisted upon. And if seventeen professors need it, how more, seventeen hundred, or seventeen thousand schoolboys. Suggestions have been made by heads of schools as to future methods. A crisis is of no use if it has not taught anything; and this particular crisis will have been of no avail if it has not urged Heads of Schools, teachers, the Education Department, and the members of the Education Board, to take serious thought for the morrow and to see wherein it is possible to lead to a reasonable state of efficiency. The nation that has the schools has the future, said Bismarck. In the case of Hongkong and the larger case of China, that has still to be proved.

headline: FATAL DIVE.
text:
INQUEST ON INDIAN DRIVER.

An Indian mule driver attached to the Army Service Corps-dived from a barge into the R.A.S.C. camber at the Hongkong Naval Yard on July 7 and was drowned. An inquest was held yesterday at the Kowloon Magistracy to inquire into the circumstances.

A fellow Indian mule driver said that he, the deceased and four other men were on guard at the Naval Yard in connection with the strike. After the tiffin interval on the day in question witness went to the camber for a swim, and while on an anchored steamer to which he had swum he observed deceased about to pump into, the water. Witness called to him that the water was deep but he took no notice. He rose to the surface once and then disappeared. Witness swam to the spot but could find no trace of the body.

L/Cpl. C. F. Masters, East Surreys, who was N.C.O. in charge of the guards, said he saw the deceased jump into the water from a barge and as he did not re-appear, witness had the barge removed, thinking that he might have been caught underneath. He then dived into the water followed by others and grappleings were obtained from the water police. Nothing was seen of the body, however, until it rose to the surface 24 hours afterwards.

Staff Sergt. Finlayson, of the Royal Army Service Corps, in reply to a question by the Coroner, Mr. E. W. Hamilton, as to whether he had received orders regarding swimming in the camber, said that no one was supposed to unless a life boat was in attendance.

Capt. E. W. Morris, in command of the corps, said that he was not aware that Indians bathed in the camber. Since the fatality strict orders had been issued that nobody was allowed to bathe in the Naval Yard basin.

The Coroner found that the deceased met his death through an accident. If the unfortunate man had not either deliberately or ignorantly disobeyed orders the accident would not have occurred. No blame could be attached to anyone.

headline: POETIC CHINA. / RAILWAY CENTENARY; TRIBUTE.
text:
On July 3 the delegates to the tenth International Railway Congress were entertained at the waggon works by the London and North-Eastern railway—an event which explains why the railway centenary is being celebrated now instead of in September. Railwaymen from most countries where the steel offspring of Stephenson's genius link town and country and sea together have met in England for that conference. Mainly through the initiative of workmen on the Italian railways, a handsome bronze shield was presented in recognition of Great Britain's record as the railway pioneer. But another tribute, sent all the way from China, is of at least equal interest. It takes the form of three exquisitely embroidered scrolls, the black Chinese characters showing in bold relief against the golden background. Mr. Chin Chun Wang, chief delegate of the Chinese Government to the International Railway Congress, has translated the message of the scrolls as follows:— In celebration of the centenary of the first British railway:

Here a century ago was born the world-wida system of rail

Here to-day are gathered representatives of all nations in praise and celebration, conquering spaces and linking seas and land. Leading progress and prosperity hand to hand. Oh! yo' inventor, great benefactor of mankind. Yea, we shall ever enshrine thee in our hearts and grateful mind. With hearty congratulations, KUNG CHAO YEN, Minister of Communications, Peking.

headline: SCHOOLS AND THE STRIKE.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—First of all let me say that I think the students in the Hongkong Schools had very little to do with and very little influence in the strike, and that any students who caused trouble should be treated as children and punished accordingly. Secondly, the fees at all Government Schools should be carefully revised. The trouble began in the Government School, Queen's College, where the fees are much too low and are the same as they were in 1910, viz. $60 per annum for a Day Boy. Several other schools in the Colony, Church and Mission Schools and Private Schools, have much higher fees and have raised their fees in recent years; for example, the fees at some schools are as high as $160 or more per annum for a Day Boy. I do not advocate that all fees should be the same, but it is worthy of note that to educate a boy in a Grant-in-Aid Non-Government School costs the Government, on the average, about one-quarter the cost in a Government School like Queen's College, for the same type of education.

I beg to suggest that the Government should

(1) Fine $10 all boys who were absent from Queen's College on June 18, and refuse them admittance to all other schools in the Colony.

(2) In future, charge an Entrance Fee of $10 for all new boys at Queen's College.

(3) Double or increase the fees at all Government Schools.

(4) Forbid all other schools in the Colony, Grant-in-Aid and Private Schools, to admit boys who leave Queen's College without meeting the conditions laid down.

(5). Have a more strict inspection of all schools teaching work up to Matriculation Standard, and not controlled by and/or staffed with at least one Euro-

(6) Keep in touch more closely, through English Inspectors, with the Vernacular Schools.

(7) Give the Heads of Shoals regular opportunities of discussing educational matters with the Education Department and have several Heads of Schools on the Board of Education.—Yours, etc.,

headline: DRIVER'S CLAIM.
text:
A taxi-cab driver claimed in the Summary Court yesterday, $100 deposited with his previous employers, the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxicab Company.

This money was deposited by him when he signed a contract with the Company and if his service had been continued would have been returned to him at the end of three years.

His Lordship held that the contract covered the action of the employers and that the man could not claim the return of the money.

Mr. M. K. Lo applied for permission to amend his claim to one of damages for wrongful dismissal and this was granted, the case being adjourned sine die.

Mr. Turner, of Messrs. Johnson, Stokes & Master, represented the Taxi-Cab Company.

headline: MOMENTOUS MATTERS.
text:
All eyes now, and for some time to come, should be on Shanghai. We must remember that if there had been no outbreak at Shanghai, there would probably have been no trouble—or the Canton "Government" would have had no immediate cause to provoke trouble with a place that has been consistently friendly with the Cantonese and has, at various times, proved a safe harbourage for absconding officials, some of whom have not been courageous enough to face music of which they have called the tune. The enquiry into the Shanghai outbreak will, we hope, lead to a satisfactory peace. If an unconscionable time has been taken in fixing up preliminaries, we must reconcile ourselves to the fact that it is the way of diplomacy to be slow, and that with a people prone to be slow themselves, caution is the first necessity. Hongkong shot to be deeply interested in the coming enquiry. It is likely that the Colony will be represented on the enquiry and it is

ability its representative will be the Chief Justice, Sir Henry Gollan. This would be an excellent appointment. The thing demands the calm and legal mind, able to sift evidence and to weigh it. But Hongkong's interest is beyond the question of a local appointment. Given a " satisfactory issue out of the enquiry, Canton has nothing to fall back upon in the way of excuses for encouraging strikers, fostering hatred, and ruining itself into the bargain. The result of the enquiry suggests another aspect. It suggests the reunification of the different and warring Chinese elements, who in their own antagonisms have done so much to place China where she is at the moment—the wilful child in the family of nations. It suggests China sober instead of China drunk. It suggests China developing her incomparable and vast natural resources; a competitor in the world's trade rightly demanding and meeting, respect; contributing not merely to the trade of the world, but to its arts and sciences. It is this China that foreigners desire to meet, to which end such institutions as the Hongkong University stand. The picture may suggest a measure of hyper-optimism; but without optimism there is no hope in Hongkong or China for anyone. Officials from Canton brave the journey to Peking. In ordinary circumstances a visit to Peking by a Cantonese official would be fraught with the gravest consequences—to his head! All this is altered. Factions and fractions can meet on what they believe is common ground—to resist the alleged intrusions of the perinacious foreigner. If they can be led to believe that the best weapon with which to resist, or meet the foreigner, is that of copying his trade methods—putting it on a material basis only—that will be great rain. It will be a great rain for Hongkong.

headline: Once Again.
text: Revolutions in Greece have become the veriest commonplace. As often as not almost Government succeeds Government in that unhappy country not by the constitutionally expressed wish of the people, but as the result of a coup d'etat. During mail week Greece experienced her seventh revolution in the space of 21 years. On this occasion naval and military leaders, in the persons of General Pangalos and Admiral Hadji Kyriakos, backed by the sailors and soldiers, simply walked in and took possession of the Government departments. For once, happily, there was no bloodshed. The usurpers, having made themselves masters of the situation by the mere demonstration of force, announced their willingness to approve of a Cabinet in which the two leaders of the revolt should hold respectively the portfolios of the Army and Navy—in other words, be virtual dictators. Whether Greece would be better off under a Dictatorship as in the case of Italy, or a Directorate, as in the case of Spain, it is not easy to say. What can be said is that, since the downfall of Venizelos, there has not been a more sadly misgoverned country in Europe—Russia hardly excepted—than Greece, and none which has become a more negligible factor in European councils. "Tis Greece, but living Greece no more."

thought of reason and no thought of the future, that future which we are helping to shape so that others may enjoy it,—or rue it? We have settled the servant question, after a fashion. It is the belief of many that it has not been settled; that there has been too much insistence on punishment and less on Christian justice, on which after all our laws are based. We have treated the servant in a manner that should make him sit up and take notice of himself; as an equal in intelligence and as an indispensable. We venture to suggest that the servant question will never be settled until a Commission of Enquiry has gone fully into the question of the status of servants; hours of labour and rates of pay, and until the Government-despised registration scheme is in operation. In a word the matter demands sympathy. Similarly with regard to schoolboys—the striking variety. We have been greatly moved by the speech of Dr. Wan Man-kai at the meeting of the Education Board. Dr. Wan combines in himself all the elements of Chinese courtesy, dignity and commonsense. It is but a truism to say so. And he is entitled to be heard, not merely by reason of the above, but by his work along social, religious and medical lines. He rightly diagnoses the case but pleads for that sympathy with which even insane cases should be treated. We are not to be taken as retracting the approval that striking schoolboys should be punished. Dr. Wan favours that. But it is not weakness to agree that a considerable measure of sympathy should be tinged with the discussions and decisions which occupy this particular matter. That the Government has it under consideration is a matter of satisfaction. That its decision will be accepted without reproach—we hope goes without saying. It is not likely we think to make the mistake of treating fervour-stricken schoolboys as if they

were over-grown men of degenerate and tainted outlook. Make the punishment fit the crime by all means, but do not let it be such that in the future it can be said of patriotism that it is the last resort of a schoolboy.

headline: SYMPATHY.
text:
There is a saying that it is nice to have a giant's strength, but better still not to use it as a giant. Something of this feeling comes to us as the various aspects of the strike or boycott thrust themselves upon us. We are too prone to make this a personal or local affair—dwelling on our inconveniences, losses and worries—forgetting that the root cause is outside and beyond our boundaries and confines, and—we had almost written, our influence. But influence, even local, must have a great bearing, not merely on the ultimate issue, but on the future as well. We are agreed that Hongkong has no case of any sort to answer. We reiterate that our hands our clean, and that as exemplars we are beyond reproach. The Chinese—of all classes—have rights of domicile, freedom of action and justice, denied them in their own domain. We are, if the simile can be granted, giants, with the strength of giants. headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text:
STRIKE LIFE. yet to rise to give us the funny side of the strike—if there is one. There have been many interesting items noticed. Take for instance the instruction being given daily to would-be tram drivers and the eager way in which the newcomers are quick to grasp the details necessary to a successful driving of a tram car. There was the geyser-like eruption of water in the Wanchai district the other afternoon. The jet rose and maintained itself to the height of the shops and was a suspended piece of silver, and of sheer beauty. It lasted some time and must have helped to alter the overflow figures of the Water Authority. Curiosity has had great play wondering who the young lady is who was seen on certain afternoons perched on a Pedder Street verandah twanging a guitar or a ukulele, and the sight of fish vendors selling their catches from the sea to those of the Praya wall. There is also the newspaper man whose feats of ice-carrying, hosing the garden, buying food, deserve to be written in imperishable prose or poetry—at least he says so. He has discovered the ideal way of assisting in the washing. Handkerchiefs, for instance, can more easily be done when one is sitting in the bath. Also socks can be easily cleansed if they are on the feet with the wearer again sitting in the bath. The ability to meet troubles can be tested by the measure of looking on the humorous side of things. And—note this—it is not the humorous people who cause trouble; but the sad "serious" people, who, seeing through a glass darkly, and unable to measure their own insignificance; step in where angels fear to tread.
STUDENT BANDSComplaint is made that the organ of the students' Union is finding harbourage in the Colony
through a slackness in the censorship. Perhaps this particular journal is of the "Red Hot" variety. It should be if it portrays the feeling of the body of young men who take charge of China's destinies on the slightest provocation. This student body has sent forth preaching bands, although there is no evidence to show that any band has reached Hongkong to proselytise and convert—and raise funds. Manila has had a visit and presumably Singapore is next on the list. How much money is raised and what becomes of it? "Red Hot" blood needs sustenance, and doubtless there is a large expenditure in feasting—feasting let us readily admit of a simple character. It is well that the faithful who enjoy the privileges of foreign imperialism in other places should be made to realise that there is such a thing as a student Body. Britain having taken Hongkong, the Kowloon, then the New Territory and made every effort to extend her railway beyond Canton—the France and Britain have ever intention of extending their power over South China and even acquiring more of Chinese territory." Again:—"Canton is determined that Hongkong shall no dominate the situation in South China, Hongkong seems equally determined that it will, and it goes a long way toward balking many of Canton's ambitions' (italics ours). The preacher—o. speaker—goes on to allege that talk of a discreditable nature goes on in Hongkong against whatever party is in power in Canton Hongkong's failure to win the confidence and goodwill of South China, is ascribed in part to our alleged "inability to see things from the point of view of China as a republic." Hongkong has had "too much control of navigation of censorship of mails and cables control of news and almost of Canton's connections with the rest of China and of the world." Such things, it is said, counteract the good effect of the justice Chinese receive in Hongkong courts, "of the fair and even generous treatment of organizations like the Confucian Society....". These things, are forgotten, we are told "when there is too much condemnation of the Government of Canton or too much repression of news or rough treatment of coolies..." "Boy Scouts, rather than swear allegiance to King George, give up their organization." "The strike has been very effective." "Bolshevist influence is unquestionably great ever among educated people and right in Hongkong." "A cable from Hongkong says that they have begun to flog the strike leaders and that it is having a salutary effect." We could add to these quotations. We refrain even from commenting on them, merely pointing to their controversial aspect, to say nothing of the obvious falsity of some of them. We are merely charitable and say that here is yet another—an "Old China Hand"—who has "spoken unadvisedly with his lips."

headline: SHAMEEN AFFAIR. DANISH CONSUL'S REPORT.
text:
FIRST SHOTS FIRED BY CHINASE.

"Not A Shadow Of Doubt."

Further evidence that the firing in the Shameen incident began from the Chinese side is contained in the report of the Royal Danish Consul at Canton on the matter. The Consul writes:

By the present I have the honour to report on what took place here on the afternoon of Tuesday, the 23rd inst. when the Chinese held a procession demonstrating against the foreigners for the abolition of the existing treaties and extraterritorial rights.

To start with it is as well to mention the events leading up to the unfortunate affair on Tuesday, the 23rd.

On the 6th June a battle started between the Canton Government troops and the Yunnanese, who had occupied Canton city in an endeavour to overthrow the existing red Government headed by Civil Governor Hu Han-min. The Yunnanese were defeated and driven out on the 12th June, and the Canton Government proclaimed that peace and order would now be restored for the benefit of the people. However, towards the end of the following week it was clear that student agitators were busy fomenting a strike against the foreigners under the pretext of sympathizing with those killed in the Shanghai affair of 30th May, and on Saturday, the 20th the usual British river steamer from Hongkong failed to put in an appearance, the crew having gone out on strike in Hongkong. At the same time rumours got about that all Chinese servants employed by foreigners on Shameen would cease work the following day, and on Sunday morning, the 21st at 9 a.m. all servants left their employ. On Monday all crews employed on foreign-owned motor-boats and launches walked out, so that by this time the Island was entirely deserted of Chinese and the foreigners practically cut off from communication with the outside world. On Monday it was further known that the Chinese students and others intended holding a procession the following day as a demonstration against the foreigners, and it leaked out that at a meeting held at the Kwangtung University the agitators were determined to enter Shameen and/or would create an incident for propaganda purposes. H.B.M. Consul-General on hearing this immediately warned the Secretary for Foreign Affairs that any attempt made on Shameen would be met by armed forces.

Forewarmed Forearmed. Preparations to meet any emergency were already made during the previous weeks' fighting by the Municipal Council of the British Concession of Shameen by calling up Volunteers for Special Police duty, and the actual defence of the Island was in the hands of British and French naval forces, who had erected sand-bagged machine-gun posts at various points along the creek facing the city. During the morning of Tuesday, the 23rd it was noticed from Shameen that motor-cars passing along Shakee Street—the street on the Canton side of the creek separating the island from the city—were distributing circulars and leaflets, which later on proved to be inflammatory pamphlets calling upon all and sundry to rise against the foreigners and drive them out of Shameen.

The procession commenced shortly after 2 o'clock and I personally watched the demonstration from the verandah of the "Victoria Hotel," facing Shakee from the beginning and was therefore an eye-witness of all that happened. The procession was headed by mounted and dismounted police, and then came on in sections consisting of various units comprising students of different schools, labourers, boy scouts, and a sprinkling of girl students, all waving flags and banners and shouting towards Shameen. One of the last units was headed by a brass band of small boys, this being said to be the Canton Christian College students. First Shots Up to this time the procession was perfectly orderly and just resembled any ordinary similar political demonstration in Europe in fact so much so that I remarked to a bystander on the orderly behavior of the crowd. But at

labourers gesticulated more threatening towards Shameen and yelled fierce than their predecessors, and the next I saw was that a fully armed military force with arms at the slope and led by mounted officers followed in their rear. When these had reached up to the corner of the lane leading into the city from Messrs Li and Fung's I suddenly saw the Chinese crowd of spectators stampede in wild panic, as if being warned of danger, and simultaneously the soldiers got their arms from the slope, cocked rifles and the first shots rang out. Bullets were flying all over where I was standing, and I leaped for safety in through the hotel window where I had to take cover behind pillars against the rain of bullets aimed at the hotel. The fire was immediately returned by the British and French naval machine gun units posted along Shameen followed by the Shameen Police force in the Police Station and Hotel, and was aimed entirely at the attacking military forces across the creek, which were said to be the Whampoa cadets under their Russian leaders. The Procession proper had, when firing started, reached the English bridge, and was therefore out of the danger zone. The actual firing took place between the French and the English bridge and was kept up by the Shameen defenders for about 10 minutes, while the troops on Shakee kept up intermittent snip-ing from the house tops for about an hour and a half after Shameen had ceased firing. The French gunboat stationed off the French concession participated with about 8 shots from their heavy artillery, but these I was later told were blank rounds. The casualties on the Shameen side numbered one French civilian killed outright and two British civilians wounded. As to the casualties on the other side the figures are very conflicting, but must have been heavy.

Later in the afternoon when firing had ceased I observed from the Shameen Police Station how the Chinese collected a large number of dead bodies stripped of their clothes in a small side street just opposite and brought a photographer along to photograph the scene. It is, of course, superfluous to enlarge on the purpose for this action.

In view of the fact that the Canton Government immediately after the incident saw fit to notify the Consular Body, and in particular the British and French Consular Representatives, that the firing had started from Shameen and that therefore the foreign authorities were responsible for the affair, I have availed myself of this opportunity to bring before His Danish Majesty's Government the actual facts as seen by myself. There is not a shadow of doubt in my mind that the affair was pre-arranged; and the fact that fully armed troops in great numbers took part in an otherwise peaceful demonstration precludes any doubt as to the intentions of the organisers, for which the Chinese Government must be held responsible the more so as they were previously warned against the consequences of such an action.

CANTON, 25th June, 1925, (Sd.) WALLACE J. HANSEN, Consul.

The Hongkong Trading Co. Ltd.

Take, for instance, the case of European importing and exporting firms in Hongkong. In the volume of business done in the ordinary course with the Chinese there is proof of the desire on the part of China for the materials that British firms supply. Through the machinations of an alien Power the Chinese are prevented from exercising a free choice, and so long as the Canton Government remains under the influence of Bolshevist agitators it is doubtful if any trade at all in the generally accepted sense of the word will be possible. Meanwhile, with the gravity of the situation as regards financial obligations increasing with every week that the present state of affairs is allowed to continue, the merchant has cause to wonder if there is not something wrong with an organisation which does not permit of Hongkong making direct representations to the Home Government on matters concerning South China, unless they occur within the territory within its jurisdiction. It is this lack of coordination which has been responsible to a considerable extent for the delay which may mean financial ruin for firms even of considerable standing. Shameen being under the Foreign Office, the Consul General there has to conduct all negotiations through the Ambassador in Peking, he in turn has to negotiate with a Government which is supposed to have recognised a southern Government

In any event, representations it wishes to make officially, must go through the Colonial Office which has no power but may, if it chooses, pass such on to the Foreign Office. Thus it comes about that when Hongkong desires to represent its views to the Home Government direct on happenings at Shameen and Canton which directly concerns it, for Canton is South China so far as business is concerned and trade with Canton is almost entirely directed from Hongkong, a public meeting has to be called and cablegrams despatched on the initiative of the conveners.

It would perhaps be too much to expect the Home Government to establish what might become an awkward precedent in placing a Crown Colony under the administration of the Foreign Office, but Hongkong's opinion must in the future be more clearly voiced in councils of deliberation at Home on affairs concerning it. Such a vital matter may well be one to commend to the consideration of our new Governor, the Hon. Mr. C. Clementi.

headline: A BEGINNING.
text:
Straws are said to show which way the wind is blowing. The first of what we may call a series of settlements in the north, may be taken to show that a beginning is being made in a return to reason. After three weeks' negotiations an agreement has been reached which provides, for resumption of work at the Japanese Cotton Mills. Nine companies, owning forty factories and employing 50,000 hands, are concerned. Three weeks may seen a considerable length of time in which to settle a presumably simple matter—the antagonism having been on one side only. The agreement puts the Japanese owners in a very creditable light. It must, at the outset, cause the indifferent and the ignorant to think that capitalists are not so bad as Bolsheviks and a certain type of Socialist would have us believe. The owners of the mill where rioting took place have offered the wounded and relatives of those killed $10,000. We trust this offer will not be taken as a sign of weakness. It seems easy to convince the unlettered, untutored, and unthinking mass of labour in China that its ends can easily be attained by a "little" strike, and possibly a "little" bloodshed. If such is the case it should be quickly contradicted. Think of Chinese capitalists acting similarly! The further clauses of the agreement suggest that there is not one of them that could not have been obtained by peaceful, if persistent representations. The Labour movement in China is likely to approximate to that which exists elsewhere: numbers of guilds or unions, controlled by paid officers, who, in order to "earn their salt" are likely to exert undue influence and willfully foment unnecessary trouble. Peaceful representations would, in time, have gained such things as increase in wages where such was found to be necessary; the recognition of organised Labour Unions; and the other things included in the agreement. The vexed question of strike pay enters into the matter and here there seems a diplomatic victory for both sides. No strike pay is to be given, but as the reluctant strikers suffered through the loss of wages during the long strike, the millowners will compassionately extend reasonable help to the workers. Hongkong should be particularly interested in this part of the agreement; for it establishes a precedent from which it will be difficult to get away, if, and we do not suggest it, it is desired to do so. For Hongkong cannot ignore the fact that many of its strikers have been reluctant, although it can be argued, and probably proved, that they suffered no particularly big loss, seeing that many of them have been shepherded in Canton and enjoyed notoriety so much enamoured of certain types of Chinese minds. The money question is likely to play a great part in any effort at settlement which may come from the other side and those called upon to negotiate should know what they are likely to think about before entering any meeting room. headline: PLAIN FACTS.
text:
It is not certain if the proposed meeting of farewell to H.E. the Governor before he leaves Hongkong is to take place. Sir Edward Stubbs's departure cannot be long delayed. He is due to receive certain addresses which have already been prepared and extensively signed. We trust the proposed meetings will not be abandoned but that the Colony will have an opportunity, in true British fashion, of voicing its feelings of appreciation of His Excellency's great services. Painting the lily is not an attracted pastive; therefore we desist from an occupation which has become frequent in regard to departing officials. Our desire for at least one farewell meeting is selfish—if this is the correct word to use. We desire to hear more of the representations which have been made to the Home Government and the steps taken if any, to bring order out of an unnecessary chaos. If we cannot hear all that has been told and

done, or contemplated, we can at least be told of some of the things, and, coming from His Excellency's own lips, this should give the assurance and confidence that the Colony seems to need. For the spirit of restlessness is abroad. Impatience is rife. There is a temptation to judge harshly, to speak unadvisedly, and to suggest extreme measures. The plain man cannot always grasp the ways of diplomacy; or see the sense of a policy of what he describes as drift. The issues are plain. They demand plain measures. If we had less of diplomacy and more of the courage of conviction and the sense of the righteousness of a cause, there would be no loss of time in right-ing wrings. It is along such lines as these that the individual is inclined to think; and the thinking expands with a continuance of silence. It may be that His Excellency has nothing to add to what he presumes is known, and feels no good would be done by reiterating it. This may be so, but a word from the Governor would have enormous effect, even if couched in the language of diplomacy. His "rose-water" methods have so far been successful. They were brought into force to make strikers and intimidators feel that Hongkong was not a safe place for them. It was not expected that in the larger issues they would have any effect except that of helping to stiffen the "stiff-necks" of the present Canton Government. In the larger spheres, the work of conciliation or of the use of force is in other hands. Can His Excellency tell us that they are in good hands, and that wildness of utterance—and action—should be curbed to the limit? His Excellency being a man of like passions will readily understand the plight of the plain man in attempting to understand conditions. He has heard of the plight of his nation as in Switton.

headline: HOBBS.
text:
The impetus which has been given to golf, bathing and other pastimes in Hongkong since the first strenuous weeks following the strike bespeaks the involuntary call for temporary forgetfulness in times of prolonged depressing circumstances. It was probably with something of the same sort of feeling that most of us turned from matters admittedly of more pressing importance to the news contained in yesterday's cable of the fine accomplishment of Jack Hobbs, the cricketer. By scoring two centuries for Surrey against Somerset he has beaten Dr. W. G. Grace's record of 126 centuries in first-class cricket. It does not necessarily follow, of course that he qualifies by reason of this record for a place of equal eminence in the history of batting to the great "W.G." who is looked upon as the "unapproachable," but apart from the question of relative merit with batsmen of past ages one thing is certain and that is that Hobbs must always rank with the great ones and that he is the greatest batsman of the day. Modest, quiet and typical when in action of the very poetry of batting he has become the idol of present day cricket, and the thousands who congest the tube from the City when there is a chance of seeing him at the wicket, also thousands of others to whom he is only a name, will join in congratulating him on carving an even more secure niche for himself in the ladder of fame. He has not, in the opinion of those best qualified to judge, played at a time to give him the chance of doing full justice to his exceptional powers. When he forced himself into the first place the great bowlers had either ceased to bowl or were yielding reluctantly to the claims of age, but from the manner in which he tackled the googlies he then received and in the light of his demonstrations since, there appears to be no reason for holding any belief other than that if he had played for Surrey in the closing years of the nineteenth century he would have treated the fine bowling he would then have had every whit as cavalierly as he does the more mediocre bowling of the present day. One is reminded in thinking of the way in which he deals almost as he likes with the best bowlers of the day of the story of Shaw and "W.G." Shaw was asked if he was the better bowler or "W.G." the better bat, and in his reply he gave a definition of a great batsman which will last for all time: "I put them where I like, and he puts them where he likes." In that he treats the very best balls delivered in that way and has every stroke at his command it may be said of Hobbs that he will assuredly go down to fame somewhere among such names as the great W.G. BRASS TACKS. Redeeming a promise he made at Monday's public meeting to give the community an early opportunity to express its voice should London's reply to Hongkong's representations prove unfavourable, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Hqlyoak, who has become the Colony's mouthpiece, has duly called another public meeting for Tuesday to protest against the Home Government's apathy and to express our views in a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner. By holding such a meeting we may be said to be getting down to "brass tacks" to essentials of the gravest kind, from which we cannot and dare not depart—and what is more important—from which we do not want to escape. The most rapid practice must across that a won

patience has been shown by Hong- kong, and that the plea for inter- vention—by force if necessary— holds in it a great amount of justification. It is for these and other reasons that could, be ad- vanced, that we trust some clear and definite thought will be behind the meeting; that its resolutions will not be a collection of indignant words only, but that some plan of action will follow them as a matter of course. It might be argued that in holding these meetings and letting loose the vials of wrath, we are treating the “Government” at Canton a little too seriously; that we show an absence of knowledge of the mentality of Chinese, whose methods in “ways that are dark” has, are this, been noticed. The “utter ruin” of trade to which Mr. Holyoak refers, may counter this line of thought, and is prob- ably unanswerable. We can only suggest that when a settlement does come, the fact of this almost “utter ruin” will come into the settlement in no uncertain fashion: If mistakes are to be made by the other side: if they are wilful acts of malice? so much the worse will the reckoning be. Acts of war have already been committed; Shamean has been fired on; Chinese soldiers have crossed the border; supplies of merchandise from Hongkong have been looted; and crowning act of all, British and Japanese steamers have been banned from Canton and an embargo has been imposed against Hongkong. Almost every known law recognised by nations of standing has been broken, without any attempt at reprisal, and seemingly, without any official remonstrance with the exception of that given over the Shamean incident. We are peak once more for word from His Excellence the Governor. It is possible for him to do so, we trust his public meeting will have the presence or falling that that the resolutions will have as a result.

against the Colony, but in a greater degree it is an attack against the British Empire and for what it stands. The Colony should press the Premier to take action in the matter of the enquiry into the happenings at Shanghai which proved such an opening for action on the part of the self-styled Government at Canton. The delay in this particular matter has had its own evil effect on minds already evilly-disposed. As to Hongkong's position we have Mr. Holyoak's words that "it cannot be too clearly stated again that it is apparently still not realised that this is no question of a'strike' but of an organised and inspired attack upon British trade and interests in all our Treaty Ports and Concessions and upon this Colony in particular." This utterance cannot be questioned. It gives justification for the holding of a meeting to enable the Colony to voice its views and to dispel the apathy at Home. If it can do that it will undoubtedly bring matters to a head, and—who knows?—save the Chinese from themselves. But it is apparent that the Chinese need to be saved from the class of person who, almost without let or hindrance, constitutes himself a ruler—but not a leader—the class of person, who like a certain Duke of Plaza Toro, led his regiment from behind "because he found it less exciting."

It is probably as a result of similar doubts as to the effect of the application of the Cristian ethic to Chinese mentality which has led to conferences being held by foreign missionary bodies in China to consider whether the time has not yet arrived for the spiritual and secular education of China to be left with the Chinese themselves. "The Bulletin," an Australian paper of considerable standing, in reviewing the China situation and considering the effects of the introduction of an alien religion to China, uses words, which although referring to things spiritual rather than secular may be compared in general principle to those used by Dr. Tso.—"The Oriental teaching is that the individual's sole religious function is to provide in this world the means whereby his father and the myriads of his forefathers shall be kept in ease and plenty in the next. The missionary teaches that it is right for the son to leave his father, and follow a higher master and any member of an Asiatic family who finds the pressure of this system irks some can always secure a refuge in the Christian church. Thus it comes about that the missionary is feared and hated by every Eastern patriot for precisely the same reason as the early Christian socialists were feared and hated by every Roman patrician." The obvious reply to what may be considered a condemnation as a disintegrating force of the work of Christian bodies in China, is that their institutions and those under British Government supervision represent the only bulwark in China against the creed of Bolsheviks which is surely the greatest menace possible to Oriental ethics. According to these latter the father is the guardian of his family, the headman is the father of the village, the magistrate is the father of his province, and the ruler who derives his power from heaven is the parent of the lot, and the right to wield authority is based on the possession of a "superior" or educated mind.
