headline: URGENT NEEDS
text:
THE POLICY OF DRIFT CONDEMNED.

READER'S STRONG VIEWS.

From a correspondent who signs himself "J.C." we have received a letter dealing with local problems of the first importance. Owing to the pressure on our space to-day we are unable to publish the letter in full. Referring to the growing atmosphere of "tiredness and drift," J.C. writes:

"There is no excuse for any policy of drift, or for any easing down of our standards as regards the governance of the Colony. In one's wanderings round the city in the course of the day, one seems to notice everywhere a slovenliness and a slackness in the way that public work is being carried on. For example, the streets, before the strike, were always clean and well swept. Now, particularly at tram stops, they look as if they were never swept, or as if the cleaning up and washing away of rubbish depended on the wind and rain. Let one cast one's eyes up the side streets when going along the Praya East on a tram, and notice what a fearful state some of them are in. Not to spin out, what I have said about street cleaning, applies to most of the jobs that are in progress."

"Now let us leave the present and take a long view of the future of Hongkong. Surely by now the Government must have realised the public are not children and that it is quite safe to take them into their confidence as regards the broad outlines of their policy. We all applauded when the rounding up policy was inaugurated, and we can all see what a beneficial effect it has had, particularly in the criminal courts. What we would all like to know—and undoubtedly we are entitled to know—is what the policy is going to be in the future. Are we going to drift back to that miserable policy of admitting the lame, the halt and the blind, the criminals and Bolsheviks, who all make of Hongkong a happy hunting ground? Or are we going to continue the policy of frequent cleanups, followed by the deportation of undesirables? What is the real objection to a poll-tax?"

J.C. points out that the French and Americans are both able to collect a poll tax in neighbouring colonies and suggests that the revenue, amounting to millions even with the poll tax as low as $2 per head, would go a long way to fill “the nasty gap” the depression will make in the Colony's revenue.

"Is one a pessimist if one assumes that British business houses, both old and new, are going to be very badly hit in some cases, perhaps, even to drop out?" J.C. asks next. "Granted that, it means a big reduction of staffs, from top to bottom. One knows, also, that a very large proportion of British coast shipping is laid up, and that Norwegian, Japanese and others have got such a footing that it will be a long time before British shipping is running again at any profit. That means, in conjunction with the starvation wages paid in Norwegian and Japanese ships, that there will be any number of Britishers out of jobs on the China Coast."

Is it not time that some notice was taken of the increasing numbers of Russians who are flocking into the Colony? There was a time when Russians were forbidden to land here on the ground that Hongkong did not wish to have to face the problem that Shanghai was up against. It is quite time that our own problem of what is going to happen to our own people, who will be axed, during the coming winter, were thoroughly gone into. After pointing to the fact that Russians are doing work which could be done by Britons, J.C. remarks: It is quite time that the Government began to get busy on this problem of unemployment. They have the example of Singapore before them, and there is at present nothing to show that Hongkong may not have to endure just as long and severe a storm as Singapore faced, with practically the same problems. "Turning to another side of the problem, are the public not entitled to know what the Government are doing to trim ship and shorten sail, to meet the storm? After the recent inquests, with the summings up and the Juries riders, we all know that things in the P.W.D. are pretty rotten. Is the Government going to ignore the suggestion for an expert's inquiry into the working of the P.W.D.? With the lean times ahead, such inquiry should be extended into the whole question of whether the Colony is getting anything. It is getting either in the professional capabilities of the men engaged for their

headline: IN ROYAL ESTATE.
text:
KARAKHAN'S ARRIVAL IN HARBIN.

V SUMPTION'S CAR FROM C. H. R.

Just two years ago, Mr. L. M. Karukhan was met in Harbin, on his arrival from Moscow, by an enormous crowd of people. He was yesterday greeted by the Soviet citizens's of Harbin in such a manner as Kings and Emperors are accustomed to. A special train of eight cars, including the now celebrated No 56, was sent specially to Chingchun to bring him to Harbin and many representatives of the Russian Consulate and the C. B. R. went to meet him. Thousands of people crowded the roads to the Harbin railway station and literally hundreds of motor cars fought their way through the crowd. As the train steamed into the station, the symphony orchestra played the strains of the "International" and all eyes were fixed on car 56, where, however, only a Russian soldier was to be seen. Mr. Karukhan and suite happened to be in the observation car at the end of the train. As he descended from the curring, the air was rent with motor sirens and horns and the hurrabs of the thousands of people. He entered the large arrival room where fruit and champagne were served and he was introduced to heads of the Railway Departments and to the Chinese administrative chiefs. During this reception the brass band from the Railway Club played selections. After a quarter of an hour, the police made a road for the Soviet ambassador and his family, who entered motor cars and drove to a railway house which has been put at his disposal. Last night a banquet was served at the Chinese Administration quarters, and to-day there are three special fetings to Mr. Karakhan. The first is a lunch at the Railway Workman's Club, the first that this Club has ever given, the second a five o'clock ten at the Railway Club for the hands of all the railway departments and this evening a grand banquet at the Railway Club. To-morrow morning Mr. Karakhan leaves for Moscow, travelling in the special train as far as the frontier and in his special car right through to the end of the journey. The fitting up of this car has cost the C. B. R. a sum of thirty thousand dollars and no crowned head, has ever had such a sumptuous carriage to travel in.

"Finally, what about the servant question? The request for Registration was passed at the meeting with no dissentient voice. What is the use of girding at the Home Government for ignoring our united voice on Imperial affairs, if we are going to allow ourselves to be completely and contemptuously ignored by the local government in domestic affairs? headline: TOUGH BABY."
text:
8. "TRAFFIC COP" WHO SHOOTS TO KILL

TAMINO THIRE REDUL DUYBN.

London's traffic problem is a puzzling which seems to do the solution, yet Chief Constable Bassam, the Scotland Yard expert on street congestion, can at least be thankful that he has not the additional burdens imposed by America's epidemic of motor-car mania, writes Sir Percival Phillips in the "Daily Mail."

If ever the British working-man takes to motoring to and from his daily toil like the artisans in this country Mr. Bussom may well call for help. If ever the British motorist secumbs to the craze for speed minus regard for his fellow-men and with open contempt for the law, London will begin to realise that the age of petrol is not a blessing but a curse. The symbol of authority in this city of much made millionaires is a broad-shouldered, heavy-jawed individual of dangerously forbidding aspect, officially designated in our own language as a policeman on point duty, but known here as a "traffic cop," and by general consent admitted to be what Americans call a "long/baby."

Includers AND THE DEAD LINE. Invariably he looks like a prize-fighter, with a touch of the Wild West about him. "Toying with this person is akin to flirting with Death."

He wears semi-riding breeches and leggings and a close-fitting flannel shirt. Around his ample waist is strapped a belt filled with curtridges and on one hip reposes a heavy service revolver ready for action.

The whistle clenched between his teeth rules the world of trudlie. Trumwaly-ears, motor-ears, pedestrians move and halt and move again in obedience to its short, shrill blast.

Obedience is instant and complete — as a rule. But the motorist herabouts is naturally a rebellions individual—performs because this is technically a land of liberty—and he is inclined to drive when and where he pleases, regardless of others. But the "tough baby" has turned him. The loaded revolver is a more powerful independent to be good than a thousand municipal regulations.

The road bog and the blind breaker of traffic rules know that if they cross the dead line when halted trouble instant and devastating will follow.

It happened only this morning. A deerepit car, careened wildly through a maze of locked traffic, past the "tough baby" and his whistly, and staggered on its uncertain way. The three Nogroes inside may have been too frightened or too satiristed with near-gin to head the ominous shout. No Western sheriff ever "drew" quicker from the hip or fired more deliberately after the fugitives. Lead pattered on the roadway. No one was hit, but no blame for that attaches to the "traffic cop." He did his best.

These point-duty sharpshooters are hand-picked for the job. They are not interchangeable with ordinary policemen. Their sole duty is to rule the crowded streets. And they do.

America is "motor-car mad." The disease is having a profound effect on the whole social structure, and the "shoot-to-kill" traffic police represent only one phase of this change for the worse in everyday life. Crime has increased by leaps and bounds—crime of a highly specialised kind, involving the use of first cars:

London, September 15.—The “Times”. Manchester correspondent says one effect of the duties on imported artificial silk is the formulation of plans for its manufacture in Lancashire. It is understood that Sir Edwin Stockton will be chairman of one new company which is at present negotiating for a suitable factory. —Reuter.

headline: SOCIAL & PERSONAL
text:
A fiancée organised by the ship's company of H.M.S. "Ambrose" was held at the Royal Naval Canteen Theatre last night.

Lieutenant Michael O'Leary, V.C., has been appointed chief of police at Crystal Beach, near Buffalo, U.S.A.

His Excellency the Governor has been pleased to appoint Supper Frederick Wentworth Foster-Turner to be Second Lieutenant in the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps, with effect from September 13, 1925.

Between December and May next at least eight large tourist ships are due to arrive in Hongkong, each vessel carrying up to 400 or 500 round-the-world passengers. Arrangements are already being made by the local agencies in control of the tours.

The 'congregation of the Union Church, Kowloon, are celebrating the first Anniversary of the Church with a series of special services, commencing to-morrow with a service of thanksgiving and re-dedication. Any visitors who wish to join their anniversary celebrations will doubtless be gladly welcomed.

The following candidates in the China Command were successful in passing the officer's examination for promotion held in April:—Captains R. A. F. Montanaro, M.C., J. O. Carpenter, M.C., W. G. Kent, the East Surrey Regt. and J. E. Hume, D.S.O. the Loyal Regt. Lieut. J. R. A. Cockayne, the East Surrey Regt.

Captain J. P. Somerville, who originally went Home on retirement in September, 1920, after over 20 years' service on the China Coast is leaving by the six "Khyber. Capt. Somerville returned to the East in October, 1924, and has been employed on various coastal boats. Recently, he has had the misfortune to suffer bad health and has been in the Government Civil Hospital.

headline: FRENCH DEBT. / U.S. EXPERT'S 450-PAGE BOOK.
text: The report of Professor Harold Moulton on the French debt, consisting of 450 pages, which will be distributed to officials of the Commission, insists that it will be ruinous to ask France to pay according to the principle adopted in the negotiations with Great Britain. The author insists that France's budget must be adjusted. He recognises that France is unable to for several years. Professor Moulton concludes that the French people are as heavily taxed as are: the British and considerably more than the Americans.

headline: NIGHT ATTACK. / FIGHT RAGES UNTIL MORNING / FRENCH SYRIAN SUCCESS
text:
A message from Beirut states that a strong force of Druses last night attacked the French Garrison at Moussefre.

The fight raged until ten o'clock in the morning. The Druses retired leaving several hundred dead.

The French, who claim to have captured a Druse standard, suffered few casualties.

Belenguered Garrison.

The newspapers' reports from Beirut describe the situation at Jebel Druse as unsettled as ever. The new chief commander Gamelin is organising a force to relieve the Suieda garrison which is "daily reprovisioned and it is hoped will hold out.

headline: THE RIFF WAR. / ANOTHER SPANISH LANDING.
dateline: Paris, Sept. 18. CARLIEM CABLES. Paris, Sept
text:
FLANK LINE HELD.

(Reuter's Service.) Denis Sankt 10

A message from Fez says that the Spaniards effected another landing at Alhucemas Bay where they disembarked troops at Frailes, a point at the western extremity of Alhucemas Bay. They occupied a position three kilometres wide on the flank of the line already held by the Spanish troops in the Morronuevo peninsula.

French victory at Ribane has had a great effect on the Riffs. The news of its spread like wildfire among the insurrectionaries with the result that numerous negotiations for submission were opened by tribes along the whole front, who sent emissaries for that purpose.

The French casualties at Bibane were only thirty despite the vigorous resistance. In the meanwhile consolidation is continuing. The French artillery and aircraft are bombarding enemy concentrations. The French captured some perfectly and most modernly organised munition dumps near Amjot. The enemy moved some of the large munition dumps northward.

"The Journal" publishes a report from Melilla that a proclamation has been issued by the Sultan of Morocco offering 500,000 francs for the capture of Abd el Krim or his brother, alive or dead. The proclamation has been broadcast among the tribes, including the insurgents.

headline: TSARIST PLOT
text: Three Tsarist Russians (all white guardists) and two from Bulgaria have been arrested at the instance of the Soviet Embassy which alleges that they were concerned in a plot to murder the new Soviet Minister, Bersin, at Bucharest.

headline: THE IMMEDIATE PROBLEMS.
text:
First, with regard to Shanghai we are about to hold a public judicial inquiry into the riots. This is not an attempt to whitewash anybody, but is designed to bring all the facts out and ensure that justice shall be done. We have tried to get the Chinese Government to appoint representatives, but, much to our regret, the Chinese Government has refused.

Secondly, negotiations have been begun between the diplomatic bodies at Peking and the Chinese Government on subjects connected with Shanghai though not in connection with the actual riots. One of the subjects so discussed is the representation of the Chinese on the Municipal Council of Shanghai. At present the rate-payers elect the Council, which in practice means the Europeans. The Council consists of Europeans, Americans, and Japanese, and its present chairman is an American.

Thirdly, the British Government seeks to arrange a collective answer by all the Powers to the various Chinese Notes that have been presented, and particularly to the Note of July 24, in which the Chinese complained of the unfairness of the various treaties. Our wish is that this Note should be a declaration of policy by all the Powers. The first thing is to carry out the conclusions of the Washington Conference, and the first step is the Tariff Conference, which is now very soon to be held. At the same time there follows the setting up of a commission to inquire into the whole subject of extraterritoriality.

The collective answer of the Powers to the Chinese Notes is still under consideration. It will be a slow business, because a complete consultation involves sixteen Powers with a right to be consulted. The British Government lays the great stress upon this collective action, and has the greatest interest in any action being collective, because there is an attempt in China, largely due, as the Foreign Office believes, to Russian Influence, to isolate Great Britain and represent her as the villain of the piece. headline: COAL THEFT. / LAUNCH MEN IN TROUBLE.
text:
IMPORTANT KOWLOON CASE

Fraudulent conversion of five tons of coal entrusted to their care, with the alternative charge of larceny of the coal, was preferred against three men from the Blue Funnel launch "Poseidon" at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday. Two other members of Messrs. A. S. Watson's launch "Tai Yuk Fong" were charged with receiving the coal knowing the same to have been stolen or unlawfully obtained.

Mr. D. McCallum, appearing for the three Blue Funnel launch men, objected to two charges being preferred against his clients in alternative forms, but this was not upheld.

Mr. J. M. d'Almada Renedios defended the alleged receivers.

Mr. T. G. Bennett, who prosecuted on behalf of the complainants, the Ocean Steamship Company, asked for a committed to the Sessions.

The story for the prosecution was that the transfer of coal was noticed to be going on from the "Posidon" to the "Tai Yuk Fong." The superintendent of Holt's wharf was informed and on an inspection being made it was discovered that about five tons of coal had been transferred from the Blue Funnel launch. The boatswain was paid $860 per month to purchase coal and pay the wages of the crew of the "Tai Yuk Fong," while the requirements of the "Posidon" were attended to by the Company.

After evidence had been called the case was adjourned till this afternoon.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / LINER SAILS FROM CAPE TOWN.
text:
Cape Town, September 21. The Arundel Castle sailed for England with 130 passengers, carrying 120 firemen and trimmers recruited locally, many of them Dutch-speaking South Africans.

Allen, chairman of the Shipping Federation, in a long statement declares that "the so-called weamens' strike is really a reconnaissance in force in connection with" the general communist offensive by direct action against the existing order of society." headline: YEAR'S TOUR.
text:
HONGKONG'S INTERESTING VISITOR.

An interesting visitor to Hongkong is Dr. Maurice Parmelee, Ph.D., the well-known sociologist, psychologist and author, who is making a year's tour of the East to study the political problems of Japan, China, India and Egypt as they affect his special subjects.

Dr. Parmelee is one of the most distinguished of the younger thinkers in the field of social and psychological science.

His books are lucid expositions of subjects of the deepest human interest. His principal lifework is a series of treatises, of which his "Science of Human Behaviour" is the first, upon the evolution of human nature and culture culminating in our civilisation.

He is a graduate of Yale and Columbia Universities and has been professor of sociology, economics and anthropology, at the Universities of Minnesota, Missouri, and Kansas, and the College of the City of New York. He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and a member of the Institut International de Sociologie.

His lectures before scientific and lay audiences both in Europe and America have, for years been models of ease and clarity, combined with sound scholarship and stimulating originality.

A representative of the United States War Trade Board in London and taking part in the administration of the Blockade, Dr. Parmelee was the only American who was Chairman of an Allied committee—the Allied Rationing Committee. From 1920 to 1923 he was an economic adviser in the Department of State and conducted investigations for the Department, travelling extensively in Europe. His new book, "Blockade And Sea Power," is the result of this unusual experience. Dr. Parmelee's book is of great historical importance and a valuable contribution to the discussion of the problems of sea power, imperialism, and the evolution of a world state which are of the utmost significance for the prevention of war and the promotion of harmonious international relations.

Among the subjects on which Dr. Parmelee lectures are: the development of "personality, the conflicts in human nature, art and the natural life, the modern Humanitarian Movement, the abolition of poverty, the influence of civilisation upon crime, sea power and the world state, and the economic collapse of Europe.

Described by Havelock Ellis as possessing "a temperamentally cool, judicial, deliberate mind, with a seemingly instinctive impulse to balance and weigh all the considerations that are brought before him, Dr. Parmelee's books include "The Science of Human Behaviour," "Criminology," "Poverty and Social Progress," and "Personality and Conduct," all of which have been highly praised in the Press, especially his book on criminology which presents a comprehensive survey of the whole field of criminology from the point of view of Social Control. A recent issue of the "Times Literary Supplement" mentions that Dr. Parmelee's "Blockade and Sea Power" will be published in London during the autumn by Messrs. Hutchinson.

Dr. Parmelee, after visiting Japan, went to Peking, and there met most of the outstanding personalities in the present situation including Karakhan himself. Dr. Parmelee went to Kalgan to see General Feng Yu-hsiang. Other places he visited were Shanghai, Soochow, and Hankow. In Shanghai he narrowly escaped being involved in the rioting of the 7th — had he been two minutes earlier he would certainly have shared the fate of the American who was brutally assaulted—and in Soochow he narrowly escaped serious trouble through a ricsha-coolie trying to exploit the strong anti-foreign feeling to extort exorbitant squeeze.

Dr. Parmelee leaves Hongkong to-morrow for Java, whence he goes to Malaya, Burma and India. He proposes to spend several months in India and then to go to Egypt, returning to America after nearly a year's absence travelling. As soon as he returns to America, in February, Dr. Parmelee will begin a lecture tour in which his Impressions of the East will play a large part.

headline: Rensons for Acquisition.
text:
The reason why the Tug and Lighter Co., Ltd., is willing to sell and we are desirous of buying is that the tendency is for more and more of the lighterage business to come to us, as, since the boycott and scarcity of labour, storers of cargo have begun to rely on us to do the whole business of landing and storing in one transaction rather than lose time in going to the one Company for the landing and to the other for the storing. Lighterage has thus become a part of our business and for it tugs and lighters must be obtained. As to build is out of the question, we approached the Tug and Lighter Company and the present proposal is the result.

The arrangement is one which I feel sure will be for the benefit of the shareholders of both Companies, and I have no hesitation in recommending it to you although as you know I am also interested in the Tug and Lighter Company, being in fact its Chairman and it is difficult to serve two masters.

As we have to create 60,000 new shares for the purpose of the amalgamation which would bring the capital up to $6,600,000, we thought we might as well take advantage of the opportunity to raise the nominal capital to $7,500,000 in case of need in the future.

The agreement referred to in the resolution is now on the table here and can be inspected by anyone present.

headline: CAPETOWN INCIDENT. / AUSTRALIAN PREMIER'S FIGHTING SPEECH.
text:
Capetown: Sept. 22.

The departure of the “Arundel Castle” wirelessing “This is the way to go home” had an immediate effect on ports in South Africa, especially Durban.

The number of vessels held up dwindled from 25 to 18. A further two vessels are expected to sail this afternoon.

The sailing of the “Arundel Castle” is the most important event since the seamen's strike began, and, has immensely perturbed the strikers who hitherto regarded it impossible to secure South African crews; but hundreds of suitable men are now offering their services.

The crews of several other ships are conferring on the position as a result of the sailing of the Arundel Castle.

Capetown, Sept. 22. Recruiting of crews continues freely. The crew of the “Edinburgh Castle” which has just arrived, have announced that they do not intend to join the strikers.

headline: GERMAN DYES / IMPORTANT BUSINESS MISSION
text:
Negotiations with a view to the fusion of all important dye works in Germany has led to a provisional result which will shortly be submitted to the Boards of companies concerned, including the Baden Aniline, Berlin Aniline, Hoechst, and Elberfeld dyeworks.

A final decision will rest with the general meetings of companies in the spring.

There is little doubt that the fusion will materialise with a view to eliminating competition and regulating consumption.

headline: FRESH CRISIS?
text:
HOME COAT TRUCF HITCH

An important conference between Mr. Baldwin and the Executive of the Miners' Federation was held in Downing Street to day, with regard to the coal truce hitch arising from the miners' contention that the owners, by varying the district base rates, had committed a breach of the understanding with the Premier when the truce was arranged, viz., that wages should not be reduced from the rates existing in July before the 1924 agreement ended.

After the conference it was officially announced that the Premier had agreed to consider the miners' arguments and to meet them on September 24.

It is noteworthy that the conf- owners contend that a variation of the district rates is permissible under the 1924 agreement and does not infringe the terms of the settlement.

It is understood the Mines Department agrees with the coal-owners.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
TRADE UNION CONGRESS DECISION.

STRIKERS GETTING TIRED.

The General Council of the Trade Union Congress has declined to interfere in the Seamen's strike.

Seventeen shipyard trade unions were invited to participate in the conference which decided to approach the Council, but the communication forwarded to the Council emanated from only six of the smaller unions. The remaining eleven refused to be parties to the request.

There are indications, as a result of the cumulative effect of the departures of vessels from Capetown, Durban and Delagoa Bay that the strike is rapidly breaking.

The majority of the men admit that they are sick of idleness, and are anxious to alleviate the sufferings of their families.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
The early end of the shipping strike is predicted, the only outstanding point being the strikers' demand for full pay during the strike which is likely to be waived. It is believed that the unanimous decision of the waterside workers to work all ships even if the strikers have been replaced will profoundly affect the situation.

-Reuter.

The steamers "Portcurno" and "Largolaw" have sailed from Durban. The steamer "Garth Castle," which was held up at Lourenco Marques, owing to the refusal of the crew to take the ship to sea unless the strike is settled, sailed with her original crew.

headline: OFF THE RAILS. / UNUSUAL PRAYA SMASH. / TRAM AND CAR DAMAGED.
text:
An extraordinary accident took place yesterday afternoon at Praya East near the Seamen's Institute when a tram car ran backwards and left the rails. The situation became further complicated when a motor car which had been following in the wake of the tram car before the latter made its backward run failed to pull up in time to avert a collision with the derailed vehicle.

Both the tram car and the motor car suffered considerable damage, but the occupants escaped with nothing more serious than a severe shaking.

Another tram car arrived later on the scene and placed the derail-ed vehicle on its track with the aid of a tow rope.

headline: TRAIL OF A PIN.
text:
BOY UNDER X-RAYS FOR TWO DAYS.

For two days doctors at the Metropolitan Hospital, Kingsland-road, N., have watched, by the aid of X-rays, a pin passing through, a five-veurs-old boy's body.

Albert Smith, of 4, Watson-place, Kingsland-road, swallowed the pin, which he was using as a toothpick, on Tuesday when he was left in the house alone. He went to a neighbour's house and told what had happened.

He was taken at once to the Metropolitan Hospital, where he was kept without food for two days, while the doctors watched the progress of the pin.

He was discharged cured and he went home to a big meal. If he had eaten anything after swallowing the pin, a "Daily Mail" reporter was informed, he might have pushed the point into the wall of his stomach and set up peritonitis.

headline: FINGER-PRINTS
text:
INTERNATIONAL SYSTEM ON IDENTIFICATION

A system of recording fingerprints by series of numbers and thereby enabling the police to identify a certain type of criminal in a few minutes by reference to a code-book was described at a gathering of delegates to the International Prison Congress, says the "Manchester Guardian." A demonstration of the method was given by Mr. and Mrs. Erek Schaffer, of the Bureau Internationale d'Identification. Those who saw it were so impressed by the value of the invention that the Congress to-day carried a resolution recommending that every delegate should bring it to the notice of his Government and that two finger-print experts should be sent to Copenhagen to study the system there.

Mr. and Mrs. Schaffer explained that the system was invented in 1914 by Mr. Hakon Joergensen. Sub-Commissioner of Police in Copenhagen, but it could not be put into operation then as the war stopped communication with foreign countries. Mr. Joergensen has written a pamphlet about the system, which has been translated into several languages and is being translated into others. The police in a few Continental countries are now using his method.

The idea is this: that there are a number of international crooks —Mr. Schaffer thinks probably 20,000 of them—who travel about from one country to another; preying on society wherever they go. Such a crook may be well known to the police in more than one town and they probably have his finger-prints. But often when a man is arrested, in a new place the police have to wait to identify him till the finger-prints they take have been compared with those in another country. The difficulty is, of course, increased when he gives false information and the police perhaps send to Boulogne for news about a man from America.

It occurred to Mr. Joergensen that while in all the great cities of the world there were enormous collections of finger-prints—New York and London had nearly, half a million—there was not any close communication between the police in these different towns and most of the finger-prints were gathering dust. It must be possible he thought, to collect all the most important finger-prints from all the bureaux, and by means of his system publish them in a book which would be a general denominator of travelling criminals for all the countries in the world. He had invented an elaborate method of describing finger-prints by numbers—a great many numbers going to each finger-print. Most countries have sent him finger prints to study, and they keep the Bureau supplied with their new ones, but so far London has not contributed to its collection.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
WASHINGTON CONFERENCE OPENS.

"FAIR AND WORKABLE."

(Reuter's American Service.

The Franco-American Debt negotiations were formally opened to-day.

Later.

The negotiations opened with a speech by M. Caillaux, hoping that the settlement would not only be of a practicable nature, but worthy of the past of the two great nations and paying a tribute to America's wartime efforts. Mr. Mellon, replying, declared that America did not minimise the burdens France had borne nor the difficulties menacing her future, but this condition was not permanent. France will emerge successfully from them. Mr. Mellon knew. The present conference may greatly influence the peace of the world, therefore he felt a great responsibility resting upon him. "It is our duty to reach a conclusion which in the estimation of both our peoples is fair and in the practical test of time, workable."

headline: THE SECURITY PACT. / GERMANY TO ATTEND CONFERENCE.
text:

headline: SAYINGPUN SCHOOL
text:
QUARTERLY REPORT.

Asked at the Legislative Council meeting yesterday by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyonk as to when the work on the new Sayingpun School was expected to be completed, the Director of Public Works said he had not the papers with him to refer to the date on which the contract had to be completed but as work had been delayed two months because of the strike it would probably be two months later.

H.E. the Governor suggested that the hon. member should put a question down in order that the Director might answer it at the next meeting.

The following quarterly report on the work on this new school was laid before the Council.

Satisfactory progress was being made until the commencement of the present unsettled labour conditions; workmen have left the site and the work is necessarily proceeding very slowly at present.

The brickwork has been completed to the roof level and the tower has been carried up to a few feet higher than roof. The floor to top storey and also the verandah roofs are completed. Steel trusses over Science Block have been fixed and the roof timbering to both N. and S. Blocks is practically finished. Roof tiling has been commenced on the South Block.

The steel roof trusses over Assembly Hall are in position and internal plastering has progressed favourably.

The standard of work is good.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE.
text:
SPECIAL FIRST NATIONAL FEATURE

To night and tomorrow there is screened at the Queen's Theatre a first National feature which was well received last night by reason of the finer points of appeal which those favourite screen artists, Anna C. Nilsson and Milton Miles, were able to do full justice to—"Flowing Gold," a drama of the oil fields.

The vindication of the honour of an ex-army officer to whom attaches the stigma of dismissal and his victory over his enemy in the struggle for supremacy in the oil fields plays an important part in the development of the story which is concerned with the fortunes of a family which after years of labour eventually hit it rich.

There are some fine scenic effects which are a triumph of the film producer's art, that, for instance, when the lightning strikes an oilwell and it disappears in a cloud of smoke comprising within wrecked timber those with whose fortunes the story is primarily concerned. Again there is the thrilling rescue scene when a cloud burst carries death and destruction with it by reason of the burning oil borne on the surface of the floods.

headline: HARBOUR RESCUES
text:
WOMAN'S INSANE IDHA

A Chinese coolie who had slept overnight on the edge of the sea wall in Connaught Road West near Jardine's wharf rolled in his sleep and dropped into the harbour early yesterday morning.

The man's cries for help attracted the attention of those near the scene and he was dragged out of the water, alive but in a serious condition. He died on the way to hospital.

What would have proved another tragedy was averted later in the day by the prompt action of boat people in rescuing a Chinese woman who jumped into the harbour with the intention of putting an end to her life.

On being taken to the hospital the woman was found to be none the worse for her immersion, but she showed signs of insanity, which accounts for her act. She was despatched to the Laumatic Asylum.

headline: BOLSHEVISTS IN CANTON.
text: Through a movement engineered from Canton, the trade of the British island colony at the mouth of the river is paralysed, and the daily losses now amount to several hundred thousand pounds. This movement is associated with the general anti-British movement in China, of which the Whit-suntide incident in Shanghai was made the pretext. But in Canton the opportunity was seized to give it a specific direction. Canton happens to be the birthplace and the home of the Kuomintang Party, which, in the declining years of its late leader, Sun Yat-sen, established a very intimate connection with the Russian Soviet Government. The extremist wing of this party, after strange vicissitudes during the chaotic civil war of the last few years, succeeded, also about Whit-suntide, in recovering control in Canton with Bolshevist aid. A confessedly Red Government is now established in Canton. It is supported by Soviet Russians who act as instructors in the Wham-poa Cadet School and as advisers in administrative and revolutionary technique. Steamers from Vladivostok have passed Hongkong conveying to Canton Bolshevik agents and Bolshevik supplies. The Canton merchants probably object to the present régime and would like to side with the more moderate but now apparently helpless wing of the Kuomintang. But the merchants can do little now, less even than when, in the days of the civil war, the Volunteer Corps financed by them was thrust aside. The Red faction, reinforced by Russian revolutionary and military aid, is in complete control of Canton and the Kwangtung region. The activities of this Government are now violently directed against Great Britain, the immediate object being the British colony of Hongkong at the mouth of the river.

headline: THAT DECREE.
text:
The general strike among the large population of Chinese workers in Hongkong and the irregular boycott of British goods have already done great harm to the colony. The Canton revolutionaries have something to show for their efforts. Now they have been emboldened to take a new step. They have published decrees forbidding the approach of British and Japanese ships to Canton and permitting other foreign ships to come only if they have avoided calling at Hongkong on their way. The penalty for infraction of the decree seems to be some activity of labour pickets and the prevention of loading or unloading. The decree is an open challenge. It is tantamount to defiant repudiation of treaties that have governed for decades the relations between the European Powers and America on the one hand and Southern China on the other. What can the Powers do about it, for if Great Britain and Japan are defied directly, all other Powers are indirectly condemned by the prohibition of access to any foreign ships that may dare to call at British Hongkong on their way up the river? This typically Bolshovist challenge must be confined warily. The Admiral Commanding the

China Station has gone up the river to investigate, and in the British concession on the island of Shameen, facing the city of Canton, we have a very gallant Consul-General, Sir James Jamieson, who knows his Cantonese through and through and is facing the extraordinary situation with great courage and unruffled humour. It would be the simplest thing in the world to retort by blockading the mouth of the river, admitting those who may be our friends and refusing access to declared enemies. But it must be remembered that the real object of our enemies in issuing these decrees may be to provoke Great Britain into taking exactly some such step as might be construed as a war measure. The Nationalist extremists in China, the Bolsheviks, and their friends throughout the world are using all their resources of propaganda to demonstrate the ridiculous thesis that Great Britain has aggressive, military or imperialistic designs on China. Our Australian Correspondent reported that even a broadcasting centre in Queensland has been used for this purpose. The situation in Hongkong is only too distressing. The effrontery of the Red Government of Canton is hardly to be borne. For that very reason great circumspection is necessary. While the Admiral investigates and while Sir James Jamieson remonstrates with Dr. Wu, the Canton Foreign Commissioner, son of the well-known Dr. Wu Ting-fang, it will be well to let ships of all nations go up the river and test in practice the actual efficacy of this impudent decree.

headline: PROVOKING.
text:
There is the more need to proceed cautiously since the Bolsheviks in Canton are obviously anxious to provoke some action by Great Britain that would turn the uncertain situation throughout China more definitely in their favour. Canton is practically independent, and its military forces are pushing out into Yunnan and Fukien. But the Yangtsze Governors seem to be combining to maintain order and to check the dangerous and destructive anti-foreign agitation. In the north, so far as Chang Tso-lin, the Lord of Manchuria, is disposed to exert his influence, the situation is comparatively favourable for the moment. But near Peking, Feng Yu-hsiang, the general of Christian professions, Bolshevik associations, and violently anti-British sentiments, is steadily strengthening his position, securing control of Shensi and Kiangsu, pushing out towards the Musulman West, and all the time vigilantly maintaining his communications, not alone with Karakhan and Borodin in Peking, but along the roads for the supply of munitions of war that lead down from Soviet Siberia through Kalgan. General Feng is in close sympathy with the Government now in power in Canton. The success of a provocative manoeuvre there might give him the opportunity, for which he is perhaps waiting, definitely to seize power in Peking. He dallies yet. In the meantime the wavering Peking Government, after having subsidized the Shanghai strike and given direct and indirect encouragement to the anti-foreign agitation, has found it possible to yield for once to an impulse of common sense. It has decided to invite the Powers to the Tariff Conference provided for in the Washington Treaty of 1922. The probability therefore is that the Conference will actually take place in October, and the Powers may at last have a real opportunity of concerting their policies in regard to China. It must be admitted that Great Britain and Japan stand somewhat alone in the intensity of their concern in the present dangerous situation, and it is something for us in these difficult days to have an old friend at our side. It must, however, be repeated again and again that while little that is effective can be done without the co-operation of all the Powers, a wise and vigorous British initiative is necessary above all. It is good news that Sir Ronald Mackay, our Minister in Peking, is so far recovered from his illness that he will shortly be able to return to his post. Mr. Austen Chamberlain came up to town specially to deal with the Chinese problem. In such a crisis as this we cannot afford for a moment to be off our guard.

headline: “THE SEA HAWK.” / BABATINI'S MASTERPIECE
text:
A fleet of five large vessels of sixteenth century design was built for First National's screen version of Rafael Sabatini's "The Sea Hawk," which comes to the World Theatre to-morrow. The picture, which has been given a great reception in America, was shown in the Albert Hall, London, on October 15. In other sea stories on the screen, schooners or steam vessels have been rented or purchased. But in "The Sea Hawk," the ships, which ranged from 90 to 192 feet in length, were specially constructed in the shipyards of San Pedro, California, under the supervision of Frederick Gabouri, an expert. Mr. Gabouri was assisted by more than 300 draftsmen, mechanics, riggers, carpenters, electricians, sailors, and labourers. With poop decks, grotesque figureheads, gaudily coloured sails, and old-fashioned cannon, the fleet affoated recalled the Pacific expeditions of Balbón, Megellan, and Cabrillo, three hundred years ago. Many of the scenes in "The Sea Hawk," as those who have read Sabatini's book will appreciate, had to be produced on the high seas. All the vessels were made seaworthy and equipped with motor power. One of the ships was a replica of an English frigate of 1500; a second, a Moorish galleas, and a third, a Moorish frigate. There was also a Spanish galleon and pirate craft. The Moorish frigate was propelled by over 200 men, four to six chained to each oar, and the other vessels had oarsmen in proportionate numbers. In order to accommodate the sailors, galley slaves, fighting men, principals, and technical workers required for the big battles at sea, Frank Lloyd producer-director, who, by the way, is a native of Glasgow, established a camp near an Algerian village on the west coast of Santa Catalina Island. Three naval speed boats and two large barges were used to carry supplies to the camp, which at times numbered as many as 750 men. Rafael Sabatini has been called the modern Dumas. His "Sea Hawk," as everyone interested in literature knows, has met with great success as a novel. Briefly, the narrative tells of a seventeenth century English baron, whose brother, seeking to divert suspicion for a murder, has him placed aboard a ship and carried to sea in the hope that he will be accused of "the crime." The British ship is captured by the crew of a Spanish vessel, and all on board become galley slaves. Later, the Spanish vessel is attacked and taken by the Moors, and among the latter, Milton Sills, leading man in a score of big productions, becomes a great chieftain and is known as "The Sea Hawk." This account falls a long way short of justice to the story, which embodies great sweeps of action, too full of detail for recital in limited space. Incident after incident of dramatic significance follow one on the other. The picture represents First National's most ambitious undertaking, which is a big statement to make on the heels of the wonderful reception accorded "Abraham Lincoln" by London and provincial newspapers.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
The joint session of the Franco-American debt funding commissioners only lasted twenty minutes, the Americans indicating that they considered the French proposals inadequate and unsatisfactory.

The Americans handed over data, which the French spent the afternoon examining and preparing further proposal for presentation at next session.

Although the members of the American commission are not at all optimistic, it is understood that the majority feel that considerable progress has been made towards reconciliation of the divergent Franco-American views.

The "Journal" publishes a report from Washington that M. Caillaux has telegraphically informed M. Painleve on the state of the debt negotiations and the concessions he reckoned on making. He stated that the American counter proposals claimed maximum annuities of $120,000,000 compared with the 80,000,000 contemplated by M. Caillaux.

The “Le Matin” publishes a report for the same capital stating that the Americans presented a totally unexpected claim for the payment of interest on $245,000,-000 which the United States treasury advanced to the Bank of France which it demanded should not be regarded as a political loan but a commercial loan, similar to the Bank of England's credit to the Bank of France.

headline: HOCKEY.
text:
CLUB'S TRIAL MATCH.

Yesterday afternoon at the Marina Ground, Kowloon, a trial Hockey match was played between two teams of the Hongkong Hockey Club.

The Match was fairly well contested, although "Whites" captained by J. Lammert had the lead throughout the whole game, and eventually won by three goals to one. The late start made play towards the end very difficult owing to approaching darkness.

The match started with Whites pressing and after ten minutes' play, from a good forward movement Faers opened the score. The game then settled down to a very evenly contested match, neither side adding any further score before halftime. The second half opened with a brilliant rush by Vallack and Lammert, the latter netting, giving Whites an additional lead. This woke Colours up and they pressed hard with the result that they scored. Lammert, however, once more got going and put through another goal five minutes later. Lammert had the misfortune to lose a fine opportunity just before the end when after a fine run down, owing to the failing light, he just missed an open goal. The whistle blew shortly after.

headline: NEEDS OF THE PRESS
text:
IMPORTANT EMPIRE CONFERENCE

VISCOUNT BURNHAM'S VIEW.

Lord Forster, Governor-General of Australia, opening the Imperial Press Conference, emphasised the immense importance of the Conference for the Empire and Australia.

Mr. S. M. Bruce, Premier, in a forty minutes' speech, dwelt on the Empire and the importance of the subjects to be discussed by the Conference.

He emphasised that Empire communication was most important as it was vital to maintain the communications of the Empire in order to promote better understanding between its component parts.

The Australian Government desired to see the cost of communications reduced to the lowest possible level.

Viscount Burnham was elected President amid acclamation.

He said the Conference, though unofficial, had the approbation and good wishes of all the Governments of the Empire, and likened the Empire Press Union to the League of Nations.

He recalled the work of the Union for the advancement of the Press, especially in obtaining adequate recognition of Dominion newspapers by the authorities at Home, and breaking down obsolete barriers, so that Departments of State and Houses of Parliament now received Dominion newspaper representatives on equal terms with the British Press; but the best work, he said, had been in cheapening and accelerating the means of communication, especially the recent reduction of the cable rate to Australia to sixpence, which was an earnest of better things in the future which the competition, between directional wireless and renovated cables was bound to produce.

He described broadcasting as possible real rival of newspapers

The vexed question of the recruitment of an army supplementary to the service which raised such an outcry among Trade's Unions early in the year was again raised at the Labour Conference when a resolution calling on all members of the Party to refuse to join was unanimously adopted.

headline: OPEN LETTER. / CHINESE ADDRESS TO SOLDIERY.
text:
THE CANTONESE PEOPLE.

Mr. Leo Chung-jun's second letter to the soldiers in Kwang-tung has been translated and sent to the "China Mail" for publication, inter alia, as follows:—

Since the arrival of Red Russians in Kwangtung through the invitation of Cheung Kai-shek, Wong Ching-wai and others, they are regarded as “wolves getting admission into the house.” The Cantonese version that Cheung and Wong are fond of Communism which would menace Kwangtung does not sufficiently describe their faults and disclose their secrets. Speaking truly, they are taking the country's goods to be changed for. Soviet Russia's money and they are under the shelter of Soviet Russia. They are obeying the order of aliens.

Though I am not a wise man, I cannot keep in silence. I have repeatedly applied to my elders and brethren for their prompt action to save themselves from the fire and the deep and have earnest expectation towards the forceful soldiers. I have urged them to expel the bad elements by united strength and to relieve the villages without taking discrimination.

Now the Kwangtung Army of Chiu Yeung and Mui Yuen is advancing westward. The dawn of light appears in the clouds of East Kwangtung and the evil mist will soon dissipate. Then the thirty million people of Kwangtung will come to life again. The Kwangtung Army will not hesitate to relieve their brethren from danger and the Kwangtung people will prepare to welcome them having for long hoped to do so.

My elders and brethren, you should get up quickly to follow them. Do not put your hands into your sleeves and look on. If every man can exert his ability, the campaign to expel Reds will be successful. It is the action of self-salvation and not helping others. My elders and brethren are aware of this idea, of which I need not say any more. What I want to state is that all soldiers in Kwangtung, whether hosts or guests, who are being supplied by the Kwangtung people, have to do their duty by protecting the people. Seeing that the people are in such a wretched position, how can you delay your operations to relieve them? Moreover the Reds are pressing forward to exterminate the dissenters. Can you bend down your head to suffer; the rough treatment of Russian officers? To fight for the Cantonese who will extol your merit is better than to serve under the bad elements who are hated by many persons. It is unnecessary to argue which is right or wrong. To relieve Kwangtung is to relieve your country and to help others is to help yourselves. Our military officers must have understood this point. I hope you will rise up quickly to help the soldiers in the East River and to expel the bad elements from the Five-Rams City. You may attack them from different directions or start the battle in an inner part. The present time is the only opportunity of settling the whole province of Kwangtung and it is also the day on which the Cantonese are applying for your relief. If you still take no notice of their supplications, you will not be allowed to keep your present position on the other hand you will be eventually exterminated by those whom you keep company with. Every person beags the responsibility of the rise and fall of his province. You cannot force the public to follow your opinion on your certainly can choose the way of popularity. I expose my views for your decision.

You may ask why, if the Company is now working at a profit, we should sell out to the Provident Company; but we have only made money since the outbreak of the boycott when cargo boats were very scarce, and should only have to face a struggle with the Provident Company later on. when business resumes its norma course. In every way it seems to us that the arrangement is for the mutual benefit of both Companies and as such we put it before you

The remaining clauses are of no special importance, but as I said before, the agreement is lying on the table and can be inspected by any shareholder who cares to do so.

RESOLUTIONS APPROVED. No questions being asked by those present, the Chairman proposed the adoption of the two resolutions as extraordinary resolutions. Mr. W. J. Hawker and Mr. S. C. Cook seconded and the proposals were carried unanimously.

Notice was also given of a further extraordinary general meeting to be held on October 17, 1925, for the purpose of receiving a report of the proceedings of the above mentioned meeting and of confirming, if thought fit, as special resolutions the above mentioned resolutions.

headline: HONAM DEATH / SECOND ENGINEER IOST OVERBOARD.
text:
A EONCKONG RESIDENT

A distressing fatality involving the loss of the second engineer of the s.s. "Honum," Mr. David Mason, was reported on the return of that ship to Hongkong from Canton yesterday afternoon. It occurred in the early hours of yesterday morning as the "Honum" was lying at anchor off Shameen. The Second Engineer had attended ashoro n. performance of the "Broadensters" and was at the time (shortly after 1 a.m.) about to make fast to the "Honum" the painter of the sumpan which conveyed him from the shore. He is stated to have lost his balance and fallen overboard, disappearing from view at once.

As soon as those on board were aware of the disaster the alarm was raised and gunbouts in the vicinity trained searchlights on the spot, without, however, resulting in any sign of the missing engineer who, it is presumed, was drowned.

Mr. Mason had not been long in the employ of the Steambolt Company but was an old resident of Hongkong and has many friends here. The deepest sympathy is extended to the relatives, who include Mrs. D. Harvey, of Kowloon.

Apart from this distressing mishap the voyage of the s.s. "Honum" was without untoward incident. The same conditions prevail as heretofore, namely the strike pickets continue to patrol with vigilance in the vicinity of the steamer and prevent passengers being taken off. Chinese merchants and others who had made their own arrangements were able to leave the ship but some of the poorer class Chinese passengers were unable to do so and were obliged to return. 22 Europeans and 61 Chinese were carried on the voyage to Hongkong.

headline: NANKING RIOT.
text:
FIRING FOLLOWS PAY DAY.

Messages received from Nanking state that a dispute arose there at six o'clock last evening at the International Export Company regarding wages payments. A riot ensued in which it is reported one Briton was killed, whereupon the British are reported to have fired, killing four and wounding several rioters. The British were taken on board the warships there and British naval ratings were landed and are guarding the Company's factory. One Briton is reported to be a prisoner, being taken to the University.

headline: OFFICIAL REPORTS
text: The official reports from Nanking differ considerably from the earlier version. No Briton was killed. It was the Chinese Police and not the Britons who fired on the mob.

headline: -NAVAL VERSION.
text: British Naval wireless messages from Nanking report that on Friday the International Export Company reduced its Chinese staff. Those dismissed became disgruntled and assumed a threatening attitude. British naval ratings landed. The mob mauled the Chinese Police, whose officer ordered them to open fire. Three words killed and four wounded, one seriously after wards a Briton, who was going home, was attacked in the street and injured, being taken to hospital. To day all is quiet and the Chinese Police appear to have the situation well in hand.

headline: JAPAN'S PREMIER.
text:
VISCOUNT KATO FILLS CABINET.

V.V.count Xato has been, re-ap- pointed Premier.

Vesant Kato has been summoned. He completed the Cabinet by assigning the portfolio of Justice, Commerce, and Agriculture to the Kenseikai members Egi, Hayumi and Katokoi respectively. The other ministers are as before.

Viscount Kuto's re-appointment fully accords with the expectations of the Press and others who are particularly scornful of the political manoeuvring of the Seiyuhai, who, by breaking up the Coalition and immediately making overtures to the Seiyuhonto, evidenced their real intentions of bidding for power. The Kenseikai Government party is the largest in the Lower House, but does not command an absolute majority.

Emen, August 1.—The miners unions have given notice to end the present wages agreement on August 31, unless wages are increased, it is improbable the mine-owners will agree owing to the depression due to the inability to dispose of huge stacks of coal at the pithoide.—Reuter.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
SETTLEMENT "ONLY AN ARMISTIC."

Mr. Cook, the miners' secretary, has received letters and telegrams from trade unionists all over the country congratulating him on his great initial triumph for solidarity.

Mr. Cook has issued a manifesto describing the settlement as merely an armistice. Great issues must still be faced, including the complete feorganisation of the in-diatry, the elimination of royalty to the owner and of private ownership in order to prevent the exploitation of the consumer and give the nation in return its ten millions subsidy.

The Chairman of the South Wales Coalowners' Association, interviewed, said the Government had allowed the country to be coerced. It was a disaster and was only deferring the evil day. The President of the Cardiff Chamber of Commerce, interviewed, said that if the coal trade needed a subsidy so did the steel, shipping and other industries.

Hague, August 1.—The foreign ministry announces that the British and Netherlands arbitration treaty of February 2, 1925, which has expired, has been renewed for a further five years, with the proviso that matters for arbitration be submitted to the Court of International Justice.—Renter.

Heijyo, August 1.—The “Asahi” aeropalnes which departed for Harbin this morning have returned owing to bad weather.—Reuter.

headline: SECRET SOCIETIES.
text:
UNDERWORLD HELP FOR STRIKERS.

It is reported that two secret societies, the membership of which is largely of the criminal class, have joined forces with labour agitators in the Chinese city and sworn allegiance to one of the most notorious labour leaders. It is believed that their intention is to blackmail Chinese firms and shops dealing in foreign goods, and Chinese in foreign employ.

A Japanese paper asserts that the Far Eastern Committee of the Third Internationale recently petitioned Vladivostok for 50,000,000 roubles for propaganda purposes in China, which petition was duly granted by the Bureau of Asiatic Propaganda.

MILL WORKERS STABBED. Five strike breakers from a Japanese mill have been stabbed in a teashop by loafers, who are probably strikers. Two of the injured men have been removed to hospital.

headline: COAL DISPUTE.
text:
SIX MONTHS INTERIM CONTRACT

Halifax (Nova Scotia), August 3. —With a view to terminate the dispute between the British Empire Steel Corporation and the striking coalminers, which has completely stopped work in the coal industry for the past five months and caused much distress and disorder, the Premier, the Hon. H. N. Rhodes, P.C., has proposed that the parties immediately arrange an interim contract for six months to embrace the 1924 working terms and the 1922 wages. Thid Provincial Government will grant a rebate of one-fifth of its coal royalties for a year, and institute a full enquiry. The Executive Pedy, representing the workers, has already recommended that the Unions should accept the proposals.

headline: WUCHOW NEWS. / NO SERIOUS TROUBLE ANTICIPATED.
text:
Although the feeling at Wuchow is not thought to indicate real danger to the foreign children, the hundred or so students were not entencing a boycott and appear to control the place, have been successful in their efforts to make things uncomfortable, and there have also been lawless acts.

The Consult at Wuchow has been away from his house to some time, and it appears that this absence something entered and removed ouries and personal belongings. A new belonging to the British American Tobacco Company was cut and drift and rescued by H.M.S. Pampanoga, but the Asiatic Petroleum Company were not so fortunate when the moorings of their landing portion were cut. It has not been seen since. Oil the property of the A.P.C., is reported to have been stolen from banks.

Chinese who have left the employ of foreigners at Wuchow and have remained, are having to justify their existence removing the City wall and building roads, the wage paid them being 60 cents a day. The work is hard and many of the strikers would leave if it were not for the fact that they know at their only haven, Canton, it would be a case of "out of the frying pan."

headline: LOCAL & GENERAL
text:
A large gang of coolies is now employed on the sandy wasted of Happy Valley.

Letters from Mr. J. Johnstone. Jr., on board the Empress of Canada, indicate plain and pleasant sailing and plenty of work. The lady Volunteers in particular are especially distinguishing themselves.

The usual weekly Public Lecture will be given at the Hongkong Lodge. The Theosophical Society, 16, Queen's Road Central, on Wednesday, August 5, at 5.45 p.m. The Public are cordially invited.

The Sanitary Department seems to exercise little control over its notice boards. We draw its attention to the one at Sai Wan Ho market which bears the name of an official as Secretary, long since defunct.

Mr. Fu Ping-sheung who continues to write letters “under direction of His Excellency Mr. Wu Hon-man, Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Nationalist Government,” is an old boy of St. Stephen's College, and was almost the first to graduate from the Hongkong University.

headline: LOCAL AND
text:
The return of notifiable diseases for the 21 hours ended Wednesday, shows three cases of enteric fever—one Indian and two Chinese.

The Broadensters gave another enjoyable entertainment in the Theatre Royal last night. They perform again this evening and to-morrow.

Rescission of all rules that women teachers must resign their posts on marriage must be made by the London County Council and other education authorities who have made them. In future there will be many marriages by women teachers. This, it was stated by an L.C.C. official, is an inevitable sequel to the result of the test case in which a woman teacher won her action against Poole Corporation.

Touring Canada to study farm methods, four English lads selected by the English Minister of Agriculture, have arrived at Toronto. They are winners of a travelling scholarship donated by E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Besides visiting the various Government demonstration farms in Canada, they will spend a month at the Canadian Pacific Railway demonstration farm in Alberta. They are also stopping off at typical farming districts, and visiting agricultural colleges. The lads are Jack Hitchings, 16 years old; Leslie Anstey, 15; Alfred Belchin, 16, and Roney Howe, 17 years of age.

A Chinese women's daily newspaper, one of the first of its kind in the country, has made its appearance its Shanghai. It is owned, edited, and published by Chinese and deals almost exclusively in news and articles of interest to women. The new daily is called the "Woman's Daily News." It is a two-sheet paper about half the size of the average Chinese newspaper issued in Shanghai. Its columns contained several feature articles on household economy, education, fine arts, ethics, women's professions, and news stories covering women's activities in the city, outports, and abroad. “New hats! Why, a new hat would cause as much commotion as an earthquake in our road,” said a woman debtor in the Bow County Court.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Commander Bivar of the "Patria" and Mrs. Bivar are to leave Macao for Portugal shortly.

Mr. H. E. Morrisz owner of the race horse Manna writes that he expects to leave England for the Far East by the "Empress of Scotland," connecting with the "Empress of Canada," on September 19.

A dance is to be given at the Macao Club to-morrow in honour of the officers of the cruiser "Republica" and the transport "Gil Eanes." In honour of the occasion a special form of lighting is to be introduced which promises to be most attractive. Tommy Milligan, the European boxing champion, whose reported intention to become a member of the Jesuit Order has caused widespread interest, would neither deny nor confirm the report when questioned. The blind students of Worcester College for the sons of gentlemen dug the excavations for their swimming bath, which was opened by Viscount Cobham. There was not a single accident, and when a wheelbarrow load of soil got off the track and tipped it only added to the enjoyment of the boys, who found great fun in doing laborious work to keep down the cost of the swimming bath.

An heroic bronze monument to Mr. John F. Stevens, engineer who is well known throughout the Far East and in Siberia in connection with his railway building, was recently unveiled on the crest of the Continental Divide in the United States. Mr. Stevens, who is now 72 years old, built a railroad through the northern Rocky Mountains at an altitude lower than any other. He was formerly chief engineer of the Panama Canal.

Dr. Ryozo Torii, one of the leading authorities on anthropology, has been invited to attend the celebration of the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the Royal Academy of Russia, which is to take place in Moscow beginning September 15. Professor Matsumura, of the Hokkaido Imperial University, and Dr. Fukuda, a member of the Imperial Academy, who is visiting in Europe, are to attend the celebration too.

The possibility of the Duke and Duchess of York paying a visit shortly to the West Indies is being discussed about the Court at the present time. It is a suggestion of much more feasibility than some tours for the Duke which have been recently suggested. The visit paid to East Africa by the Duke and Duchess has made them anxious to see more of the Empire, and it is quite likely that another visit abroad may be arranged which will enable them to winter abroad. Lady Patricia Earney, who goes back to Bernolda now, is very anxious to

A distinguished name appeared amongst those seeking their call to the Bar early in May. And the bearer of it was moreover a woman—Miss Gladys Steyn. Miss Steyn is a daughter of Martinus T. Steyn who was President of the Orange Free State when the South African war broke out. A hundred members of the Irish Bar were listed for call to the English Bar, and among them figured the name of Sir James O'Connor, who held the posts of Attorney-General and Lord Justice of Appeal before the Irish Free State came into being.

Sir Alfred Fripp, the famous senior surgeon at Guy's, who is retiring about the end of this month, made his first step to fame by a lucky chance. For he was in practice at York, still quite unknown, when the late Duke of Clarence, elder brother of the King, was stationed there. "Prince Eddy" injured his ankle, and Fripp was called in. He made so good an impression, as much by his confident and reassuring manner as his skill—at school they called him "Jehovah Junior"—that the Duke mentioned him to King Edward, to whom he was subsequently appointed Surgeon-in-Ordinary, and his future was assured. Such Coupets are honorary, but the recommendation and introduction are naturally invaluable. DINNER DANCE SATURDAY, 12th SEPTEMBER AND EVERY SATURDAY. FROM 8 p.m. to 12 Midnight.
