The next production of the Hongkong A.D.C. is likely to be "A Little Bit of Fluff."

The Gannow Engineering Co., Manchester, obtained an order recently for pulverising plant for a Portuguese corR factory.

Furness shipyard on the Tyne has achieved a remarkable feat in rapid ship construction. Fifteen weeks ago the keel was laid of a 2,500-ton vessel for service on the Canadian Lakes. She is now loading her first cargo in the Tyne, having successfully passed her trials.

The new Chinese Minister to Moscow, Mr. Sun Pao-chi, received a letter wrapped round a live cartridge. The letter said that on arrival in Moscow he must demand that the Russian Government make good to the Chinese losses through depreciated roubles, or he would be shot. It is reported that Dr. C. T. Wang received a similar postal packet, says the "Central China Post."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
The Italian Premier, 'Benito Mussolini, has approved a plan for the transformation of the Palazzo Venezia into an establishment to house the offices of the Premier of Italy. It will be called the Government Palace. The palace for many years belonged to Austria and served as the Austrian Embassy.

The Archbishop of Tuam, Co. Galway, Ireland, has delivered a smashing attack at evil literature from his pulpit. The Archbishop appealed to the Free State Government for protection against the flood of filthy and degrading literature which is imported into Ireland each year.

A movement is on foot to introduce policewomen in Berlin according to the American and English example. The pioneer cities in this matter are Cologne and Leipzig, where permission and sympathy were only obtained after a hard struggle on the part of great-hearted women workers in the field of social welfare. In Berlin, although there is still some opposition, the majority of the city council are in favour of the innovation. The opinion of Israel Zangwill as to the American actors and American plays that are sent to England was given by him at the meeting held in London not long since of the Theatrical Managers Association. After telling the managers they didn't know a really good play when they saw it, he switched to the subject of the American products with a characteristically impromptu epigram saying: "America sends us her stars—and tripe." Which is reminiscent of another Zangwillian retort. In his early days the novelist always signed his name "I Zangwill" and few lines which first name was "At an after-day's"

Plans for a nation-wide drive to raise funds for a memorial to William Jennings Bryan in Florida have been discountenanced by Mrs. Bryan. A memorial in Arlington, Cemetery at Washington is the only one she has approved.

“Every church in the United States should provide a hall with a good floor and music for old-fashioned dancing, which should be heartily encouraged by all religious, moral and educational leaders of the country.” Henry Ford has declared.

Mr. J. L. Berns, for many years resident in Shanghai, having resigned his position as manager of the Credit Foncier d'Extreme-Orient, has been appointed inspector for the Societe Francaise de Gerance de la Banque Industrielle de Chine as from September 1. Mr. Bernis will shortly leave for Tientsin in connection with his new appointment. Mr. William Joynson Hicks, the Home Secretary, in a speech at Althorp, near Northampton, stated that the "Pravda" one of the greatest newspapers in Russia, had published recently what they called "the true gospel and life of Christ." It was so, you, so blasphemous, so bestial that he had thought it his duty to prohibit that newspaper from coming into the country at all. The last census were taken in 1921 and the summarizing of the figures shows that the tendency of London's population is to move outward. Of the 26 administrative areas in the county of London, 20 show decreases and has increases. The net decrease is that over 87,000 Districts where first housing schemes have been set up. Now do not have the same for administrative areas on which the 10-mile road is the most important.

The Rev. T. Campbell Gibson, M.A. and Mrs. Gibson have come from Swatow to assist in the work of the English Presbyterian Mission, Singapore.

The diplomatic correspondent of the “Daily Express” says a strong Canadian influence is being exercised on the British Government to appoint as next Governor-General of Canada, Earl Beatty, admiral of the fleet, or Field-Marshal Earl Haig.

More Women drive Buicks than any other car because of the striking appearance of this famous motor car. Then comes Buick dependability. A woman knows when she starts out with her Buick that she will "get there and back." Other reasons are—the comfort in driving a Buick—the velvet clutch action, easy steering; then the power and quietness of Buick's Valve-in-Head engine and the safety of Buick mechanical four-wheel brakes.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. E. B. MacNaghters of the B.A.T. Co. left by the "Siberia Maru" on Monday.

Major Victor Coates, commnendant, 5th Batt., 2nd Punjab Regiment, is promoted Lieut.-Colonel as from August 1.

Captain W. J. Thompson, R.A.S.C., has been granted leave of absence from this station from September 19 till October 3.

The forthcoming marriage is announced of Mr. Alexander William George Herder Grantham, of Hongkong, to Miss Maurine Sumsun, of Sin Francisco, U.S.A.

A marriage will take place in October between Mr. Ross St. John Gore, of Kunlu Lumpur, and Miss Florence Doreen Egan, elder daughter of Mr. Michael Egan, Pyrford, Surrey.

The Rev. W. T. Lindsay, M.A., has assumed the duties of Officating Clergymen to the troops of the Wesleyan denomination, Hongkong. His address is Lee Buildings, Wanchai Gap.

Three Shanghai senior police officers—Supt. A. H. Aiers, Chief Inspr. E. H. Lynch and Inspr. G. Jc nston—are roliring next spring on pension. Mr. Aires has been in the force for over 40 years. His two colleagues have scarcely less service to their credit.

Miss Louise Gaster, Secretary to Sir Ernest Wilton, Chief of ho Salt Inspectorate is resigning from the secretaryship of the British Woman's League in Peking. The Peking "Lender" states that Miss Gaster, who has rendered most valuable service to the League, is being replaced by Mrs. Pridaux-Brune.

The marriage of Mr. Alexander Graham Wallin, Acting Deputy Commissioner of Shanghai Native Customs, and Miss Joan Macdonald, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. John A. Macdonald, of 1670 Harwood Street, Vancouver, British Columbia, was expected to take place quietly at Yokohama on the 16th instant.

Mr. Li Yik-moy, a well-known Chinese rice merchant, has been appointed by His Excellency the Governor as a permanent member of the Po Leung Kok Committee to succeed the late Mr. Chau Sik-ki. "Chinese immigrants arriving at Singapore in August numbered 6,833, making 140,889 for this year up to the end of August. During the eight months 46,893 left Singapore for China.

The marriage of Miss A. M. Lee, daughter of Mrs. M. Lee, to Mr. Benjamin Randall, takes place at St. John's Cathedral on Saturday at 3.30 p.m. A reception is to be held after the ceremony at the Hongkong Hotel.

Another dance under the auspices of H.M.S. "Hermes" is to be held in the Seamen's Institute to-night.. The Jazz Band of the "Hermes" will be in attendance and dancing will be from 8.30 p.m. to midnight.

The memebers at the Hongkong Philharmonic Society are busily engaged in rehearsing Gilbert and Sullivan's "Iolanthe," to be produced at the Theatre Royal in December. There are a few vacancies for ladies in the chorus.

Maurice Tate, the Sussex cricketer, is the father of twins. He seems to have had some idea before they were born that there would be more than one, for he went to a doctor friend and said, "Two fast bowlers, I hope." But alas! He returned, not long after, and said, "It's only a couple of lawn tennis players." He meant they were girls.

An early morning visit to the Zoological Gardens has become the fashion among many hundreds of Berliners who cannot take a holiday. The beautiful grounds are at their best at 7 a.m., and to the strains of a good band the visitors march slowly up, and down, the promenade greeting their friends. The animals are a secondary consideration; as the majority of them are not yet up and on view.

Australians are hoping that the Duke and Duchess of York will be present at the opening of the Federal Parliament at Canberra next year, and a Melbourne message states that the Commonwealth Government would welcome a Royal visit with the utmost enthusiasm. Nothing has been definitely arranged, but it is regarded as more than probable that the Duke and Duchess will visit Australia together with the Empire Parliamentary Association representatives.

André Gide, who has long been the leader of a French school of literateurs, has grown tired of Paris life and has left his house, after selling many of his books, for a secret retreat. He announced that he wished to be forgotten. The sight of his name in the journals had grown distasteful to him, and the constant controversies of which he was the centre, had prevented him from doing his best work. Unhappily, his disappearance has provoked still more talk about him. He has gone without leaving an address, but it remains to be seen how long he can stay away from the city in which he has enjoyed for many years a remarkable prestige. WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 1925.

The sympathy of all who're member Dr. G. H. Bateson Wright, and particularly of members of the Queen's College Old Boys' Association will be extended to him in the loss of his wife. They had been married for 44½ years, and on Dr. Wright's retirement from Hongkong, they settled down at Bournemouth where Mrs. Wright passed away on August 17.

Oxford bags have introduced themselves into Paris. It is from England that men's fashions come to France, and the tailors have tried to keep up with the new mode and have made trousers ten inches wide at the bottom and much too long. But they do not like the introduction of these English-cut clothes. Smartly dressed Frenchmen prefer tight well-fitted clothes and it is with some reluctance that they adopt the Oxford bags and the loose-fitting cants. They do so merely because such is the decree, but they will abandon them as quickly as possible.

Eels when they come down the rivers to the seas " swim at once to the Atlantic Ocean to a secret rendezvous near the Antilles, between longitude 48 and 60, and there lay their eggs. This statement was made to the French Academy of Science by Dr. Schmidt, of Copenhagen University.

Another witness has come forward to testify to the reality of the much-debated sea-serpent. This is Sir Henry F. Woods, K.C.V.O., who, while serving in the British Navy in the old sailing days, distinctly saw the monster at close quarters while cruising off the Javanese coast. In the newly-published book, "Spunyarn," he describes it as being fully 50ft. long, and of girth proportionate.

Dublin saw its busiest and gayest week in its annual Horse Show. Visitors came from all parts of Ireland and Great Britain, for the Dublin Horse Show is now a national event. The decline in popular favour of this animal has made no appreciable difference to the show, nor, so far as one could judge from the congested condition of the streets, in the attendance. The effects of the troubled political times of recent years have worn off, and the city has regained its wonted gaiety.

Undiscouraged by the failure of their campaign to banish alcohol, the Soviet authorities are now tackling the problem of profanity—a large scale task. Under a new ordinance the use of a curse in public is liable to a fine of one gold ruble for each curse. Students of Russian swearing are inclined to believe that the Government will have to compromise by introducing the ration system. Managers of the telephone system have placed a taboo on "Miss" as a term of address to the telephone girls on the ground that this is a bourgeois title.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
The Shanghai Community Church celebrated its fifth birthday yesterday. The evening's programme was divided into two parts, a "Tour of Pleasureland," and a musical and miscellaneous programme. The return of the Citroën Mission, which traversed Africa, has been greeted with enthusiasm in the French Press. For nine months MN. Haardt and Audin-Dubreuil have, with their collaborators, penetrated into the most difficult regions of central Africa and have shown that the automobile has a special value as a vehicle of exploration. Their journey has been followed with the utmost interest. There were many sceptics, but it has been proved that the roads traced by René Caille, Stanley, Livingstone and others can now be taken with comparative security and ease, thanks to the motor car. The Sahara is no longer an obstacle. As the result of this mission, many interesting specimens and a wealth of documentation have been acquired. Thousands of photographs and tens of thousands of yards of cinematographic films have been produced.

Paavo Nurmi, the champion distance runner, is now a Finnish knight and the possessor of the White Rose. These honours were conferred upon the athlete by President Retander upon Nurmi's return from America and were in recognition of his advancement of Finnish interests through his athletic prowess.

It was due chiefly to the strenuous efforts of Mr. H. Ellis, local manager of Linotype and Machinery, Ltd., who, it is stated in Editor and Publisher (New York), acted as linotype operator and pressman, that two British and one American newspapers in Shanghai were able to appear when the Chinese employees suddenly walked out. White members of the editorial and reporting staffs assisted as linotype operators.

Dr. O'Hara, Shanghai interport cricketer, was complainant at the Mixed Court against a Chinese who had stolen the radiator top off his car while it was standing in front of the American Club. The watchman at the Club had seen the accused take the top from the radiator and when he was searched it was found in his pocket. The Court records showed a previous conviction against this man. A sentence of one month's imprisonment was imposed. Two English and two American motor omnibuses, the latter from New York and Chicago, can now be seen in the streets of Berlin, where they make a very favourable impression. They were imported by the General Omnibus Company of Berlin, which wants to try them out in the city. So far, the public appears to prefer them to the omnibuses of German make, but it is difficult to say whether this is due to any advantages they may offer or whether this liking is merely an outcome of curiosity on the part of the public. At any rate, the London omnibuses appear to make less noise than the German ones, and the American omnibuses are generally noted for their brilliant illumination in the evening.

A picturesque wedding took place at St Joseph's Church, Shanghai, when Miss Ru Kathleen Carter, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Carter of Dunedin, New Zealand, became the bride of Mr. Charles Frederick Taylor son of the late Mr. J. F. Taylor and Mrs. Taylor of Suffolk. Mr. D. McAllister gave the bride away and the matron of houdier was Miss M.A. Pollock whose daughter, Vonnie, and Cecilia, was a power girls. M. W. O'Neil was best man.

"A Syncopated Cocktail" is the title of a musical revue staged by the men of the U.S.S. "Black Hawk" at Garrison Hall, Taing-tao. The Druses, with whom the French are now involved in Syria, are one of the most mysterious races of the world. They are believed to have sprung from a mixture of Eastern tribes with a strong Arab infusion, though Druse tradition asserts a Chinese connection. When, in 1016, Hakim Biamrillah declared himself in Cairo to be an incarnation of the Deity there was a violent reaction, he was killed, and his follower, Duruzi, fled into Syria; hence the Druses. Their faith has been described as a mixture of Mohammedanism, Judaism, Christianity, Greek philosophy, Persian mysticism, and certain Chinese beliefs.

Mr. Eric Rice, Special Commissioner for the Overseas League, and formerly of Hongkong, organised two delightful concerts in June, at Vernon House, London, at which a large number of visitors from overseas were present, and a sum of nearly £40 was placed to the War Memorial Fund as a result.

Word has come from Africa that Stewart Edward White, the American novelist and sportsman, was recently badly mauled by a leopard at which he was aiming. Mr. White, accompanied by Dr. Arthur H. Young, and Dr. T. Saxton Pope, left last March on a six months' expedition to hunt wild game with bow and arrows only

M. Briand, a leading figure in the news, has been credited with Irish ancestry. According to one French genealogist, the ex-Premier is descended from one Conell Briand, who migrated from Ireland to Nantes, where he became overseer in a bleaching factory. According to Conell Briand's story, he was a descendant of the great King Brian Boru.

Miss Marcella Duggan, being still a schoolgirl, finds no use for Naldera, the house bequeathed to her by her late stepfather, Lord Curzon, and it has come into the market. Containing about 16 rooms and fitted with all necessary modern conveniences, it is pleasantly situated on the cliffs of the North Foreland, with a great view out to sea. Lord Curzon likes the late Lord Northlife, aware by the building quality of Thanet alr. That the King and Queen share the conviction was proved when they sent their younger sons to school there. It was at Broadstairs the Queen enjoyed her one and only risks on a tram. Mrs. Woodrow Wilson, widow of the late President, was among the visitors at a recent meeting of the League of Nations Assembly at Geneva.

"The immediate cause of the present difficulties in China is national pride," according to Archibald Bullock, head of the department of education in the Centra China Teachers' College for the last 20 years, who has just returned to the United States on furlough. The Shanghai riot he declared to be "comparable to the battle of Lexington and Concord."

On the authority of the London Chamber of Commerce it is learned that during the holiday months more especially, the demand for young male shorthand writers is greater than the supply. The reason is not that there are no unemployed in that calling, but that there is a surplus of inefficients.

A lady reader confesses that she is anxious for the time to come round when she can get to work with her almond-scented whitewash. Is there not, quite seriously, a future for the firm that can perfume its paints? Size and turpentine in particular cry aloud for the sachet treatment. There seems no more reason for nasty smelling paints than for nasty tasting physic.

Philatelists have paid subscriptions to everything from a public park to a consumptives' home. Mexico is now overrun with grasshoppers, but is without money to combat the plague. So they have issued a special set of stamps which have to be fixed to every letter and parcel, thus producing some revenue, but the plague will really be "stamped" out in order that philatelists' collections may be complete.

The German Foreign Office has instructed its representatives throughout Europe and North America to grant visas free of charge to all foreign sportsmen coming to Germany for sporting competitions of any description. The measure is the result of a request by the German Sporting Union, which also had asked that the Foreign Office take up with other governments the question of reciprocal passports for German sportsmen taking part in foreign competitions.

More Women drive Buicks than any other car because of the striking appearance of this famous motor car. Then comes Buick dependability. A woman knows when she starts out with her Buick that she will "get there and back." Other reasons are—the comfort in driving a Buick—the velvet clutch action, easy steering; then the power and quietness of Buick's Valve-in-Head engine and the safety of Buick mechanical four-wheel brakes.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
Two of the public bathing beaches, those at Stonecutter's and Kennedy Town, are to be closed at the end of the present month. Launches will not be available to these beaches after Wednesday evening. September 30, and the matsheds will be dismantled. Other public beaches remain open.

At a dinner given at Wellington to delegates of the Empire Press Union, who are visiting New Zealand, Sir Harry Brittain mentioned the increasing fact that New Zealand's 1,250,000 population did more trade with Great Britain than the 400,000,000 of China. This must not however, be taken as underrating the importance of certain branches of China trade to England and of China as a field for British manufactures.

Malaya and Hongkong "are both represented in a large Empire's delegation which is visiting Hull to see for themselves how comprehensive are the quays for handling fruit, the warehouses for storing grain and meat, the sheds for holding wool, and how expeditiously, with the aid of the London and North-Eastern Railway, can large cargoes be unloaded and transported over the greater part of northern England.

At the annual meeting at Auckland on August 4 of the New Zealand Insurance Company, whose local agents are Messrs. Holyoak, Massey and Co., the shareholders were informed that the directors felt justified in recommending an increase of the rate of dividend, and they accordingly recommended that a sum of £118,750 should be distributed by way of dividend for the year, being equivalent to a dividend at the rate of 1/7 per share. In order to meet this increase in dividend it would not be necessary to draw on the underwriting profits for more than £7,154, as the income derived from investments was only short of the dividend by that amount.

The case against a Chinese revenue officer, who is charged with attempting to obtain by threats a sum of $100 from a distiller, was continued before the Kowloon Magistrate and again adjourned. A scheme was alleged to have been suggested to the distiller by which he could defraud the Revenue Department.

Since the recent unpleasant incidents due to the appearance of sharks and crocodiles at favourite bathing resorts, the increase in the number of bathing pagars at Port Dickson is very noticeable. Nowadays scarcely any bathers are seen in the open sea. A very striking addition to these pagars is that adjoining the fine new bungalow recently erected at the fifth mile on the Coast Road, by a well-known Pasir Panjang towkay.

Among interesting items referred to in an article in the "Ice Cream Trade Journal" are the following: If the ice cream consumed in the United States in one year were put into one cone, it would tower over the Washington Monument; that more than 700,000 cows supply the cream, and that most of the eggs used in the trade come from China. All of which is highly interesting; comments the "N. C. Daily News," but are we to draw the conclusion from these latter facts that honest-to-goodness cream and eggs really enter into the composition of everything sold as ice cream? Alas, we wish we could believe it.

The cruiser “Diomede,” Captain C. E. Kennedy-Purvis, arrived at Portsmouth on August 29 from China, where she has been serving since her completion in 1922. The vessel was commissioned for the first time for service on October 2, 1922, so that by the time she is paid off her term will have extended to nearly three years instead of the normal two-and-a-half. The place of the “Diomede” has temporarily been taken by the “Concord,” Captain A. R. W. Woods, D.S.O., from the Mediterranean, until such time as the large cruiser “Vindictive,” Captain G. F. Hyde, R.A.N., arrives on the station. The “Diomede” will be transferred to the New Zealand Government, which a year ago offered to maintain a second cruiser of the same type as the “Dunedin,” already out there.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Joseph Conrad is the inspiration for the new library and reading room in the annex to the Seamen's Church institute at 25 South Street, New York. The memorial room will cost approximately $100,000 (G.) It is planned to make it a shrine for all Conrad lovers.

Mr. F. J. Benton, formerly of the E. E. A. and C. Telegraph Co., Ltd., in Singapore, is now settled in Sydney and is a director of the Rural Estate and Development Co., Ltd., and the Federal Building Loan Co., Ltd. He writes to say that if any Straits men require information regarding real estate in Australia he will be pleased to answer letters addressed to the offices of the companies, 251, George Street, Sydney.

A wedding of especial interest to the younger set was solemnized at St. Joseph's Church, Shanghai, when Miss Marguerite Tahaney, of San Francisco, became the bride of Mr. Lewis Jackson Peoples, of Townsville, North Carolina, who is Han River manager of the British Cigarette Company. The bride was given away by Mr. Otis D. Terell, and Mrs. C. F. Wolsiffer attended as matron of honour, while Miss Ramona Gray acted as brides-maid. The Very Rev. Dean Symons has been elected an honorary life member of the Shanghai Football Association. Dean Symons has always been a keen patron of sport, and on most Saturday afternoons is to be found at the Race Course, watching the games.

Three men who in the last few years have been unofficial advisors to Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce, and the Administration at Washington regarding Russian affairs, are going again to Soviet Russia. They are James P. Goodrich, formerly Governor of Indiana; William N. Haskell and Dr. F. A. Golder of Stanford University. Colonel Haskell, who directed the American relief administration in Russia, already has sailed from New York.

Mr. A. H. F. Edwards, who was Commissioner of Customs, at Canton at the time of the attack on Shameen, and was shot in the knee, has been undergoing medical treatment at home. It was found inadvisable to extract the bullet which was in the centre of the bone, but success was attained in the difficult and painful process of joining up the severed portions of a tendon which had been shot away. Mr. Edwards is shortly returning to the Far East via Siberia together with Mrs. Edwards, but his future sphere of activities is not yet known.

A woman knows when she starts out with her Buick that she will "get there and back." Other reasons are—the comfort in driving a Buick—the velvet clutch action, easy steering; then the power and quietness of Buick's Valve-in-Head engine and the safety of Buick mechanical four-wheel brakes.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL. GREEN ISLAND CEMENT CO LTD
text:
"Messrs. Mackintosh & Co., Ltd. issue an attractive folder called 'Dress of To-day.'

、Subscriptions to the local Garrison· Recreation Club, per quarter, are:—Officers $2; other ranks 20 cents.

During the weak ended Sept. 26, the only case of notifiable disease was of enteric fever, a Russian (imported). There was a clean sheet for Monday.

According to latest reliable information the employees of Chinese Telegraph Administration in Canton went on strike on the 28th inst. in support of their fellow-workers. in Shanghai to enforce their demands for increase of wages and better treatment.

. Reuter cables that the Peking Government has received a telegram stating that the telegraph strike at Tsingtao has ended. The Cabinet to-day discussed the strike but it is understood that it is left to Chiao Tung-pu to decide whether or not to accept the strikers terms.

A meeting of the Legislative Council will be held to-morrow when the following resolution will be moved by the Colonial Secretary: "Resolved by the Legislative Council that the percentages on the valuation of tenements on the following lots on Kowloon Bay Reclamation shall be 13 percent: New Kowloon Inland Lots Nos. 132, 227, 228, 238, 239 and 251." The following questions will be asked: By Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird.—"Has the Government considered the advisability of establishing a Labour Bureau for the voluntary registration of domestic servants and others? If so with what result?" By Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak.—"Will the Government state when it is hoped to complete and open the new 'Saiyingpun' School?" The Orders of the Day contain the second reading of five Bills which were introduced at the last meeting of the Council. “The Motion Picture Industry in China” was discussed at the last weekly meeting of the Shanghai Rotary Club held at the Astor House by Roturian Luther Jee of the Pencock Motion Picture Corporation.

Messrs. Wm. Powell, Ltd. announce the engagement of Mr. E. Broadberry as a cutter in charge of their tailoring department.

The annual general meeting of the Hongkong Philharmonic Society is announced to be held on Monday, October 5 next at 9 p.m. in St. John's Cathedral Hall.

Babies' finger prints are to be taken in Ireland when they leave workhouses. This decision was made by the Union Commissioners in consequence of large increases in the number of babies, living and dead, found in the streets, shops, and elsewhere in Dublin. It is hoped that the finger prints will enable the police to trace the mothers or foster mothers abandoning children.

A peculiar incident was brought to light at Vigo when a girl of 18 jumped into the sea. Her act was in consequence of apparently insuperable obstacles to her marriage to a youth who was wrongly registered as a girl at birth. The authorities refused to certify him as anything but a female, and it was thus impossible to obtain the necessary documents for the marriage. Two sailors saved the would-be suicide.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Reuter cables that Wu Kuang-hsin has arrived at Hankow to interview Hsiao Yao-nan.

The leave granted to Captain L. W. Smith, R.A. has been changed to "from October 5 to October 11."

Professor Danenberg cables from Tokyo that the recital given by young Emil has been a great success. Emil is to play in Osaka, Kobe and Shanghai.

The marriage of Mr. Chia Powhin, of the Hongkong University, formerly assistant master of St. John's Institution, Kuala Lumpur, to Miss Lye Nyon Keow, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lye Ah Yew, of Singapore, has taken place at Singapore.

News to hand from Liemchow indicates the collapse of part of the roof of the C. E. Church outside the city, through the work of white ants. The Church was the gift of Miss A. M. Bakewell, so well known in Hongkong, who is a C.M.S. missionary at Liemchow. The foundation stone was laid by Miss Marguerite Bradley, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. Bradley, of Yunnanfu, also well known in the Colony.

Lieut. G. H. Sloane-Stanley, R.A., Lieut. E. L. E. Davies, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. H. C. Gould, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. B. Aucott, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. G. M. S. Webb, 5/2nd Punjab Regt., and Lieut. E. A. S. Cope, 1st Batt. East Surrey Regt. will be examined for promotion on Friday; Captain L. D. Joll, M.C., R.A., Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman and Captain D. J. Allfree of the Surrey Regt. will be examined on Thursday week.

Justice E. Finley Johnson, member for the United States at the International Commission, was the honour guest, with Mrs. Johnson, at a notable dinner given by Consul General for China Mr. Lingui Wang at the Manila Hotel Mr. Wang's other invited guests were the Honourable Robert M. Bacon and Mrs. Bacon, Admiral and Mrs. W. Bullard, Colonel, and Mrs. Arthur W. Yates, Colonel and Mrs. C. M. National Dr. and Mrs. H. Sugeno Stafford Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Zoninger Mr. and Mr. C. G. Brinsney Mr. and Mrs. W. The Hongkong Technical Institute re-opens next Monday. Students joining classes held at Queen's College will be enrolled at the Education Department only, but those joining classes to be held at the Central British School, Kowloon, may be enrolled at the school. Entry forms can be obtained from the Education Department or the Central British School.

Mr. D. F. Dunn of the Hongkong Taxi Cab Co., Ltd. returned to the Colony from Manila yesterday by the "President Madison."

Mr. R. J. Farrar, President of the Municipal Commissioners, has arrived at Singapore by the "d'Artagnan" from home leave.

H.E. Major-General Sir T. Fraser, K.C.B., arrived in Kuala Lumpur on the morning of September 20, and is staying at the British Residency.

Reuter cables that Messrs. Abe and Kawachi, the Japanese aviators "who are flying from Japan to London, have arrived at Le Bourget.

The engagement is announced between Mr. Lionel Van Geyzel, son of Dr. Van Geyzel, of Seremban, and Miss Dorothy Marks, eldest daughter of Mr. John Marks of Digwarah group, Sungkai.

The Rev. P. B. Clayton, the founder and the first padre of Toc H, who is now in Australia is expected to arrive in Singapore on October 2 and will be in Penang on the 14, 15 and 16, leaving following day for Calcutta.

The following were among the candidates declared successful at the recent examination by the Civil Service Commissioners for admission to the Police Force of Ceylon, the Straits Settlements, the Federated Malay States, and Hongkong: T. D. Ogier, F. O. Mell), A. R. H. Anderson, H. P. Waights, L. F. Knight, H. R. Bond, L. R. Barnett-Smith, O. E. M. de Bretton, A. R. MacKillop, H. M. Smith, and L. A. Ives.

Mr. G. W. King, O.B.E., Registrar of H.M. Supreme Court (Shanghai), who wound up the estate of the late Mr. Patrick Reilly who died on February 22, 1925, has received a letter from the deceased's alster, Mrs. Downie, expressing appreciation in the following words: "I wish that you could thank the many friends of my late brother for the lovely wreaths and the interest they look in him," only wish I could thank each one personally but may be your could not some way to thank them for me. The late Mr. Reilly was employed in the Shanghai War. Mr. A. B. M. Mr. F. A. Walls, of H.B.M. Consulate-General, accompanied by his wife, is on a trip to Baguio for his health.

Uniformed interpreters for the convenience of tourists have been stationed at the three principal terminals in Berlin. They are on hand at the arrival and departure of all trains and their services are given to the travelling public without charge.

In spite of unrest and anti-foreign agitation, more books are said to have been sold in China lately by the British and Foreign Bible Society. Out of every ten books sold in 1924 about four were sold in China. Half of their increased circulation last year took place there.

Among the passengers who arrived Home by the "Mantua" was Mrs. Mackenzie, widow of the Englishman who was shot dead by Chinese rebels while motoring outside Shanghai. She has gone to London with her little daughter. Another passenger was Sergeant Gavan, of Shanghai Police Force, who has been invalidated home as the result of wounds inflicted by women who, armed with knives, were in the front of the strike crowds.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
Comm. Maxwell Scott, the Senior Naval Officer at Canton, has been promoted to the rank of captain.

Says Dr. Inge (the Gloomy Dean) on his visit to America:—I met with nothing but courtesy from high and low. The good American is a great gentleman; and this quality seems to be widely diffused, irrespective of differences in social position.

It is not without significance that, when a procession of Chinese paraded the streets the other day in Kobe in order to encourage the strike of Chinese semmen, some of the most prominent in the procession were employees of British firms, and these prominent patriots were not themselves on strike.

A Naval flight is projected from Yokosuka to Maizuru and across the Japan Sea to Vladivostok, to take place in either July or September. The return trip is expected to take a week. The seaplanes will participate.

The British American Tobacco Co. (China), Ltd., announces that as so much unjust pro-paganda is being directed against it by competitive interests in an effort to boycott the products of the Company, the Company has felt justified in calling the attention of the public to the great quantity of charitable work it has done in China. A list of its charities follows, making a very large total.

President von Hindenburg has objected to the paintings hung by President Ebert in the rooms of the Presidential Palace. President Ebert, who was a great lover of nature, had decorated his rooms almost exclusively with landscape pictures. In his working room hung a large landscape, a woman's portrait by Rembrandt and two small water colours. President von Hindenburg, however, declared they were not cheerful enough for his taste, and has chosen several new pictures at the state picture galleries.

headline: 一
text: The Chinese Communists, arrested after the attack on the Chinese Legation at Paris, were taken to the frontier of Belgium to be dumped in that friendly State. As a rule, the Belgian police do not object, but these undesirables were too much for them. John Chinaman was promptly pounted back into France. A French Commissary tried several points along the Belgian frontier; but each time the yellow Reds were returned to him (without thanks). He resolved to try Germany. From Strasbourg he took his proteges to the nearest point of the frontier beyond the Rhine, and told them to go straight on. They did not return. The new Chinese puzzle was solved.

Fifty Boy Scouts from Japan will go to China this summer to spend several weeks in camps there, says an American paper. At the same time some two dozen Chinese Boy Scouts will come to Japan for a visit. This plan of exchanging Boy Scouts with various countries has aroused considerable enthusiasm among Scout leaders in Tokyo. It was stated that the Boy Scout organisation of Hungary has begun negotiations with the Japanese organisation with the view of exchanging visits.

A driver of a taxicab goes to the Chamber of Deputies in Paris, and when he arrives he places a black cover over the flag of his taximeter. This indicates that he is not soliciting fares. He puts his cwb on the rank and enters the Chamber. He takes his seat on the parliamentary benches, listens to the discussions and sometimes intervenes. When the sitting is over, or when he considers that his presence is not required, he leaves, returns to his cab, takes off the black cover, and plies for hire. For the taxi driver is a Deputy, but because he is a Deputy he does not therefore cease to follow his occupation. For a number of hours every day he drives for a living. The cab is his own property and he is therefore under no restrictions as to hours. His name is Monsieur Adam, and he sits as a Communist in the Department of the Seine.

After the lapse of seventeen years, Lord Burnham held a Court Baron at Hall Barn, Beaconsfield (Bucks), in connection with the manorial rights and customs. Lord Burnham, as Lord of the Manor of Beaconsfield, appointed his hayward, scalers of leather, ale-tasters, bailiff, constables; and bellman. The ale-tasters appointed were Mr. Charles Allen Bennet, K.C., and Mr. G. K. Chesterton.

The King of Spain, who is 39, has, with rather grim humour, formed a collection of relics of the various attempts which have been made to cut short his career. The collection is a considerable one, and its contents range from the test of a feeding-bottle used in an attempt to poison him at the age of eight, to pieces of the Barcelona bomb, the skeleton of a horse killed by another bomb, and a fragment of the landau in which he was riding with President Loubet at the time of the attempted assassination in the Rue de Rivoli, Paris. Of late years, happily, the additions to, the museum have been few.

headline: HOCKEY PROSPECTS. / DISCUSSED AT ANNUAL MEETING.
text:
Confidence in the prospects for another successful season was expressed at the annual meeting yesterday of the Hongkong Hockey Club. - This took place at Volunteer Headquarters, and was presided over by Lieut. Col. L. G. Bird, D.S.O., the attendance not being large owing to the coincidence of the Rugby match between the Volunteers and H.M.S. "Hermes."

After a balance in hand of $238.88 had been reported, last season's excellent record was read and the revival of meetings between the Club and Shameen was referred to. As regarded the future, the Club would have three representatives at a meeting on Monday of the Recreation Grounds Committee which would consider a request for a double plot to serve as sports ground for the Volunteers. During the coming season there would again be three teams and playing days would be the same. The resignation of Mr. Bower from the Club was received with regret and for his organisation which had made possible the playing by the A team of 18 matches the thanks of the Club were recorded.

Present officers willing to serve again were Hon. Secretary, P.W. F. Mills; Captain, E.J. R. Mitchell; and Vice-Captain, W. Woodward. Mr. J. Wedlake was elected Captain of the second XI. and Mr. L. H. Kearne of the "A" team. Mr. G. H. Piercy who had signified his inability to continue in the office of Hon. Treasurer was succeeded by Mr. L. H. Ralphs.

The thanks of the Club were recorded to the United Services Recreation Club for the use of grounds and entertainment of visitors.

headline: WANT MORE PAY.
text:
SOME CANTON RATEWAY WORKKR

K.C.R.—CHINESE BACTION.

The demand for an increase of wages by the Canton. Kowloon Railway workers was forwarded to the Railway Authorities for over a fortnight. Proposals were made by representatives from both parties. A reply was recently given by the Railway authorities to the workers saying that owing to financial stringency the railway cannot meet the demands of the workers, for while the railway may easily make promises it will not be able to carry them out. Besides, the demands for a reply in so short a time means danger to the welfare of the railway. In response, a letter was addressed to the Railway authorities yesterday (says Monday's "Canton Guiehte") by the workers stating, "With regard to financial stringency, the Kwangtung Yuch Hani Railway and the Canton Samshui Railway are in worse condition than the Canton Kowloon Railway, yet the wages of the workers of these two railways are nearly double that of ours. We do not see the reason why you cannot meet the demand of the workers while other railways can. As to the limit of time for a reply from you, our subject is to get an early settlement. There is nothing threatening in it."

It is said that the workers are preparing to take other measures to urge an early settlement, as they regard the attitude of the Railway Authorities as insincere.

headline: S.S. "WAH SHAN."
text:
CANTON ACKNOWLEDGES SEIZURE.

POLITICS BLAMED.

In connection with the seizure of the s.s. "Wah Shan," the "Canton Gazette" of Monday says:—

A special correspondent reports that the steamer "Wah Shan" was found transporting provisions to Hongkong. "She was seized by the pickets immediately. Several officers under Tang Poon-yan were arrested on board the steamer. They were brought to the Strike Committee at Canton.

The Nationalist Government has ordered the Strike Committee to transfer the case, including criminals and steamer, to the Government for judgment, as documents relating to political matters were found on the criminals when their arrest was effected.

[Commander Tang Pun-yan is the pro-Chan Kwing-ming ruler of Hainan and the Lui Chow peninsula. The "Wah Shan" did not touch his territory nor is it a passenger steamer. The only ports of call were Hongkong (British), Kwong Chow Wan (French) and Macao (Portuguese).]

headline: LEGACY OF ERRORS. / MISPRINTS THAT PERSIST IN SHAKESPEARE.
text:
For some years past it has been increasingly recognised in England that anyone who sets out to edit or annotate Elizabethan or Jacobean plays without an adequate knowledge of the handwritings of the period is not likely to do much to improve his author's text. Dramatic texts, including Shakespeare's, despite all the work which has been done on them during the last two centuries, still stand in need of further corrections, because while in other forms of literature many, perhaps most, authors corrected their proofs, most dramatists did not. The main reason for this was, doubtless, that as a rule they had no pecuniary interest in printed editions of their plays, all the rights (as far as the extent evidence shows) having passed to the companies of actors for which the plays were written. Proof-reading in those days, moreover, seems to have involved frequent attendance at the printing house; and for an actor-dramatist, with performances in the afternoon and rehearsals (presumably) in the morning, this would have been especially inconvenient. The blame cast on the printers for the misprints which resulted from their being left to do the best they could is thus largely unjust; but the misprints were made, and undoubtedly many of them still disfigure current texts, some as recognised difficulties and others as poor readings which editors are too conservative to alter.

If more of the corruptions which still linger in dramatic texts are to be eliminated, emendation must be inspired and controlled by a knowledge (1) of the different kinds of misprints which have already been corrected, (2) of the various ways in which letters were formed, more especially by the dramatist himself, but also by other authors of the period, (3) of the various ways in which words could be spelt. Dr. Keilner, who has issued a work entitled "Restoring Shakespeare" prefaces it by saying that "from 1914 to this day" he has been "busy to the exclusion of all other work, applying the key of the elizabetthan handwriting to the unexplained passages in Shakespeare's works"; and he ventures a modest hope that as a result of his labours he has "arrived at a number of satisfactory readings." headline: HOME RUGBY
text:
RESULT AHEAD OF THE MAIL.

In the Rugby Union match played to-day, Pontypool beat Aberavon by three points to nil.

By 10 goals to 1, the Kowloon British School Former Pupils Association defeated the Hong Kong Electric Co. In the Water Polo League, at the VRC last night.

Some of the heats in the annual aquatic sports of the V.R.O.V.Ch. including the Colony's champion ships) will be decided this afternoon.

(Times of Ceylon.)

The “Auto” learns that the Rugby Unions of Australia and New Zealand have officially asked the French Rugby Federation whether it would welcome representative teams in 1926-27.

It is impossible for the Federation to receive both teams simultaneously, but it is understood that it has agreed to invite the Australians in 1926-27 and the New Zealanders during 1927-28 to play a number of matches in Paris and the provinces.

headline: RUGBY RULES.
text:
INTERNATIONAL BOARD'S CHANGES.

SCRUMS, OFFSIDE, THROW-OUT.

In order that all players may familiarise themselves with the changes in the laws of the game recently passed by the International Board, the Home Rugby Union have just issued a resume of such changes.

In regard to a scrummage, the team not responsible for the stoppage now has the right of putting the ball into the scrummage on either side, and the ball is not to be considered fairly in the scrummage until it has passed a player on each side.

An offside player is not to be put onside when the ball is touched by an opponent, but only when the ball is intentionally so touched. No charge is to be allowed when a penalty kick is taken.

Another interesting change is in the throw-out law. The ball must now be thrown out so as to alight at least five yards at right angles to the touch-line.

What is the best of all exercises from the point of view of health and fitness? The Lord Mayor of London (Sir Alfred Bowar)

headline: TRADE ROMANCE
text:
The enterprise of these responsible for the founding of the English India Company and the patented and bravery of those responsible for carrying on its work forms the subject of an article in the Scottish Educational Journal. The story whilst being of educational value, it states, is also sufficiently colourful to attract the youthful student. After dealing with the first efforts of London merchants to secure a portion of the profitable business which was being carried on in the East India by the Portuguese and Dutch and the bestowal on them by Queen Elizabeth of a special monopoly, the efforts of the leading members of the association to obtain funds for the equipping of a commercial squadron are referred to. Large numbers shrank from the risk, and at last there was nothing for it but to create a separate association of the more enterprising and start business on much smaller scale than was originally intended.

On February 18, 1601, therefore, five small ships, the largest of which was only 600 tons, weighed anchor at Tor Bay, and steered on that amazing course which was to lead to the conquest of an empire. Of the many adventuring banks that have left our shores, not one has opened a story to equal the strangeness, the romance, the magnificence, of the events that were ushered in by the sailing of those five ships. Patience must have been one of the finest assets of the little group of merchants who undertook the first expedition, for they had to wait two years and seven months before their ships came home. Captain James Lancaster, under whose command they had sailed, had already been in India, but so slightly was he acquainted with the geography of the regions into which his argosies were sailing that he did not reach his destination. Acheen in Sumatra, till June 5, 1602—one year and a half after leaving England. In spite of successful business done, the wake of his five ships was not followed with much enthusiasm, the result being that for about ten years no great advance was made. Then, in 1812, a Captain Best secured privileges from the ruler at Delhi, which included the right to establish a factory at Surat, and the connection with the mainland thus made, was greatly strengthened three years later, when James I. sent Sir Thomas Roe as his ambassador to Delhi. He was received with the highest honours, and English trade with India was much encouraged. But in viewing the story of the advance of the British in the land of the Moguls, we have always to bear in mind that the distance between the two scenes of the Company's activities, together with ever changing circumstance in both places, did much to dislocate their arrangements. While the pioneers, far from the home base, were opening up fresh sources of prosperity, the Governor and his Directors in London were facing and overcoming a variety of difficulties. Increasing success (somewhat slow, however), brought competitors into the field who sought to ignore the Charter which James I. had renewed; and these competitors were not discouraged by Charles I. In spite of the monopoly that the Company legally possessed, the King last named—doubtless on account of his own need for money—granted a second Charter to a separate association, and the trade thus divided was of little profit to either, till they were finally amalgamated into one company.

headline: TIENTSIN MILL STRIKE.
text:
The "Perking and Pfeiss Times" states that the workers at Paocheng Mill, outside Tientsin, struck work on Saturday and other mills ceased work on Sunday.

It is reported that trouble arose over the fining of two men for being late, though the authorities state that the workers are demanding an increase of wages. The Chinese Police acted promptly; and there were practically no disturbances beyond the early breaking of windows.

The student delegates played a prominent part at meetings of workers, last evening.

headline: MISSION SCHOOLS.
text:
Considerable interest and importance attaches to the various Missionary Conferences to be held at summer resorts, near Shanghai and elsewhere, this month to discuss the future of Mission Schools in China, in view of the widespread movement among students not to return to such institutions owing to nationalistic and anti-foreign agitation.

It is understood that some missionaries favour opening next term, hoping that a good number of pupils will return.

returning will probably be subjected to considerable annoyance and persecution by students of non-Mission Colleges; and possibly forced to leave. Many Missionaries, therefore, advocate the closing of the schools for 8 months, a year, or more; others suggest the handing over of the schools to the Chinese for a period of one to three years so as to give the native Christian teachers an opportunity of conducting them. The problem not only concerns education; for there are numerous cases of Chinese withdrawing from the Mission. Churches and forning Independent Churches of their own. The question there was also a crisis whether to hand the Chinese to native.

headline: SYRIAN FIGHTING.
text:
General Surrail's despatch, regarding the fighting in Syria was read to a party of pressmen by M. Painlevé, late last evening. It stated that the Druse attack on the French troops originated in discussions among members of the family of the aggressor. Some of them wanted a French Governor: others, favouring independence, clamoured for a Native Governor. As the agitation grew more lively, small columns were sent to inspire respect and order. One immediately entered Jebeldruse and was enveloped, and submerged by the flood of aggressors. The troops fought most valiantly, but were crushed by numbers. Sixty managed to escape massacre.

A large column, commanded by General Michaud, was sent to exact reparation. This action of General Michaud's column was followed by a convoy of mule and camel transport, protected by Mulagasy and Syrian Tiraillens, who fled in the face of a violent Druse attack. The convoy was captured and the officer in command of the convoy was wounded and committed suicide. The infantry column was thus deprived of ammunition, but was able to retire fighting.

M. Painlevé added that he was unable to state the losses of General-Michaud's column as General Serruil's despatch was unfinished.

“Le Journal,” commenting on the above, says that the despatch throws an expected light on the Jebeldruse incidents, their causes and effects, and demands a full and impartial enquiry.

headline: CHINA AND POWERS.
text:
Following two previous communications M. Pajaret on the 7th sent a further note to the Wachiaopul in regard to the bayoneting of a Chinese at Chungking last month, forwarding a memorandum summarising the detailed report from the Consul. The note mentions the receipt of the Wachiaopul's note of the 27th July quoting telegrams from the Szechuan provincial authorities but questions the accuracy of these accounts and expresses surprise that the reports, which are in complete contradiction, to the facts, should in this, as other cases, be accepted as genuine.

The note claims that the action of the gunboat in landing four sailors under a petty officer, who dispersed the mob, wounding one Chinese, in the stomach and slightly wounding three others, was taken in view of the imminent danger threatening the lives of British subjects and the failure of the Chinese authorities to take require-site action.

While commending the praiseworthy efforts of two Chinese officers, General Wang Ling-chi and Captain Lei, to avert trouble and to protect Britons, M. Palairet protests most strongly against the "disgraceful conduct of the Chungking authorities as a whole, who, with the exception of the officers named, were guilty of willful neglect of duty and more or less open encouragement of the rioters."

headline: PEKING'S TROUBLES.
text:
Peking, August 10. Two-thirds of the British Legation employees are still on strike, though a few of the office staff and servants returned this morning. The lighting was yesterday linked up with the Legation quarter supply and little inconvenience was caused.

Some instances of subotage were discovered, including damage to the pump providing houses in the Legation with artesian water.

Mr. Pulariet, is interviewing the Chief Executive, His Excellency Tuan Chi-jui, with regard to the strike this afternoon. Legation officials are optimistic that the interview will result in ending the strike.

The British and other foreigners are daily growing more indignant at the seeming'indifference of the Chinese Authorities with regard to the strike which, it is felt, they could have ended promptly if they had desired.

headline: FOOD RIOTS.
text:
SHANGHAI CHINESE CITY OVER-RUN.

Bands of striking wharf and godown coolies this morning overran the Chinese city creating a riot during which they looted the foodshops.

The demonstrations were the result of strike pay not being forthcoming.

The police were helpless. They fired once, wounding one man.

The afternoon was quieter. A mob of a few hundreds started for the Settlement and demonstrated at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. They were pacified by labour officials. The municipal police prevented trouble.

headline: NO DEADLOCK.
text:
THE BELGIAN DEBT NEGOTIATIONS.

PRESIDENT COOLIDGE'S STATEMENT.

After two hours conference at the Presidential homestead with Mr. Mellon and Senator Smoot who reported on the Belgian Debt negotiations, President Coolidge made a statement to pressmen that progress was satisfactory and that no deadlock had developed.

The conference is reassembling to-morrow when a final agreement is expected.

Reuter learns that a gigantic financial deal, probably the biggest since the war will presently be negotiated, whereby an Anglo-American syndicate, the names of the members of which are not disclosed, will purchase the entire property of Mannesmann Brothers in the Spanish zone of Morocco and Riff.

The vast property includes the harbour works of Alhucemas, and elsewhere, zinc, sulphur, and other mines and large tracts of agricultural land.

headline: BOLSHEVIK MENACE.
text:
A reduction in the population of St. Petersburg from two millions before the war to 400,000 and 500,000 now and its ruined state were also referred to by the lecturer, the matter arising out of a question by the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster.

In reply to another member of the audience who quoted the "China Mail" and asked the lecturer if he had heard the rumour with regard to the opening of the gates of Shameen, Mr. Hellstrom said that he had, but it was only a rumour. When the rumour had got about before the Bolsheviks had caused to be re-erected some kind of barrier outside the Chinese's Customs and had warned the Chinese that they were liable to be killed if they had anything to do with Europeans.

His reference to barricades was challenged by a member of the audience and the lecturer admitted that it was perhaps too strong a term to use in indicating duck and pig baskets near some newly laid cement although they had been strengthened somewhat after the rumour about the gates being opened. He did not think Shameen would be attacked by the Bolshevik Government as they preferred to kill trade rather than risk defeat by war.

The meeting applauded an answer given by the lecturer to Mr. M. Manuk who asked what remedy he would suggest for the present state of affairs. A voice interpolated with "British intervention" but Mr. Hellstrom answered that it was not for him to tell Britain how to put her own house in order.

Conditions in Swatow were referred to by Mr. A. Macgown of that port. He referred to the taxes imposed by whatever military leader happened to have control at the time and said that the taxes were collected by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce whose representatives were accompanied by military. Up to the present house rents (one method of taxation) had been collected three years in advance (ltr.) Mr. Macgown referred to the impossible treatment of the British Consul at Swatow who received no replies to his despatches to the Chinese representatives and was not received when he called personally. Examples were given of the intense anti-British feeling in existence there.

More questions were invited at the end and speaking from the audience, Sir Henry Pollock was received with applause when he remarked that the time for drift and inaction was past. A minority in Canton were defying treaties by which it was stipulated that Canton was an open port to Great Britain for trade not only with Canton but with the interior. He felt he was expressing the feelings of those present when he said that they would be grateful to the Committee of the Chamber of Commerce if they would at an early date call a public meeting with a view to definite action being suggested to the British Government.

Thanks to Mr. Hellstrom, the Chairman and the Hon. Mr. Holyoak for getting into touch with Mr. Hellstrom, concluded the meeting.

It is time Britain intervened and showed a lead to other nations. A large body of influential Chinese should welcome British intervention to help China put her house in order. We can intervene with every justification. Now is our opportunity. Wake up England and fight this blasted Bolshevism. Let's have War and occupy Canton to start with. We have a wonderful record. Let's live up to it and be men, not cowardly politicians.

Will all who want to join an Anti-Bolshevik Association whose objects are to forcibly eject all Bolshevism from China and every other part of the world, send their names in to me care of the "China Mail" as soon as possible, with a view to a mass meeting to ask the Government to declare war on the present Canton Government. This is the only possible solution to the present situation, and the only way to restore our prestige in China.

headline: Two Different Views.
text:
M. Caillaux and Mr. Churchill met at the Treasury at noon to discuss the payment of France's debt to Britain, amounting to £623,000,000.

The contrast between British and French viewpoints is illustrated by the respective Press comments to-day.

The British newspapers emphasise that Britain expects to receive payments equal to those paid to America.

“L'Echo de Paris” says the agreement is impossible unless it is admitted that France is unable to assume a burden beyond her strength.

"Gaulois" says that statistics prove that the French are indirectly heavier taxed than the British; moreover the British must not consider the question from purely a fiscal viewpoint.

"L'Ere Nouvelle" says the success of M. Callaux's mission depends on whether he meets a gentleman or a shopkeeper. Referring to the situation in China and India "L'Ere Nouvelle" says this is not the time to discuss bills but to close the ranks in the face of a threatening world conflagration.

“Le Matin” denies that M. Callaux is disposed to offer $15,000,000 annually. It declares that the last offer of French experts was the maximum of $10,000,000. The negotiations were adjourned because this was declined.

headline: SHIPPING STRIKE:
text:
NEWS FROM ALL OVER

AUSTRALIAN EMERGENCY

The Federal Cabinet, at a special meeting to consider the difficult situation arising out of the strike of British seamen, subsequently issued a proclamation declaring a serious industrial disturbance exists.

This empowers the Federal authorities to deal with those who continue to obstruct the conveyance of goods and passengers.

Later Melbourne August 24

Highly important developments are expected to follow the issue of a proclamation which sets in motion the machinery of the Immigration Act, empowering the Government to deport persons not born in Australia who are responsible for obstructing transport.

headline: Ten Ships Held Up.
text:
Ten British steamers are idle. Their crews total 2,000 of whom 1,600 are practically nomiess and the remaining 400 are allowed aboard pending a settlement.

Spreads To New Zealand.

headline: (Earlier Cable.)
text: At the headquarters of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union it was said to-day that all the ships effected by the trouble at the London Docks sailed and no men left their ships. An official of the Tibbury branch said "our fellows are good men and are acting very decently. There is nothing Bolshevik about them."

headline: HONGKONG SAFE.
text: on that "very damaging weapon" the boycott does not convey very clearly what was in the mind of the writer, and those who delight in our "confused British ways" have waxed profanely playful on the subject, remarks the "Peking and Tientsin Times." It is stated that the boycott "is maintained by an idea or an obsession, and it should be the definite object of British policy to dispel the obsession by all possible means." It is not always easy to suppress an idea, and still harder to dispel it when it comes out of the chrysalis and becomes an obsession. But the boycott idea is not among the difficult category. It usually suppresses itself, and it will do so as it has done before, because it is essentially contrary to self-interest. It is pre-eminently the boomerang of economic politics, inflicting hardships quite as severe on the boycotters as upon the boycotted.

headline: RETAILATION?
text: which the dispelling of the obsession may be assisted. Some of them have been openly discussed in Shanghai, and in a restricted sense practised, with notably healthy reactions. There is an unexploited field for retaliation in the Straits Settlements, for instance, where many thousands of Chinese are making their fortunes, and, instead of distributing most of their incomes in the country wherein they are made, as the vast majority of foreigners do in China, send large sums annually to their native land. Enormous sums of money in the aggregate leave the United States in this way for Europe. The same circumstances apply in the Straits. Life could be made very uncomfortable for the large Chinese population in these Settlements. We do not suppose it would ever be made as impossible and, in supportable as in Soviet Siberia, where Chinese traders who have not been kicked out of the country have to carry on under extreme difficulties. It would not be necessary to go farther than the Government of the Philippines, whose book-keeping laws, directed wholly against the Chinese traders, aroused a storm of indignation among the latter. It is not to be supposed that the indigenous population of the Straits is less jealous of the Chinese than are the Filipinos. When the representatives of the British Government in the Peking Legation are boycotted, and attempts are made to starve them out, countermeasures of a salutary description are unquestionably warrantable. However, we do not suppose such reprisals, which are entirely against our traditional Colonial policy, will ever be necessary, or adopted. But some of the fanatics, who, like their ancestors, think they can do without foreigners, the trade they bring, and the employment they afford to thousands of Chinese, and would yell with diabolical glee if they saw the last of us embark for our homelands, might occasionally give a thought to their own countrymen, vastly outnumbering us, who obtain their livelihood and amass wealth — some of which found its way to the coffers of the Kuomintang before the Party went over to the Communists — under the British flag.

And when the Governor of Hongkong declared that he would stay and see it through, he was promptly declared, not a coward, but a bully. We think that Hongkong will prove to be quite able to take care of itself, and will crush once and for all this officially engineered assault upon a Government that has always treated the Chinese perfectly fairly, and to whom Sun Yat-sen paid a glowing tribute in a rare moment of fair-mindedness.

headline: CANTON'S LOSSES.
text:
The strike and boycott are slowly killing themselves. Hongkong has been put to great inconvenience, but Canton has suffered no less. The great silk trade of the city is at a standstill, together with most of the foreign trade. Many large consignments of silk warehoused in Canton for shipment to foreign markets have had to be sent back to the producing districts, and a city whose commerce is thus temporarily ruined has, moreover, to support a veritable army of unemployed, intimidated into leaving their positions in Hongkong, and terrorised into remaining away. The boycott and the nationalist agitation have points of peculiar similarity. A constructive policy could make China independent of those facilities whose withdrawal, as the result of her own action, has paralysed her commerce. A constructive national policy would with for the Chinese people all that a nation of such vast proportions could desire. In the present at in previous agitations, the Chinese are simply kicking with blindury against the pricks. An educational boy, out with last no longer than a trade boycott. The students will are most involved in the movement have decided that they will never return in the foreign educational institutions whose principal adopted the only course consistent with this principle and

duty. Some of them undoubtedly will not, though the choice will not always be theirs. But no serious effort is being made to expand native facilities for education. The thousands who have been receiving their education at the Mission schools will have to go back to them, or consider their education completed, and set out on a fight for existence, already hard enough in this undeveloped and over-populated country, that can have but one result. If only a tithe of the effort devoted to destructive movements, from the civil wars of the Militarists to the rabid ravings of the babus, were given to creative and constructive effort, there might be some hope for the immediate future of this country, and a corresponding respect and generosity among foreign nationals. There is no better or surer way to win the goodwill of the West—or to command it—than by earning and deserving it, and that can only be done by a solid, determined patriotic national effort to introduce order and good government. The world can only respect those who respect themselves.

London, August 26.—St, Paul's Restoration Fund has reached £250,000.—Reuter.

headline: CANTON MISSION WORK.
text:
NESTERDAY'S INTERESTING CONFERENCE DEVISION.

A 'WITH DRAWAL-TEMPORALITY'

The decision come to yesterday at a Conference held in Hongkong to consider the immediate future activities of the U.M.S. in Canton and throughout Kwangtung, marks an epoch in the history of missionary work in China.

Reuter has already cabled with regard to conferences held throughout China recently the opinion that had been expressed by missionary bodies that schools and missions should be handed over to the Chinese at any rate temporarily, because, in the first place, parents of pupils would hesitate to expose their children to possible insult at mission schools, and, in the second, that it would give an opportunity to test whether the time was opportune for Chinese effort alone to carry on with the work.

The decision at the Conference held here yesterday was that the schools in Canton should re-open as under the aegis of the C.M.S. but with no foreign teachers, and as it is the first actual decision which has been reported to the "China Mail," its results as an experiment will be awaited with interest. An important member of the C.M.S. body at present in Hongkong who conversed with a "China Mail" representative this morning said that it should be made clear that the foreign teachers and missionaries were shirking nothing. In leaving and abstaining from visiting the scene of their work they were acting merely in accordance with consular instruction and they were prepared to return at any moment if it were possible and if it were thought that such action would serve a good purpose.

The Chinese masters had in the great majority of cases noted splendidly at the various missions and schools, said the "China Mail" informant, and the Mission had every confidence in them. A few, left but merely as a result of intimidation and not out of sympathy with the forces of disorder.

Missionaries whose sphere of activities have been at Foochow and Pakhoi are awaiting consular instruction before returning

The schools at Canton affected by the decision come to yesterday are Holy Trinity, St. Andrew's Hall and St. Kildn's Girls' School.

headline: KATHERINE MACDONALD in WHITE SHOULDERS / INTIMIDATION.
text:
COOLIE BRAWLS HEARD IN COURT.

ACCUSED FINED

Two Chinese were charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday with intimidating a coolie foreman.

Mr. R. E. A. Webster, defending, said that certain witnesses he wished to call had dropped out of sight, and that apparently one of the men had been threatened by the complainant not to give evidence against him.

A woman who was in Court at the last hearing was called, and she stated that she heard the complainant threatening a man outside the Court.

One of the accused stated that he had entered into a partnership with the other accused and that they went to the Ping On wharf to unload cargo. They met complainant here and had a dispute as their appearance on the wharf was resented. They were later arrested on a charge of threatening the complainant, which was denied.

The accused were each nned $25.

A similar charge against the two men in which a coolie stated that they threw stones at him and threatened to kill him if he continued in his work was dealt with by Mr. H. R. Butters.

-Both the accused were bound over on a bond of $25 to be of good behaviour for six months.

headline: SAFETY RULES.
text:
WHEN IT IS FATAL TO IGNORE THEM.

DRAIN COOLIE'S DEATH.

Non-observance of the regulation was alleged at the enquiry yesterday to have led to the death of a coolie employed on work connected with the drainage department. If the regulations were adhered to, accidents would be impossible, said Mr. D. S. Edwards, of that department, who gave evidence at the enquiry.

Under the regulations in question, which were all explained to the coolies, said Mr. Edwards, they were told that it was dangerous to descend a manhole unless more than one of the holes were opened. Sewer gas would tend to accumulate and rise and when the manholes were not opened daily the gas would escape only when they were opened.

The coolie foreman who was present at the time that the deceased went down the manhole gave evidence at the enquiry. He said that before the deceased went down, another hole in Canton Road was opened and adhered to this statement, although the Coroner asked him how he could account for the fact that the drain in question in Canton Road had been examined by expert witnesses who found dirt still round the edges and were prepared to swear it had not been opened.

The regulations also emphasised the imperative necessity of a lamp being lowered before entry and the Coroner put it to the foreman that there had been one there on that day. Witness affirmed that there had been and that he had been there and saw it lowered the first time. He did not know what had happened when the deceased went down the second time. Witness had gone to shut the hole opened in Canton Road, he said, when he heard a shout that the deceased had become unconscious. On going down to pull the deceased from the hole, he himself had slipped and fallen, said the witness. They were both pulled to the surface by another foreman who arrived on the scene. The lamp which witness affirmed had been used was not to be found after the accident. As he was away at the time he could not swear that the deceased was lowered into the hole the second time with the rope around him as provided in the regulations.

Medical evidence to the effect that the death of the coolie was due to asphyxia, and that when admitted to Hospital, he had all the signs of sewer gas poisoning was given and the enquiry was adjourned until Friday.

headline: MADRAS RIOTS.
text:
TROUBLE OVER COMING ELECTIONS.

Thirty persons were injured, some seriously, as a result of hooligans attacking a procession of National Congress supporters on the eve of further city municipal elections. The as-ailants are stated to have used sticks, crowbars and mineral water bottles.

Stone-throwing and rowdyism were previously reported at some election meetings of the Congress party, following the defeat of all four non-Brahmin candidates by members of the Congress party last week.

The police mudo seven arrests.

headline: BOYCOTT IDEA.
text:
TIMES' URGES EXPERT REPORT.

Drawing attention to a "most damaging" weapon," namely, the boycott of British goods in China, the "Times," in a leader, says it is maintained by an idea or obsession, and a definite object of British policy should be to dispel the obsession by all possible means. It urges the Government to send out to China, simply to investigate and report, a very competent expert on Chinese affairs.
